fields.title: Portraits of Courage – David Livingstone
fields.subtitle: A Mill Boy from Blantyre, the Open Sore of the World, and the Faithful Hands That Carried Him Home
fields.description: A Christian biography of David Livingstone (1813–1873), the Scottish mill boy who became a doctor, a missionary to the Batswana, the first European known to cross Africa from coast to coast, and the most persistent voice of his age against the East African slave trade. Built on his own books and journals and checked against modern scholarship, it tells the real man behind the legend: brave and stubborn, devout and often unjust, loving and costly to those who loved him, and carried home at last by the African companions who would not leave him. All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of David Livingstone about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of David Livingstone (1813–1873). It follows him from a one-room home at the Blantyre cotton mill, through his years with the Bakwena and their chief Sechele, his crossing of Africa from Luanda to Quelimane, the failed Zambezi Expedition and the death of his wife Mary, to his last journey, the massacre at Nyangwe, his meeting with Stanley, and his death at Chitambo’s village in 1873. It draws mainly on his own books and journals.

qa.question: Who was David Livingstone?
qa.answer: He was a Scottish doctor and missionary who went to southern Africa for the London Missionary Society in 1841. He worked among the Batswana, crossed the continent between 1853 and 1856, led a British government expedition on the Zambezi from 1858 to 1864, and spent his last seven years searching for the sources of the Nile and exposing the slave trade. He died in what is now Zambia in 1873 and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

qa.question: Did Livingstone really make only one convert?
qa.answer: Sechele, chief of the Bakwena, is the only African he is known to have baptised, in October 1848, and Livingstone suspended him from communion a few months later. But the book shows that Sechele kept his faith, taught and led his people in it for the rest of his life, and that the missions founded after Livingstone’s death in the lands he explored grew into large African-led churches.

qa.question: How does the book treat Livingstone’s family?
qa.answer: Honestly. It tells how Mary Livingstone, herself a missionary’s daughter raised in Africa, crossed the Kalahari pregnant, spent four years wandering through English lodgings with their children, and died of fever on the Zambezi in 1862. It also tells the story of their son Robert, who died in a Confederate prison camp in 1864. The book honours Livingstone’s grief and does not hide what his calling cost them.

qa.question: How does the book handle colonialism and empire?
qa.answer: It does not separate him from it. Livingstone called for “commerce and Christianity” to open Africa and believed British influence was a Christian influence. He also opposed the seizure of African land and labour by Boers and Portuguese and wanted Africans to trade freely and govern themselves. After his death his name was used to justify British rule in what became Malawi and Zambia. The book tells both sides and draws lessons from them.

qa.question: Who were Susi, Chuma and Jacob Wainwright?
qa.answer: They were among the African companions who stayed with Livingstone to the end. Susi joined him on the Zambezi; Chuma was a boy freed from a slave caravan in 1861; Jacob Wainwright had been freed from a slave ship and educated in India. After Livingstone’s death they and their companions buried his heart at Chitambo’s village and carried his body about a thousand miles to the coast. The book treats them as people who made their own choices, not as a backdrop.

qa.question: Did Stanley really say “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?”
qa.answer: The words come from Stanley alone. The pages of his diary for those days are missing, his own versions differ in detail, and even the date of the meeting at Ujiji in late 1871 is uncertain. The book gives the greeting as Stanley reported it and explains why it should be held with some caution. It also corrects other popular claims, such as the Abbey inscription’s statement that the “open sore of the world” sentence was written with his last breath.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme, from Psalm 16’s “goodly heritage” to Jesus’s saying about the grain of wheat that dies and bears much fruit, and further passages are woven through the story. Where Livingstone himself quotes the Bible, as in his famous journal entry on Matthew 28:20, his King James wording is kept. Appendices give lessons from his life, a study guide, a chronology and a note on sources.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace, that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation, that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!”

— Isaiah 52:7, ASV

The earlier volumes of this series have told of a Chinese church leader who died in a Communist labour camp, an American who prayed his way through the villages of the Punjab, a Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews behind a false wall, a Scottish mill girl who went alone up the rivers of Calabar, an African bishop who had once been sold as a slave, an Indian widow who built a home for thousands of outcast women, an Oxford don who was found by God against his will, a young widow who walked into the Ecuadorian forest to live among the people who had killed her husband, and an Irish missionary who made a home at Dohnavur, in South India, for children rescued from temple service. This tenth volume tells the story of a man whose name, for a hundred years, was almost a synonym for the word “missionary,” and whose life, looked at closely, fits that word less neatly than his admirers liked to think.

David Livingstone was born in 1813 in a single room in a tenement at a cotton mill on the Clyde, and he went to work in the mill at the age of ten. He made himself a doctor and a minister, sailed for southern Africa in 1840 for the London Missionary Society, and spent most of the remaining thirty-two years of his life on that continent. He walked across it from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean. He led a government expedition up the Zambezi that ended in failure and in the death of his wife. He spent his last seven years wandering, ill and often lost, in search of the sources of the Nile, and he died in 1873 in a village near the swamps of Lake Bangweulu, in what is now Zambia. The men and women who had travelled with him buried his heart there and carried his body to the coast, and he was buried in Westminster Abbey.

Mary Slessor, whose story was told in the fourth volume, offered herself as a missionary when the news of his death reached Dundee. She was one of many. For two generations Livingstone’s name sent young people to Africa, raised money for missions, and stood in sermons and Sunday-school prizes for everything that was brave and selfless in the Christian life. It was also used, by people who cared little for his faith, to justify the conquest of the continent he loved.

Why Courage?

His physical courage needs no defending. He was mauled by a lion and set his own arm, badly, so that it never healed straight. He crossed country no European had mapped, often with nothing but a few beads, a sextant and the goodwill of the people whose land he was passing through. He faced down armed men more than once, and he went on travelling for years with fever, dysentery and bleeding that would have sent most people home.

But that is not the courage this book most wants to examine. Livingstone spent his life doing things that did not work. In more than thirty years in Africa he baptised one African convert whom we know of, a chief named Sechele, and he soon suspended him from communion. His great river was blocked by rapids he had not seen. The mission he called for on the Shire Highlands buried its bishop within a year. The family he loved paid for his journeys with years of poverty and separation, and his wife died beside him on the Zambezi. He quarrelled with colleagues, misjudged people, and sometimes told the story of his own failures more kindly than the facts allowed. And yet he kept going, not always wisely, in the conviction that God had given him a work to do and that its results belonged to God.

There is a harder kind of courage in that than in facing a lion. It is the courage to go on believing that faithfulness matters when success has failed to come, and to keep praying for the ending of an evil that you can see no way to end. Livingstone’s campaign against the slave trade in East and Central Africa was the steadiest thing in his unsteady life, and his last years were spent among slave traders whose cruelty he could neither stop nor escape. He died before the great Zanzibar slave market was closed, a month after his death. He never knew.

How This Book Is Written

Like the earlier volumes, this book tries to be honest about its sources.

Livingstone was a prolific writer, and nearly everything he published is now in the public domain. His Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa (1857), the Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi and Its Tributaries (1865), which he wrote with his brother Charles, and The Last Journals of David Livingstone, edited by his friend Horace Waller in 1874, let him speak for himself, and he is quoted from them throughout. So is the first full biography, W. G. Blaikie’s The Personal Life of David Livingstone (1880), which printed many of his private letters and journal entries, and Henry Morton Stanley’s How I Found Livingstone (1872).

None of these is a neutral witness. Livingstone wrote his books to be read, to raise support and to sway the government, and he left things out. Waller edited the last journals with a reverence that softened some passages. Blaikie wrote, with the family’s help, the life of a saint. Stanley was a journalist who needed a story. Modern historians, working from Livingstone’s manuscripts, his field notebooks and the letters of the people around him, have corrected much of the Victorian picture, and this book has learned from them, though it does not quote them.

Two further cautions belong here. The first is that Livingstone lived at the beginning of the age of European empire in Africa, and his life cannot be told apart from it. He wanted Britain to come to Africa, though not in the way it eventually came. A Christian biography should say so plainly. The second is that the language used about Africans in his time, his own included, was often contemptuous. This book quotes it only where it is needed to understand him, marks it when it does, and does not adopt it. It also tries to give the African men and women of his story their due, as people who made choices of their own: Sechele, who argued theology with him and evangelised his own people long after Livingstone had left; the Makololo who walked with him to the Atlantic and back; Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright and the others who brought him home.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme. Where Livingstone himself quotes the Bible, he quotes the King James Version, and his words are left as he wrote them.

The verse at the head of this preface is Isaiah’s, about the messenger whose feet bring good news across the mountains. Livingstone’s feet crossed more mountains than almost any messenger of his century. Whether he always brought good news is a question this book will keep asking. He would not have minded the question. Near the end of his life, ill and alone in the heart of the continent, he wrote in his journal that he had dedicated his whole self again to Christ, and asked only that he might be allowed to finish his task. The story that follows is about that self, and that task, and what God made of both.

fields.title: Introduction: The Saint, the Explorer, and the Record
fields.body_html:
“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:7, ASV

A Funeral in the Abbey

On 18 April 1874, David Livingstone was buried in the nave of Westminster Abbey. The coffin had come from Southampton by special train. The Prince of Wales and the Prime Minister were among the mourners, the Queen had sent a wreath, and the congregation sang the Scottish paraphrase “O God of Bethel, by whose hand.” Among the eight pallbearers were Henry Morton Stanley, the journalist who had found him alive at Ujiji, old friends and companions of his travels, and a young African named Jacob Wainwright, who had carried his body from the middle of the continent to the coast.

The black marble slab over the grave still bears the inscription chosen for it. It begins, “Brought by faithful hands over land and sea,” and calls him “Missionary, Traveller, Philanthropist.” It says that for thirty years his life was spent in an unwearied effort to evangelise the native races, to explore the undiscovered secrets, and to abolish the desolating slave trade of Central Africa, and then presents, as among the last words he wrote, a sentence that has been quoted ever since: a prayer, written in his solitude, that Heaven’s blessing would come down on everyone, of whatever nation, who would help “to heal this open sore of the world.”

The funeral was the beginning of a legend. Within a decade there were popular lives of Livingstone for every age and taste. Missions were founded in his name in what are now Malawi and Zambia, and towns, schools, hospitals and a waterfall-side city carried it. For the Victorian public he became a kind of Protestant saint: the mill boy who rose by hard work and faith, the doctor who healed Africans and freed slaves, the lonely hero who died on his knees.

What the Legend Says

A legend is not the same as a lie. Much of what the Victorians believed about Livingstone was true. He did rise from a cotton mill. He did cross Africa. He did hate the slave trade with all his heart. He did die, by the account of the men who found him, kneeling beside his bed.

But the legend says more than the evidence. It makes him a successful missionary, when he made one known convert. It makes him a discoverer of lakes and rivers that African people had lived beside for centuries, and that Portuguese and Arab traders had sometimes visited before him. It makes him a selfless family man, when his wife and children suffered for his choices. It makes him a gentle leader, when many who served with him found him hard, suspicious and unforgiving. It even improves his words. The inscription in the Abbey presents the “open sore” sentence as among his last written words, when in fact he wrote it a year before he died. A saying carved on many memorials, “I am prepared to go anywhere, provided it be forward,” is a tidied version of something he wrote in a letter. Another, “Fear God and work hard,” is often given as his motto, though its source is less certain than the many plaques suggest.

The verse at the head of this introduction is Paul’s description of the gospel and the people who carry it: a treasure in clay jars. Paul does not say that the jars are beautiful. He says they are breakable, and that this is the point, so that “the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” A legend polishes the jar until no one notices the treasure. This book tries to show the jar as it was, cracked and stubborn and brave, and to let the reader decide what treasure it carried.

The Books He Wrote

Livingstone is unusual among missionaries in how much of his own record survives. His first book, Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa, published in November 1857, was a bestseller. It told the story of his first sixteen years in Africa and his journey across the continent. It is vivid, often funny, full of natural history, and frank about many things, including the failure of his mission among the Bakwena. It is also a book written by a man who had just resigned from his missionary society and needed the public’s support for his next venture, and it is silent about much that was painful.

His second, the Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi and Its Tributaries (1865), written with his brother Charles, told the story of the government expedition of 1858 to 1864. It is a more defensive book. It says little about the quarrels that broke the expedition apart, and less than it might about how badly things went.

The third was not written as a book at all. The Last Journals of David Livingstone (1874) were edited from his notebooks and journals by Horace Waller, a former member of the Universities’ Mission who had become a close friend. Waller worked with Susi and Chuma, two of the men who had carried Livingstone’s body to the coast, to add an account of his last days. The journals are the most intimate record we have, but they passed through Waller’s hands. Modern scholars, using new imaging techniques on Livingstone’s faded field diaries, have shown that the published text sometimes smooths over what he first wrote, especially about the massacre at Nyangwe in 1871. Those discoveries are discussed in this book in their place.

The Witnesses Around Him

Two other early books are quoted here. W. G. Blaikie’s The Personal Life of David Livingstone (1880) was written with the family’s cooperation and printed many private letters and journal entries. Blaikie wanted to show the inner man, the man of prayer and family affection, and he did so, but he was protective. Henry Morton Stanley’s How I Found Livingstone (1872) is the only full eyewitness account of Livingstone in his last years by an outsider. Stanley admired him deeply and wrote well, but he was a journalist who made his fortune from the story, and his own diaries do not always agree with his book.

There are other witnesses, and they matter. Livingstone’s companions on the Zambezi expedition kept diaries and wrote letters that were not meant for publication. His wife’s family wrote to him and about him. African witnesses speak less often in the written record, but they are there: in Sechele’s own letters and statements, in the testimony of Susi, Chuma and the boy Majwara about his death, and in the diary that Jacob Wainwright kept on the journey to the coast. Where their voices survive, this book tries to listen to them.

The Historians

For more than a century after his death, Livingstone was written about mainly by admirers. In the later twentieth century, historians began to look again. They showed how his reputation had been made and used, how often his plans had failed, how hard he could be on those who worked with him, and how his call for “commerce and Christianity” was taken up by people with very different aims. Some went so far as to treat him as little more than a forerunner of empire. Others, especially historians of African Christianity, have restored a more complicated picture: a man whose campaign against the slave trade was sincere and costly, whose respect for many Africans was real, and whose example helped bring into being churches that Africans then made their own.

This book draws on that work for its facts, and it agrees with much of it. It also tells his life as a Christian biography, which means taking seriously something his critics often set aside: that Livingstone believed himself to be a servant of Christ, prayed, read his Bible, and judged himself by it. He could be wrong about what God wanted. He was rarely insincere about wanting it.

A Word About Words

Livingstone wrote in the language of his time. He used words for Africans that are offensive today, and he sometimes wrote about African customs with contempt. He also wrote, often and against the opinion of many of his countrymen, that Africans were in no way inferior to Europeans, and that the differences between peoples were the result of circumstances, not nature. Both things are true of him. This book uses the names African peoples use for themselves where it can, and gives his own words as he wrote them only where they are needed, with a note where the language needs one.

Place names are another difficulty. Livingstone wrote Zambesi, Loanda, Quilimane, Nyassa and Tette; modern maps have Zambezi, Luanda, Quelimane, Nyasa (or Lake Malawi) and Tete. This book uses the modern spellings, except inside quotations and book titles.

What This Book Is For

The purpose of telling Livingstone’s story honestly is not to bring him down. It is to see him clearly enough to learn from him. He has things to teach about perseverance, about the cost of a calling, about the slow work of God in places where nothing seems to happen, and about the ways in which good intentions can be borrowed by power. He also has things to warn us about: the danger of a vision that leaves no room for the people closest to us, and of a faith so sure of its direction that it stops listening. Paul’s clay jar is breakable. That is why the treasure in it is worth looking for.

Stanley admired him deeply and wrote well, but he was a journalist who made his fortune from the story, and his own diaries do not always agree with his book. There are other witnesses, and they matter. Livingstone’s companions on the Zambezi expedition kept diaries and wrote letters that were not meant for publication. His wife’s family wrote to him and about him. African witnesses speak less often in the written record, but they are there: in Sechele’s own letters and statements, in the testimony of Susi, Chuma and the boy Majwara about his death, and in the diary that Jacob Wainwright kept on the journey to the coast. In the later twentieth century, historians began to look again. They showed how his reputation had been made and used, how often his plans had failed, how hard he could be on those who worked with him, and how his call for “commerce and Christianity” was taken up by people with very different aims. Some went so far as to treat him as little more than a forerunner of empire. Others, especially historians of African Christianity, have restored a more complicated picture: a man whose campaign against the slave trade was sincere and costly, whose respect for many Africans was real, and whose example helped bring into being churches that Africans then made their own. This book draws on that work for its facts, and it agrees with much of it. It also tells his life as a Christian biography, which means taking seriously something his critics often set aside: that Livingstone believed himself to be a servant of Christ, prayed, read his Bible, and judged himself by it. This book uses the names African peoples use for themselves where it can, and gives his own words as he wrote them only where they are needed, with a note where the language needs one. It is to see him clearly enough to learn from him. He has things to teach about perseverance, about the cost of a calling, about the slow work of God in places where nothing seems to happen, and about the ways in which good intentions can be borrowed by power. He also has things to warn us about: the danger of a vision that leaves no room for the people closest to us, and of a faith so sure of its direction that it stops listening. Paul’s clay jar is breakable. That is why the treasure in it is worth looking for.

fields.title: Shuttle Row
fields.body_html:
“The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage.”

— Psalm 16:6, ASV

A Room Above the Clyde

David Livingstone was born on 19 March 1813 at Blantyre Works, a cotton-spinning village on the south bank of the River Clyde, about eight miles south-east of Glasgow. The mills had been built in the 1780s by the Glasgow merchant David Dale, with the help of the inventor Richard Arkwright, and by Livingstone’s childhood they belonged to the firm of Henry Monteith and Company. The village was a company village. The mill owned the houses, ran a school, and employed whole families, children included.

The Livingstones lived in Shuttle Row, a three-storey tenement built for the mill workers. Like most of its families, they had a single room. In it the parents slept, cooked, ate, read and prayed, and in it they raised their children. The room survives, as part of the David Livingstone Birthplace museum, and visitors are usually surprised by how small it is. It was a crowded, clean, disciplined home, and those who knew the family remembered it for its order.

David was the second of seven children born to Neil Livingstone and Agnes Hunter. Two of them died young. The survivors were John, the eldest, then David, then Janet, Charles and Agnes. Charles, eight years younger than David, would one day join him on the Zambezi. John emigrated to Canada. The two sisters, Janet and Agnes, never married, and in later years they kept house for their mother and looked after David’s children while he was in Africa.

Ulva and Culloden

When Livingstone came to write his first book, he began it with an apology. He would rather, he said, write about Africa than about himself, and his own inclination was to say as little as possible about himself. But he gave his readers a few pages on his family, and they show what he was proud of.

The Livingstones came from the island of Ulva, off the west coast of Mull, in the Inner Hebrides. He wrote that his great-grandfather had fallen at the battle of Culloden, fighting for the old line of kings, and that his grandfather had been a small farmer in Ulva, where his father was born. Like thousands of Highlanders in the hard years at the end of the eighteenth century, the grandfather left the land and came south to find work. He was employed at the Blantyre mill, where the owners valued him as an honest man, and his sons grew up in the Lowlands.

Livingstone remembered his grandfather as a storehouse of Highland tradition, full of legends, songs and family history. One family story he cherished above all the others. An ancestor in Ulva, renowned in the island for wisdom, had called his children around him on his deathbed and told them that he had searched through all the traditions of the family and had never found a dishonest man among their forefathers. If any of them took to dishonest ways, it would not be because it ran in their blood. The old man left them, as Livingstone told it, a single precept: to be honest.

It is the kind of story families keep because it tells them who they are. Livingstone kept it. Of all the family traditions, he wrote, this was the only point he felt proud of. He was a man who would be accused, later in life, of many things, of harshness and stubbornness and of telling the story of his journeys too kindly to himself. He was very rarely accused of dishonesty about money, and he carried the old Highland pride in plain dealing to the end.

Neil Livingstone

His father, Neil Livingstone, had been apprenticed as a tailor but disliked the trade, and for most of David’s childhood he made a small living as a travelling tea dealer, going from house to house with packets of tea. It was a poor living. It suited him, his son thought, because it gave him the chance to leave tracts at the doors where he called. Neil Livingstone was a serious, devout and somewhat stern man, a total abstainer at a time when drink was the ruin of many working families, a Sunday-school teacher, and an eager reader of theology and missionary magazines.

He was strict about books. He believed that novels and light reading wasted time and endangered the soul, and he wanted his children to read religious works. David, who loved books about travel and science, resisted, and the result was a long quiet struggle in the house. Livingstone recalled, years later, that the last time his father beat him was for refusing to read Wilberforce’s Practical Christianity, a book that he found dull and that seemed to him to set religion against the study of nature. The father won the argument about the beating and lost the argument about books. Science and travel would be the son’s lifelong passion.

Yet Livingstone wrote of his father with deep respect. He thanked him for setting before his children, from their infancy, a consistent example of piety, of the kind Robert Burns had drawn in The Cotter’s Saturday Night, the poem in which a poor Scottish father gathers his family at the end of the week to read the Bible and pray. That was the kind of home Shuttle Row was. Neil Livingstone died in February 1856, while his son was still in Africa, on the last stage of his crossing of the continent, and David learned of it only on his voyage home. He had been looking forward to telling his father the story of the journey. It was one of the griefs of his life that he never could.

Later, when Neil Livingstone left the Church of Scotland for an Independent congregation in Hamilton, his son went with him. It was through that Independent church, and its connection with the London Missionary Society, that David would eventually go to Africa. The Society was not a denominational body. It was supported mainly by Congregationalists, and it had a rule, which Livingstone liked, of sending out missionaries to preach the gospel without imposing any particular form of church government on the people who received it.

Agnes Hunter

His mother, Agnes Hunter, came from a family of small tradespeople in the district, and from a line of Scottish Presbyterians who remembered the persecuted Covenanters of the seventeenth century with pride. Those who knew her described her as a small, neat, cheerful woman, careful with every penny, devoted to her husband and children. The order of the one-room home was hers. It was she who kept the family respectable on a tea seller’s income, who cooked and mended and saved, and who sometimes, when David was older, came and took the book out of his hands at midnight so that he would go to bed.

She lived until 1865, long enough to see her son famous and to see him leave for Africa for the last time. Livingstone loved her deeply, and his letters to her, plain and affectionate, are some of the most unguarded things he wrote. His elder daughter was named after her. When he was dragging out his last years in the interior, he sometimes wrote in his journal about his mother and father, and about Blantyre, as a man thinks about home when he does not expect to see it again.

A Goodly Heritage

It would be easy to make this sound idyllic, and it was not. The mill village was a place of long hours, crowded rooms, hard discipline and frequent death. Children worked in the mill from the age of ten or younger. Two of Neil and Agnes Livingstone’s own children did not survive. The family was poor even by the standards of the village, because the father’s tea round brought in less than the mill. When David went into the factory, it was because the family needed his wages.

But the psalm at the head of this chapter is not about wealth. “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places,” the psalmist says, and he means the boundary lines of his inheritance, the portion of land that was his. His real portion, he says a verse earlier, is God himself: “Jehovah is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 16:5, ASV). Livingstone inherited no land and no money. He inherited a Highland pride in honesty, a father’s stern faith, a mother’s cheerful thrift, and a house where the Bible was read every day and missionaries were spoken of with admiration. He also inherited, from both parents, an extraordinary capacity for hard work.

Some of what he inherited was less helpful. He grew up in a family that held firm opinions and did not easily change them, and in a tradition that valued duty above feeling. He learned early to keep his own counsel, to distrust idleness in others, and to judge harshly those who did not work as hard as he did. Those habits served him well in a mill and in the African interior. They served him much less well as a husband, a father and a leader of other men.

The Victorian biographers liked to draw a straight line from Shuttle Row to Westminster Abbey: the poor boy who rose by industry and faith. The line is real, but it is not straight. The boy from the single room carried his upbringing with him everywhere, for good and ill, and much of the story that follows is the story of how God used, and sometimes had to break, the man that Blantyre made.

The Village and the World

One more thing about Blantyre deserves notice. The mill that employed the Livingstone family spun cotton, and much of the raw cotton that came up the Clyde to the Scottish mills in those years had been grown by enslaved people in the American South. Britain had abolished the slave trade in its empire in 1807, six years before Livingstone was born, and would abolish slavery itself in its colonies in 1833, when he was twenty. But the textile industry of Lancashire and Lanarkshire still depended heavily on slave-grown cotton from the United States.

Livingstone did not write about this as a boy, and there is no sign that it troubled him then. But later in life he became convinced that if Africans could grow cotton and other crops for sale to British merchants, the demand for enslaved labour in Africa would fall, and the trade would wither. He imagined African cotton feeding the very mills he had worked in. That idea, of fighting the slave trade with honest commerce, would shape his greatest journeys and his greatest failure. It had its roots, in part, in the village where he was born, where the whole of life turned on the price of cotton.

fields.title: The Piecer
fields.body_html:
“Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, whither thou goest.”

— Ecclesiastes 9:10, ASV

Six in the Morning Till Eight at Night

In 1823, at the age of ten, David Livingstone went to work in the Blantyre mill. He wrote that he was put into the factory at ten as a piecer, so that his earnings might lessen his mother’s anxiety.

A piecer’s job was to watch the threads on the spinning machines and to join them when they broke. The machines did not stop for a broken thread, so the boy had to reach in among the moving parts, catch the two ends and twist them together, then move on to the next. He spent the day walking up and down beside the machine, bending, reaching and watching. The work was not heavy, but it was relentless, and it was done in the heat and lint-filled air of a cotton mill, where the machinery roared so loudly that talk was almost impossible. The working day, Livingstone recorded, ran from six in the morning to eight at night, with short breaks for meals. He was a child. He did it for ten years.

Child labour in the mills is one of the great scandals of the British industrial revolution, and the reforming laws that began to limit it came only during Livingstone’s years in the factory. It is worth saying plainly that his childhood was hard and that it was hard because of a system that used up children for profit. Livingstone himself, characteristically, did not complain. He looked back on it as a school.

Ruddiman’s Rudiments

The mill owners provided an evening school for their young workers, and Livingstone went to it. With part of his first week’s wages, he recalled, he bought Ruddiman’s Rudiments of Latin, and he went on studying Latin for years afterwards, with undiminished enthusiasm, at an evening school that met from eight until ten.

A boy who had been on his feet since six in the morning went from the factory floor to the schoolroom, and from the schoolroom to his books at home. The dictionary work, he wrote, went on till midnight or later, unless his mother intervened by jumping up and snatching the books out of his hands. Then he slept a few hours and was back at the mill by six. In this way, he said, he read many of the classical authors, and knew Virgil and Horace better at sixteen than he did in middle age.

He read at work too. The famous picture of the boy with his book on the spinning frame comes from his own pen. He wrote that he read at work by placing his book on part of the spinning-jenny, so that he could catch a sentence at a time as he passed at his work, and in this way kept up a fairly constant study, undisturbed by the roar of the machinery. Strictly, the machines at Blantyre were spinning mules, not jennies, but Livingstone used the common word. He added that the habit of concentrating in the noise of the factory gave him a power of shutting his mind to everything around him, so that later he could read and write in the middle of a crowd of shouting people, or amid the dancing and singing of an African village, without being disturbed.

Many poor children in Scotland worked and studied in this way, and the country was proud of its self-educated working men. What marked Livingstone was not the habit but the intensity of it, and its persistence. He did not read in order to escape the mill. He read in order to master things: languages, then science, then medicine. He was already, at twelve and thirteen, a boy who would not let go of a task until it was done.

Rocks, Shells and Herbs

His great love, from boyhood, was the natural world. On the few free days of the year he went out into the country around Blantyre with his brothers, collecting plants, rocks and shells. He identified the plants he found with the help of old botany books. He was fascinated by the limestone quarries near the village, where the rock was full of fossil shells. He once asked a quarryman how the shells had got into the rocks. The man, he recalled, looked at him with the pitying expression people reserve for a harmless lunatic. The boy did not get an answer, but he never stopped asking that kind of question.

This curiosity about the created world was part of his religion, though for some years it seemed to him to be in conflict with it. His father distrusted science books. The theology of his father’s church seemed to have no room for geology. David read whatever science he could find, including books on chemistry and astronomy, and for a time he was troubled by the thought that he could not be a Christian and love these things too. How he came through that trouble is the story of the next chapter.

Promotion to the Wheel

In his nineteenth year, about 1832, he was promoted from piecer to spinner. The work was harder and the pay better. Spinning, he wrote, was exceedingly hard on a slim, loose-jointed lad, but it was well paid. The better pay was important, because by then he had decided what he wanted to do with his life, and it would cost money. For the next few years he worked in the mill in the summer and studied in Glasgow in the winter, paying his own fees and living on almost nothing.

He was proud of having done it without help. He wrote later that he had never received a farthing of aid from anyone, and that he would have reached his goal by his own efforts in the end, if friends had not advised him to apply to the London Missionary Society. There is a characteristic note in that pride. It is the pride of a man who has earned everything he has and who finds it hard to understand people who have not had to.

The Same Hardy Training

Many years later, in the opening pages of Missionary Travels, written when he was the most famous traveller in Britain, Livingstone looked back on the mill with gratitude. Looking back on that life of toil, he wrote, he could only feel thankful that it had formed so large a part of his early education, and if it were possible he would like to begin life over again in the same lowly way and pass through the same hardy training.

That passage has been quoted ever since as an example of Victorian self-help, and it is easy to be cynical about it. It was written by a man who had escaped the mill, for readers who had never been in one. It can be read as a comfortable endorsement of child labour by someone who no longer had to do it.

But Livingstone meant something more particular. He believed that the factory had given him two things that he needed in Africa. The first was endurance. He had learned, as a child, to work through tiredness for fourteen hours a day, and it was that endurance that carried him across the continent. The second was a working man’s sympathy for the poor. He said more than once that his time in the mill had taught him to respect working people and to understand their lives, and that he never forgot it. In Africa, he dealt with chiefs and porters, traders and slaves, and he was often more at ease with the porters than with the officials. He knew what it was to work for someone else.

There is a third thing the factory gave him, which he did not mention. It taught him to measure himself, and others, by work done. In the mill a man was what he produced. In Africa, Livingstone would judge his companions by the same standard, and those who could not keep up with him, or who seemed to him idle, he despised. A missionary needs endurance. He also needs patience with the weak, and that is harder to learn at a spinning frame.

With Thy Might

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Ecclesiastes, the book of the Bible most aware of the shortness and frustration of human life. “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.” The Preacher does not say this because work always succeeds. He says it because life is short and death is coming, and there will be no work in the grave. It is a sober verse, not a cheerful one.

Livingstone lived it all his life. He worked with his might in the mill, in the classroom, in the dispensary, on the road and in the swamp. The Preacher would have recognised him. He might also have reminded him of something else he says, that there is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak,” and “a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Ecclesiastes 3:5, 7, ASV). Livingstone was much better at doing things with his might than at knowing when to stop. Paul gives the same command a gentler setting: “whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, ASV). The mill taught him to work heartily. It would take the rest of his life to learn what it meant to work as unto the Lord, and to leave the results with him.

A boy who had been on his feet since six in the morning went from the factory floor to the schoolroom, and from the schoolroom to his books at home. The dictionary work, he wrote, went on till midnight or later, unless his mother intervened by jumping up and snatching the books out of his hands. Then he slept a few hours and was back at the mill by six. In this way, he said, he read many of the classical authors, and knew Virgil and Horace better at sixteen than he did in middle age. He read at work too. The famous picture of the boy with his book on the spinning frame comes from his own pen. He wrote that he read at work by placing his book on part of the spinning-jenny, so that he could catch a sentence at a time as he passed at his work, and in this way kept up a fairly constant study, undisturbed by the roar of the machinery. Strictly, the machines at Blantyre were spinning mules, not jennies, but Livingstone used the common word. He added that the habit of concentrating in the noise of the factory gave him a power of shutting his mind to everything around him, so that later he could read and write in the middle of a crowd of shouting people, or amid the dancing and singing of an African village, without being disturbed. Many poor children in Scotland worked and studied in this way, and the country was proud of its self-educated working men. What marked Livingstone was not the habit but the intensity of it, and its persistence. He did not read in order to escape the mill. He read in order to master things: languages, then science, then medicine. He was already, at twelve and thirteen, a boy who would not let go of a task until it was done. Rocks, Shells and Herbs His great love, from boyhood, was the natural world. On the few free days of the year he went out into the country around Blantyre with his brothers, collecting plants, rocks and shells. He identified the plants he found with the help of old botany books. He was fascinated by the limestone quarries near the village, where the rock was full of fossil shells. He once asked a quarryman how the shells had got into the rocks. The man, he recalled, looked at him with the pitying expression people reserve for a harmless lunatic. The boy did not get an answer, but he never stopped asking that kind of question. This curiosity about the created world was part of his religion, though for some years it seemed to him to be in conflict with it. His father distrusted science books. The theology of his father’s church seemed to have no room for geology. David read whatever science he could find, including books on chemistry and astronomy, and for a time he was troubled by the thought that he could not be a Christian and love these things too. How he came through that trouble is the story of the next chapter. Promotion to the Wheel In his nineteenth year, about 1832, he was promoted from piecer to spinner. The work was harder and the pay better. Spinning, he wrote, was exceedingly hard on a slim, loose-jointed lad, but it was well paid. The better pay was important, because by then he had decided what he wanted to do with his life, and it would cost money. For the next few years he worked in the mill in the summer and studied in Glasgow in the winter, paying his own fees and living on almost nothing. He was proud of having done it without help. He wrote later that he had never received a farthing of aid from anyone, and that he would have reached his goal by his own efforts in the end, if friends had not advised him to apply to the London Missionary Society. There is a characteristic note in that pride. It is the pride of a man who has earned everything he has and who finds it hard to understand people who have not had to. The Same Hardy Training Many years later, in the opening pages of Missionary Travels, written when he was the most famous traveller in Britain, Livingstone looked back on the mill with gratitude. Looking back on that life of toil, he wrote, he could only feel thankful that it had formed so large a part of his early education, and if it were possible he would like to begin life over again in the same lowly way and pass through the same hardy training. That passage has been quoted ever since as an example of Victorian self-help, and it is easy to be cynical about it. It was written by a man who had escaped the mill, for readers who had never been in one. It can be read as a comfortable endorsement of child labour by someone who no longer had to do it. But Livingstone meant something more particular. He believed that the factory had given him two things that he needed in Africa. The first was endurance. He had learned, as a child, to work through tiredness for fourteen hours a day, and it was that endurance that carried him across the continent. The second was a working man’s sympathy for the poor. He said more than once that his time in the mill had taught him to respect working people and to understand their lives, and that he never forgot it. In Africa, he dealt with chiefs and porters, traders and slaves, and he was often more at ease with the porters than with the officials. He knew what it was to work for someone else. There is a third thing the factory gave him, which he did not mention. It taught him to measure himself, and others, by work done. In the mill a man was what he produced. In Africa, Livingstone would judge his companions by the same standard, and those who could not keep up with him, or who seemed to him idle, he despised. A missionary needs endurance. He also needs patience with the weak, and that is harder to learn at a spinning frame. With Thy Might The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Ecclesiastes, the book of the Bible most aware of the shortness and frustration of human life. “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.” The Preacher does not say this because work always succeeds. He says it because life is short and death is coming, and there will be no work in the grave. It is a sober verse, not a cheerful one. Livingstone lived it all his life. He worked with his might in the mill, in the classroom, in the dispensary, on the road and in the swamp. The Preacher would have recognised him. He might also have reminded him of something else he says, that there is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak,” and “a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Ecclesiastes 3:5, 7, ASV). Livingstone was much better at doing things with his might than at knowing when to stop. Paul gives the same command a gentler setting: “whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, ASV). The mill taught him to work heartily. It would take the rest of his life to learn what it meant to work as unto the Lord, and to leave the results with him.

fields.title: Colour Blindness Cured
fields.body_html:
“The heavens declare the glory of God; And the firmament showeth his handiwork.”

— Psalm 19:1, ASV

Doctrine Without Life

David Livingstone grew up knowing the gospel. His parents taught it to him, he heard it every Sunday, and he could have explained the doctrines of the Scottish catechism as well as any boy in Blantyre. But in his teens he found that knowing the doctrine was not the same as possessing what it described. His account of what happened next, written twenty years later in the opening pages of Missionary Travels, is brief and careful, and it is the only account of his conversion that he ever published.

His parents, he wrote, had taken great pains to teach him the doctrines of Christianity, and he had no difficulty understanding the theory of free salvation through the atonement of Christ. But it was only at about this time, in his late teens, that he really began to feel his own need of that atonement, and the value of applying it personally to his own case.

It is the language of a nineteenth-century Scottish Protestant, and it is worth reading slowly. Livingstone does not say that he discovered a new doctrine. He says that a doctrine he already believed became his own. The atonement of Christ, which had been a theory, became something he needed and received personally. The story has none of the drama of a sudden conversion. There is no single night, no sermon, no named preacher. There is a young man who knew the truth and came, over a period of months or years, to rest his own life on it.

The Trouble With Science

What had held him back, he later suggested, was the apparent conflict between his faith and his love of the natural world. His father’s religion was suspicious of science, and some of the preachers he heard seemed to set Christianity against the study of geology and astronomy. A boy who wanted to know how shells got into limestone could easily conclude that he had to choose between his Bible and his rocks. For a time, Livingstone seems to have felt that he could not be a real Christian without giving up the questions he loved, and that he was not willing to give them up.

The book that helped him was Thomas Dick’s The Philosophy of a Future State. Dick was a Scottish minister, schoolteacher and amateur astronomer who wrote popular books arguing that science and Christianity were allies, not enemies. The universe, he taught, was God’s handiwork, and the study of it was a form of worship. The more we learn about the creation, the more we see of the wisdom and goodness of the Creator. Livingstone read Dick and found that the wall he had imagined between faith and science was not there. He could love both, because they had the same author.

He later visited Dick at his home near Dundee, and he never lost the outlook he learned from him. For the rest of his life, Livingstone saw no contradiction between his work as a missionary and his work as a naturalist and geographer. He collected plants, measured rainfall, studied the habits of animals, took astronomical observations to fix his position, and wrote about African geology and disease, and he regarded all of it as part of the same calling. The psalm at the head of this chapter would have been one of his favourites: “The heavens declare the glory of God; And the firmament showeth his handiwork.” When he lay on his back in the African night, with a sextant in his hand, working out his latitude from the stars, he was, as he understood it, reading God’s other book.

This conviction is one of the most attractive things about him, and also one of the sources of his later difficulties. Because he saw exploration and science as part of his missionary calling, he could pursue them with a clear conscience long after his supporters began to think he had stopped being a missionary at all. He was never able to see what they were complaining about.

Like Colour Blindness

He described the change that came over him with an image from medicine. It was like what might happen, he wrote, if it were possible to cure a case of colour blindness. A colour-blind person sees everything that others see, but not as they see it. Shapes and objects are all there, but something essential is missing. Then, if such a thing were possible, the colours come. Nothing new appears in the world, but the whole world looks different.

That is a striking way for a scientifically minded young man to describe conversion, and it is accurate to the experience of many believers. Livingstone did not say that he saw new things. He said that he saw the same things truly. The doctrines he had learned as a child now had colour. The created world he loved now had colour. And so, he went on to say, did the needs of other people.

The Alleviation of Human Misery

In the glow of love that Christianity inspires, he wrote, he soon resolved to devote his life to the relief of human misery.

The sentence moves directly from conversion to service. Livingstone does not describe a period of private devotion first, or a slow growth in holiness. He describes a heart warmed by love, and a resolution to spend that love on others. It is a very practical Christianity, and a very Scottish one. Love, for him, was something you did.

The question was where to do it. The answer came from China. Around 1834, an appeal was circulated in Britain by Karl Gützlaff, a German missionary in China, for medical missionaries to go to that country. Gützlaff argued that doctors could gain an entrance for the gospel where preachers could not, by healing the sick and so winning the trust of the people. The appeal reached the Livingstone household. Neil Livingstone was enthusiastic. His son, who had been thinking of a life of service but had no clear direction, now had one. He would become a doctor and go to China.

Turning the idea over, he wrote, he came to feel that to be a pioneer of Christianity in China might bring material benefit to parts of that immense empire, and so he set himself to gain a medical education to qualify for the work. The word pioneer is already there. Livingstone never wanted to go where others had been. From the beginning he wanted to be first.

Glasgow

In the winter of 1836, at the age of twenty-three, he went to Glasgow to study. He enrolled at the Andersonian University, a college founded to bring science and medicine to people who could not afford the ancient universities, and attended classes in medicine and chemistry. He also took Greek at the University of Glasgow, and theology under Ralph Wardlaw, a leading Congregational minister. He lived in a cheap rented room and walked the eight miles home to Blantyre at weekends. In the summer he went back to the mill to earn the money for the next winter’s fees.

At the Andersonian he made a lifelong friend. James Young was the assistant to the professor of chemistry, Thomas Graham, and he and Livingstone became close. Young would later make a fortune from the refining of paraffin oil, and he became one of Livingstone’s most generous supporters, paying for much of his last expedition. In the laboratory the two young men worked side by side, and Livingstone learned, among other things, to make and mend scientific instruments. It was the kind of practical skill he valued above all, and it served him in Africa, where there was no one to mend anything if he could not.

He was a serious, quiet student, more interested in learning than in making friends, and he left little mark on the college except in the memory of a few classmates. He was not brilliant. He was tenacious. He passed his examinations by the same method he had used in the mill: he simply went on working after everyone else had stopped.

The Society

By 1837 he had come to see that he could not pay for a full medical training by himself, and friends urged him to apply to a missionary society. He chose the London Missionary Society, partly because of its link with his father’s Independent church, and partly because of its principles. He approved of the Society’s own description of itself: that it sent to the heathen neither episcopacy, nor presbyterianism, nor independency, but the gospel of Christ. That, he said, agreed exactly with his idea of what a missionary society ought to do. He did not want to export a Scottish denomination. He wanted to preach Christ.

The word heathen in that description was the ordinary word of his time for people who were not Christians, Jews or Muslims, and it carried a sense of moral and cultural inferiority that most readers today would reject. Livingstone used it all his life, as almost all his contemporaries did. It is used here because it was his. It is worth noticing that his concern, even in this early statement, was that the gospel should not arrive dressed in the clothes of a particular European church. That concern did not always survive his later enthusiasm for British influence, but it was there from the beginning.

He filled in the Society’s application papers early in 1838. One of them asked about his religious experience and his motives. He answered with the same plain seriousness he would show all his life, describing his wish to make known the gospel by teaching and example, and his hope to combine it with medicine. The directors liked what they read. In the summer of 1838 he was summoned to London for interview, and accepted on probation.

The Glory of God in His Works

Psalm 19 has two halves. The first praises God for the heavens and the sun, which speak without words to every nation. The second praises God for his law: “The law of Jehovah is perfect, restoring the soul” (Psalm 19:7, ASV). The psalmist does not set the two halves against each other. The God who made the sun also gave the law, and both reveal him.

Livingstone came to faith when he saw that this was true. He did not have to choose between the God of his father’s Bible and the God of the rocks and stars. They were the same God, and he could serve him with his whole mind. That conviction made him a missionary who never stopped being a scientist, and a scientist who never stopped praying. It also gave him a confidence that God’s purposes and his own curiosity would usually point in the same direction. Sometimes they did. In the years ahead, there would be times when it was very hard to tell the difference.

fields.title: Slow of Speech
fields.body_html:
“And Moses said unto Jehovah, Oh, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”

— Exodus 4:10, ASV

Ongar

The London Missionary Society did not send its candidates straight to the field. In September 1838, Livingstone was sent with several other probationers to Chipping Ongar, a small town in Essex, to study under the Reverend Richard Cecil, a Congregational minister who prepared young men for the Society. They lived in lodgings in the town, studied Latin, Greek, Hebrew and theology with Cecil, and took turns preaching in the village chapels around about. Cecil reported on each of them to the Society’s secretary in London. Those letters survive, and they show that Livingstone came close to being sent home.

The problem was not his character, which Cecil admired, or his learning, which was adequate. It was his manner. Livingstone was awkward, shy in company, and hesitant in public prayer and speech. He spoke with a broad Lanarkshire accent and a thick, slow delivery that Londoners found hard to follow. Cecil wrote that he had sense and quiet vigour and that his temper was good, but that he was heavy in manner and his prayers were not what a minister’s should be. Early in 1839 he recommended that Livingstone’s probation should be extended before the Society made up its mind.

A Sermon Forgotten

A story told by his biographer Blaikie, from the memory of those who knew him at Ongar, shows why. Livingstone was sent one Sunday to preach in the chapel at a village near Ongar, in place of a minister who was ill. He had written out his sermon and learned it. He went into the pulpit, read out his text, and then found that his mind was completely empty. After a painful silence, by Blaikie’s account, he told the congregation that he had forgotten everything he had meant to say, and came down from the pulpit and left the chapel.

It is a story that later admirers liked to tell for its humility, and it is worth taking seriously for what it reveals. Livingstone was never a good preacher. He knew it, and so did everyone who heard him. In Africa he would preach in Setswana, a language he came to speak well, and some who heard him there found him plain and moving. But he never had the gifts that the Victorian church valued most in a minister, and he never pretended to. When he became famous and was asked to speak to great crowds in Britain, he did it badly, read his speeches, and hated it.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Moses’s protest at the burning bush. God has told him to go to Pharaoh, and Moses says that he cannot speak. God’s answer is not to make him eloquent. It is to remind him who made his mouth: “Who hath made man’s mouth? … is it not I, Jehovah? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth” (Exodus 4:11-12, ASV). Moses was given Aaron to speak for him, and he went. Livingstone was never made eloquent either. But God did not need him to be a great preacher. He needed him to walk, and to write, and to tell the world what he had seen, and he was given gifts for that.

A Night Walk

A fellow student at Ongar, Joseph Moore, later remembered another side of him. Moore told Blaikie that Livingstone once walked to London on an errand for his family, a journey of over twenty miles, and set out to walk back the same day. On the road home in the dark, he found a woman who had been thrown from a gig, and he stopped to help her, carrying her to a house nearby and making sure she was cared for before he went on. He lost his way, and reached Ongar at last in the early morning, utterly exhausted. Moore said he had never seen him look so done in. It is a small story, and we have it only at second hand, but it fits everything else we know of him: the endurance, the practical kindness, the refusal to pass by someone who was hurt. Livingstone could not preach a sermon about the Good Samaritan from memory. He could be one in the dark on a country road.

In the end the Society’s directors decided that his strengths outweighed his weaknesses. He was accepted in 1839, and sent to London to complete his medical training.

China Closed

He had offered himself for China, and while he was at Ongar the door closed. In 1839 the long dispute between Britain and China over the British opium trade turned into war. Britain was fighting to force the Chinese government to allow British merchants to sell opium, grown in British India, to Chinese people. It was one of the most shameful wars in British history, and it made missionary work in China impossible for the time being.

Livingstone could not wait. The Society suggested the West Indies, but he did not want to go where there was already an established church and a settled ministry. He wanted to go where the gospel was not known. It was in London, in the winter of 1839 to 1840, that he found his direction.

Robert Moffat

Robert Moffat was the most famous missionary in Britain. A Scottish gardener by training, he had gone to southern Africa for the London Missionary Society in 1816 and built a station at Kuruman, on the southern edge of the Kalahari, among the Batlhaping people. He had learned Setswana and was translating the Bible into it, and he was in Britain from 1839 to 1843 to raise support and see his New Testament through the press. His book Missionary Labours and Scenes in Southern Africa appeared in 1842 and was widely read.

Livingstone met him in London and was captivated. According to the account Moffat gave Blaikie many years later, Livingstone asked him whether he thought he would do for Africa. Moffat said that he would, if he would not go to an old station but would push on to the vast unoccupied country to the north, where, Moffat said, he had sometimes seen in the morning sun the smoke of a thousand villages where no missionary had ever been.

That phrase became part of the Livingstone legend, and later storytellers embroidered it. One popular version has a boy pumping the bellows of a church organ, hidden in the loft, who hears a visiting missionary describe the smoke of a thousand villages and resolves to go. There is no evidence for the organ loft. The phrase itself comes from Moffat’s later memory of a private conversation. It is the kind of thing Moffat might well have said, and it fits what Livingstone did next, but it should be held lightly.

What is certain is that Moffat pointed him north, beyond Kuruman, to the peoples of the interior who had never heard the gospel, and that Livingstone accepted the direction at once. The Society agreed to send him to southern Africa.

Doctor and Minister

He spent 1840 completing his medical studies in London, attending lectures and hospital practice, and in November he went back to Glasgow to take his medical qualification, as a Licentiate of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons of Glasgow. He had very little time at home. Blaikie records the last night: father and son sat up talking about the prospects of missions, and the next morning the family rose at five. Psalm 121 was a natural choice for a family saying goodbye to a son they did not expect to see for many years: “I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: From whence cometh my help? My help cometh from Jehovah, Who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:1-2, ASV). It ends with a promise that the Livingstones took literally: “Jehovah will keep thy going out and thy coming in From this time forth and for evermore” (Psalm 121:8, ASV).

The voyage took three months, and Livingstone used it as he used everything. In September 1838, Livingstone was sent with several other probationers to Chipping Ongar, a small town in Essex, to study under the Reverend Richard Cecil, a Congregational minister who prepared young men for the Society. They lived in lodgings in the town, studied Latin, Greek, Hebrew and theology with Cecil, and took turns preaching in the village chapels around about. Cecil reported on each of them to the Society’s secretary in London. Those letters survive, and they show that Livingstone came close to being sent home. The problem was not his character, which Cecil admired, or his learning, which was adequate. It was his manner. Livingstone was awkward, shy in company, and hesitant in public prayer and speech. He spoke with a broad Lanarkshire accent and a thick, slow delivery that Londoners found hard to follow. Cecil wrote that he had sense and quiet vigour and that his temper was good, but that he was heavy in manner and his prayers were not what a minister’s should be. Early in 1839 he recommended that Livingstone’s probation should be extended before the Society made up its mind. He went into the pulpit, read out his text, and then found that his mind was completely empty. There is no evidence for the organ loft. The phrase itself comes from Moffat’s later memory of a private conversation. fields.title: Another Man’s Foundation
fields.body_html:
“yea, making it my aim so to preach the gospel, not where Christ was already named, that I might not build upon another man’s foundation.”

— Romans 15:20, ASV

Kuruman

Kuruman, when Livingstone arrived in July 1841, was the most famous mission station in southern Africa. It lay in dry country on the southern edge of the Kalahari, where a strong spring, the “Eye” of the Kuruman River, rose out of the limestone. Robert Moffat and his colleagues had led its water into channels and planted gardens and orchards. A stone church, large enough for hundreds, had been finished in 1838. There was a printing press, on which Moffat was printing the Scriptures in Setswana, and a school. The people of the station were mostly Batlhaping, one of the Setswana-speaking peoples, and a congregation of believers had been gathered over twenty years of patient work.

Livingstone was disappointed. He had expected, perhaps from Moffat’s descriptions in London, a large population, and he found a small one, scattered across dry country. He wrote home that the number of people within reach was far smaller than he had imagined, and that the Society had too many missionaries crowded into the south while vast regions to the north had none. It was a judgement that was partly right and partly unfair, and it was typical of him. He did not see what twenty years of work had cost. He saw what had not yet been done.

Moffat himself was still in Britain, and Livingstone was under orders to wait at Kuruman until he returned, and then to go north with him to choose a new station. He did not wait long. Within a few months he was asking permission to travel, and by the end of 1841 he was on the road.

Not Where Christ Was Named

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s statement of his own missionary aim, in the letter to the Romans: to preach the gospel “not where Christ was already named, that I might not build upon another man’s foundation.” Livingstone took this as his own principle. He wanted to go where no missionary had been. It was not that he despised the work at Kuruman. He thought that it was done, or at least that it could be done by others, and that his calling was to go beyond it.

Paul’s words were not a criticism of other missionaries. Paul was explaining why he had not yet visited Rome, where a church already existed, and why he wanted to go on to Spain. He was also, in the same chapter, collecting money for the poor believers in Jerusalem, a church he had not founded, and he was eager to be refreshed by the Roman Christians on his way. Paul’s pioneering was part of a fellowship. Livingstone’s, increasingly, was not. He came to regard the established stations, and many of the men who served at them, with impatience, and he said so in letters to the Society’s directors in terms that his colleagues found hurtful when they heard of them. He was right that the interior needed the gospel. He was less right about the people who had spent their lives on the edge of it.

The First Journeys

His first journey north, late in 1841, was made with Rogers Edwards, an older missionary at Kuruman who had come out as an artisan and been ordained in the field. They travelled by ox-wagon into the country of the Bakwena and other Setswana-speaking peoples, several hundred miles to the north and north-east. Livingstone found that the people were eager to receive a missionary, and particularly a doctor, and that his medicine gave him an entrance everywhere he went.

In 1842 he went north again, this time with a few African companions from Kuruman and without any European. He travelled farther than any missionary had done in that direction, as far as the town of Sekgoma, the chief of the Bamangwato, and he visited a people called the Bakaa, who had a reputation among Europeans for violence towards travellers. He walked among them without weapons, slept in their village, and treated their sick. Nothing happened to him. It was the first of many occasions on which Livingstone found that the dangers Europeans feared in the interior were smaller than they imagined, if a traveller came openly and in peace.

It was on these early journeys that he first met Sechele, the young chief of the Bakwena, who would become the most important African in the first half of his life. That meeting, and what came of it, is the subject of a later chapter.

Six Months Without English

Livingstone saw at once that he could do nothing without the language. Setswana was the language of all the peoples of the region, and Moffat had already given it a written form. But most missionaries learned it slowly, at the station, from books and interpreters, and spoke it badly all their lives. Livingstone decided to do it differently. He wrote that he cut himself off from all European society for about six months, living among the Bakwena at a place called Lepelole, so that he would be forced to hear and speak nothing but Setswana. He gained, he said, by this ordeal, an insight into the habits, ways of thinking, laws and language of the people that proved of incalculable advantage in his later dealings with them.

It was a remarkable thing to do, and few missionaries of his time would have done it. At Lepelole he also tried to help the people with practical work, persuading them to dig a channel to bring water to their gardens. He treated the sick, who came to him in large numbers. He preached, at first through an interpreter and then in his own halting Setswana. He also watched and listened, and his letters and journals from these years are full of careful observations about the lives of the people around him: how they farmed, how they hunted, how their chiefs governed, how they settled disputes.

Native Agents

Out of these journeys came the first of Livingstone’s large ideas about missions. He became convinced that the gospel would spread through Africa not mainly by European missionaries, who were few, expensive and often sick, but by African Christians. Europeans should go ahead, open the way, and train African teachers, who would then carry the message to their own people far more effectively than any foreigner could. In the language of his time, he called them native agents.

The idea was not new. Moffat and others had used African evangelists for years, and the London Missionary Society had long believed in it. But Livingstone pressed it with unusual force. He thought that the European missionaries at Kuruman and the older stations were holding back African converts from responsibility, and he urged the Society to place African teachers in the villages of the interior. It was one of his best insights, and the later history of African Christianity proved him right: the churches of southern and central Africa were built far more by African evangelists, catechists and teachers than by Europeans. He did not always follow his own insight. In practice, as we shall see, his own work rested heavily on African Christians such as Mebalwe, and he gave them less space in his books than they deserved.

Seeing and Not Seeing

Reading Livingstone’s letters from these first years, one is struck by two things together. The first is his openness. He liked the people he met, he enjoyed their company and their humour, and he respected their intelligence. He wrote, against the racial theories that were becoming fashionable in Britain, that Africans were in no way inferior to Europeans in natural ability. He took their questions seriously, including their objections to Christianity. He was happier sleeping in an African village than at a mission station.

The second is the limits of his openness. He saw African religion almost entirely as darkness and superstition, and he had little patience with the customs that bound African societies together: the initiation schools, the role of rainmakers, the marriage of several wives by chiefs and wealthy men. He believed that Christianity would replace them, and he expected that it would come with what he called civilisation, which meant in practice many of the habits of a Scottish working family: square houses, clothes, ploughs, regular work and trade with Britain. He did not see how much of this was culture rather than gospel.

That is not a reason to dismiss him. Almost every missionary of his generation thought the same way, and so did most of their critics. But it is a reason to read him with care. Livingstone saw the people around him more clearly than most Europeans of his time. He did not see them as clearly as he thought he did.

The Edge of the Map

By 1843 he had persuaded the Society to let him found a new station in the north. With Rogers Edwards he chose a site at Mabotsa, in a pleasant valley among the Bakgatla people of a chief named Mosielele, some two hundred miles north-east of Kuruman. He built a house there with his own hands and began work.

He was thirty years old. He had been in Africa for two years. He spoke Setswana, he had travelled farther north than any other missionary from Kuruman, and he had a reputation among the Batswana as a healer. He was also restless, impatient with his colleagues, and already looking beyond the station he had just begun. Paul’s words in Romans end with a plan: “whensoever I go unto Spain” (Romans 15:24, ASV). Paul never got there, as far as we know. Livingstone’s Spain was always over the next horizon, and he would spend the rest of his life walking towards it.
