fields.title: The Lion at Mabotsa
fields.body_html:
“But the Lord stood by me, and strengthened me; that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.”

— 2 Timothy 4:17, ASV

The Lions of the Valley

Mabotsa was a beautiful place, a valley among hills, with good water and the large town of the Bakgatla people under their chief, Mosielele. It was also, in 1843 and 1844, troubled by lions. They came down at night and attacked the cattle in their enclosures, and sometimes in daylight. The Bakgatla believed, Livingstone wrote, that the lions had been sent against them by a neighbouring people, through witchcraft. He thought the real reason was simpler: the lions were bold because the people had not killed one, and if one could be killed the others would go. In February 1844, when the lions killed several cattle, he went out with the men of the town to encourage them in the hunt.

What happened next is the most famous incident in his life before Stanley, and he told it himself in Missionary Travels, thirteen years later, with a calm that is almost comic. The men surrounded a small wooded hill where the lions were lying. Livingstone saw one of them sitting on a rock, and fired both barrels of his gun into it. The men, however, did not close in to finish it, and Livingstone turned to go after them. He was reloading when he heard a shout.

Like a Terrier With a Rat

“Starting, and looking half round,” he wrote, “I saw the lion just in the act of springing upon me.” He was standing on a little rise, he went on; the lion caught him by the shoulder as it sprang, they fell to the ground together, and, growling horribly close to his ear, it shook him as a terrier shakes a rat.

He went on to describe, with a doctor’s detachment, what he felt. The shock, he said, produced a stupor like that of a mouse in the jaws of a cat. It brought on a kind of dreaminess, in which he felt neither pain nor terror, though he was fully aware of everything that was happening. He compared it to the state described by patients under chloroform, who see the surgeon’s knife but do not feel it. He was able to turn his head and see the lion’s paw on the back of his head, and its eyes directed at someone else.

The someone else was Mebalwe. Livingstone’s account names him only in passing, as the native schoolmaster, but Mebalwe was one of the most important people at Mabotsa. He was a Christian teacher from Kuruman who had come north with Livingstone to help found the station, and he was doing much of the day-to-day work of teaching and evangelism there. Standing some yards away, Mebalwe raised his gun and tried to fire at the lion. Both barrels misfired. The lion left Livingstone, sprang at Mebalwe, and bit him in the thigh. Another man, whom Livingstone had earlier rescued from a buffalo, tried to spear the lion, and the lion caught him by the shoulder. Then, at last, the bullets Livingstone had fired at the beginning took effect, and the lion fell dead.

The whole thing, Livingstone said, took only a few moments. Besides crushing the bone into splinters, he wrote, the lion left eleven tooth wounds in the upper part of his arm.

Courage That Is Not His

The lion story was told for a century as an example of Livingstone’s courage, and he was certainly brave. But it is worth noticing whose courage saved his life. Mebalwe ran towards the lion with a gun that failed, knowing what had just happened to the man on the ground. The other man ran at it with a spear. Both were badly hurt. Both, as far as we know, recovered. Neither was famous. In the Victorian retellings Mebalwe is often left out altogether, and the lion simply lets go of the missionary.

That pattern will recur throughout this book. Again and again, Livingstone’s survival depended on the courage, skill and loyalty of Africans whose names appear in his books, if at all, as footnotes. It was Mebalwe who saved him at Mabotsa, as it was Makololo men who carried him to the Atlantic and back, and Susi, Chuma and their companions who carried him, dead, to the coast. A Christian reading of his life should notice them, because God noticed them.

A Merciful Provision

Livingstone drew a theological lesson from the experience, and it is characteristic of his way of seeing the world. The dreaminess he had felt in the lion’s jaws, he thought, was probably felt by all animals killed by predators. He suggested that this strange state was probably produced in all animals killed by beasts of prey, and if so, that it was a merciful provision of a kind Creator for lessening the pain of death.

A modern reader may find that too tidy. The natural world, red in tooth and claw, raises harder questions for Christian faith than Livingstone allowed here, and he would come to see a great deal more suffering than a single lion attack. But it is worth noticing what he did. He did not see God only in his rescue. He looked for God in the experience of being attacked, and found, as he believed, a sign of kindness even there. The psalmist says, “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil; for thou art with me” (Psalm 23:4, ASV). Livingstone had walked a short way into that valley, and he reported that it was not as terrible as he had feared.

The verse at the head of this chapter is from Paul’s last letter, written from prison in Rome, near the end of his life. At his first trial, Paul says, no one stood with him; everyone deserted him. “But the Lord stood by me, and strengthened me … and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.” Paul’s lion was almost certainly a figure of speech, for danger or for the Roman authorities. Livingstone’s was real. But the point is the same in both cases: God delivered his servant, not for the servant’s sake, but “that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear.” Livingstone believed he had been spared for a purpose. That belief would carry him through many later dangers. It would also, at times, make him reckless.

A Crooked Arm

There was no other doctor within hundreds of miles, and Livingstone had to direct the setting of his own arm. It was done badly. The bone did not knit properly, and a false joint formed in the upper arm. He was ill for weeks with the wounds, and he could never afterwards lift his left arm above the level of his shoulder. He had to learn to fire a gun from his left shoulder, and every heavy load or fall reminded him of the lion. Thirty years later, when his body was brought home to London, the surgeons who examined it identified him by that false joint.

He went to Kuruman to recover. The Moffats had come back from Britain at the end of 1843, and their eldest daughter, Mary, had come with them.

Mary Moffat

Mary Moffat was born at Griquatown, in the northern Cape, in April 1821, the eldest child of Robert and Mary Moffat. She had grown up at Kuruman, been educated partly at the Cape, and spent the last few years in England with her parents. She was twenty-three, practical, capable and reserved. She spoke Setswana from childhood, knew the country and the people, and understood exactly what the life of a missionary’s wife involved, because she had watched her mother live it. She was teaching in the infant school at Kuruman.

Livingstone, recovering from the lion, spent the spring of 1844 at Kuruman, and he and Mary were engaged in the middle of the year. His letters about the engagement are notoriously unromantic. He described her to friends in terms of her practical qualities rather than her charms, and he seems to have been at least partly guided by the thought that a missionary in the interior needed a wife who knew the country. That is not the whole story. His later letters to her show real tenderness, and after her death he wrote that he had loved her when he married her and loved her more the longer he lived with her. But the marriage began with a missionary’s calculation as well as a young man’s affection, and it would be shaped all its life by the priority he gave to his work.

They were married at Kuruman on 9 January 1845, and they went north together to Mabotsa.

A Quarrel and a Departure

Mabotsa did not last. Rogers Edwards, the older missionary with whom Livingstone had founded the station, came to resent him. Edwards felt that Livingstone had taken credit for the station in his letters to the Society, and that he treated him as an inferior. Livingstone, for his part, thought Edwards slow and petty. The quarrel was bitter, and it went to the Society’s district committee. Livingstone was not wholly in the wrong; Edwards seems to have been a difficult colleague. But it was a pattern that would recur: Livingstone could not easily work beside another European as an equal.

His solution was characteristic. Rather than continue the dispute, he gave up the house he had built with his own hands and left Mabotsa to Edwards. In 1845 he and Mary moved some forty miles away, to Chonuane, the town of the Bakwena and their chief Sechele, whom Livingstone had met on his first journeys and who had asked him to come. There, at last, he would have a people and a chief of his own, and no colleague to share them with. It was there that the most important relationship of his missionary life began.

fields.title: Sechele
fields.body_html:
“And Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some one shall guide me? And he besought Philip to come up and sit with him.”

— Acts 8:30-31, ASV

A Chief Who Had Lost and Won

Sechele was about Livingstone’s age, a tall, intelligent and forceful man who had become chief of the Bakwena after a childhood of danger and exile. His father, the chief Motswasele, had been murdered by his own people when Sechele was a boy, and the young heir had grown up as a refugee. He had regained his chieftainship with the help of Sebetwane, the leader of the Makololo, a people from the south who had fought their way north across the Kalahari to the Zambezi. Sechele was a skilled hunter, a shrewd politician and, by the custom of his people, a rainmaker, responsible through ritual for bringing the rain on which everyone’s life depended. He had several wives, as chiefs did, and through them a web of alliances with leading families of the Bakwena.

He was also, as Livingstone soon discovered, one of the most eager learners he would ever meet. Livingstone wrote that Sechele learned the alphabet on the first day of his residence at Chonuane. Within a short time he was reading, and once he could read, he read the Bible with an appetite that astonished his teacher. His favourite book was Isaiah. Livingstone remembered him saying that Isaiah was a fine man who knew how to speak. Livingstone noted with amusement that from so much sitting over his books the chief, once spare and active, grew stout.

The verse at the head of this chapter is about another African statesman reading Isaiah, the treasurer of the queen of Ethiopia, sitting in his chariot on the road home from Jerusalem. Philip the evangelist ran up beside him and asked whether he understood what he was reading. “How can I,” the official replied, “except some one shall guide me?” For a few years at Chonuane and Kolobeng, Livingstone and Sechele sat side by side in the same way. It was the nearest thing to a real missionary partnership that Livingstone ever had. It ended, as we shall see, in grief on both sides.

All My Bones to Shake

Sechele did not receive the gospel passively. He asked hard questions, and Livingstone, to his credit, recorded some of them. When he first heard Livingstone describe the coming judgement, he was deeply troubled, and asked a question that missionaries have heard all over the world. As Livingstone told it, Sechele said, “You startle me: these words make all my bones to shake,” and that he had no strength left in him. Then he asked why, if Livingstone’s forefathers had been alive at the same time as his own, they had not sent word of these terrible things sooner. His ancestors, he said, had all passed away into darkness without knowing where they were going.

Livingstone did not record a satisfying answer, because there is none that removes the force of the question. He mentioned the geographical difficulties, and said that he hoped Christianity would spread. Sechele was not consoled. His question is still asked, and it deserves to be heard as he asked it: not as a debating point, but as grief for his own people, the parents and grandparents who had died without hearing what he was now being told mattered more than anything. It is also a rebuke to the Church that took eighteen centuries to reach the Bakwena.

The Whips of Rhinoceros Hide

Sechele was a chief, and he thought like one. Once he was persuaded that Christianity was true, he wanted his people to accept it, and he could not understand why Livingstone did not simply tell them to. Livingstone recorded his offer with obvious affection for the man who made it.

Did Livingstone imagine, Sechele asked, that the people would ever believe merely because he talked to them? Sechele himself could make them do nothing except by beating them. If Livingstone liked, he would call his headmen, and with their litupa, whips of rhinoceros hide, they would soon make everyone believe together.

Livingstone refused, and he was right to refuse. Faith cannot be beaten into anyone. But Sechele’s offer was not foolish. In the society he governed, a chief’s religious choices were not private. He was responsible for the rain, the harvest, the initiation of the young, and the rituals that held the people together. If he changed his religion, everything changed, and the people expected to follow their chief or to resist him. Livingstone’s idea of individual conversion, one soul at a time, each person freely choosing, was a Protestant European idea that made little sense to the Bakwena. Sechele was trying to tell him how his world worked. Livingstone heard the offer as a charming mistake. It was also good political advice, and it explains a great deal about what happened next.

The Drought

Chonuane was short of water, and in 1847 Livingstone persuaded Sechele to move the whole town forty miles to the banks of the Kolobeng River, where there was water for irrigation. Livingstone built a house there, a church and a school, much of it with his own hands, and Sechele built himself a square house in European style with Livingstone’s help.

Then the rains failed. Year after year, from about 1847 onwards, the country suffered drought. The Kolobeng River dwindled and then dried up. Gardens died, cattle grew thin, and hunger came. In a society where the chief was responsible for rain, the explanation seemed obvious to many of the Bakwena. Sechele had abandoned the rain rites under the influence of the missionary, and the rain had stopped. The new religion was killing them.

Livingstone recorded, in Missionary Travels, a long imagined conversation between a medical doctor and a rain doctor, based on the arguments he had actually heard. It is one of the fairest things he wrote. The rain doctor points out that both men use medicines, and both pray to God, and that neither can be sure what the other’s medicine does. Why should the missionary condemn the rain doctor’s medicine and expect his own to be trusted? The medical doctor’s answers are not always convincing, and Livingstone seems to have known it. He let the rain doctor have some of the best lines. He understood that, to the Bakwena, the drought was evidence, and that he had no evidence to set against it.

Baptism

Sechele asked for baptism. Livingstone was willing, but there was a difficulty. The London Missionary Society, like almost every Protestant mission of the time, would not baptise a man who had more than one wife. Sechele would have to send away all his wives but one.

It was a terrible demand, and Sechele understood its cost better than Livingstone did. His wives were not only his partners. They were women he had married by the law of his people, the mothers of his children, and the daughters of families on whom his authority rested. To send them away would humiliate them, impoverish them and enrage their relatives. Sechele hesitated for a long time. Livingstone held to the rule. In the end Sechele decided to do it. He kept his first wife and sent the others back to their families, with new clothing and the goods that had been theirs in his house, and with a message that he had nothing against them, but that he was following the word of God.

He was baptised on 1 October 1848. The Bakwena watched in dismay. Work in the town stopped, a great meeting was called to discuss what the chief had done, and many people stayed away from the services. Livingstone noted that some of the wives who had been sent away had been among the most regular hearers at the school and the church.

The question of polygamy has troubled missions in Africa ever since, and many African church leaders have argued that the missionaries got it wrong: that the demand to put away wives broke families, cast women and children into poverty, and made Christianity seem an enemy of African life. Others have argued that the missionaries were right about the ideal of marriage and wrong about how to reach it. This book cannot settle the question. It can say that Livingstone, who was rarely in doubt, did not seem to see how much he was asking, and that the women who paid the price were not asked at all.

The Fall

A few months later, early in 1849, it became known that one of Sechele’s former wives was pregnant, and that he was the father. Sechele confessed. Livingstone suspended him from communion. He wrote in sorrow, and the episode seems to have broken something in him. He had put his whole hope for the Bakwena in this one man, and the man had failed. Livingstone never again baptised a convert that we know of. Sechele is, as far as the record shows, the only African he ever baptised.

That fact is often repeated, sometimes to make Livingstone look a failure and sometimes to make him look a heroic sower who left the reaping to others. It should be repeated carefully. Livingstone was not the only missionary at work among the Batswana, and the church at Kuruman and elsewhere was growing. He had helpers, Mebalwe and others, who taught and preached. And Sechele did not abandon his faith. He went on reading the Bible, praying and holding worship for his people. In later years he invited other missionaries to the Bakwena, and he preached himself. He remained, in his own way and on his own terms, a Christian until his death in 1892, and Christianity spread among the Bakwena largely through his example and his authority, as he had always said it would. The man Livingstone suspended became, in the long run, the evangelist of his people.

Who Is Guiding Whom?

The Ethiopian official in Acts was baptised by Philip in a pool by the roadside, and then, the story says, “the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip; and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing” (Acts 8:39, ASV). The missionary disappears from the story. The African goes home with the gospel, and what he does with it there is not recorded, but the Church in Ethiopia remembers him as its first evangelist.

Livingstone, too, disappeared from Sechele’s story. Within a few years he had gone north and never came back to live among the Bakwena. What Sechele did with the gospel after that, he did without Livingstone’s guidance. He did it imperfectly, as all of us do. He also did it with a persistence that matched his teacher’s, and he did it in his own language, among his own people, in ways no foreign missionary could have managed.

It is worth asking, at the end of this chapter, who was guiding whom. Livingstone taught Sechele to read, and Sechele read Isaiah. But Sechele also taught Livingstone, or tried to: about how a chief’s faith affected a whole people, about the cost of the demands the mission made, about grief for ancestors who had died without the gospel. Livingstone did not always learn. He left Kolobeng convinced that he had failed among the Bakwena and that the way forward lay elsewhere, in the north, among peoples who had never heard a missionary. He may have been right about the north. He was wrong to think he had failed with Sechele.

They were women he had married by the law of his people, the mothers of his children, and the daughters of families on whom his authority rested. To send them away would humiliate them, impoverish them and enrage their relatives. Sechele hesitated for a long time. Livingstone held to the rule. In the end Sechele decided to do it. He kept his first wife and sent the others back to their families, with new clothing and the goods that had been theirs in his house, and with a message that he had nothing against them, but that he was following the word of God. He was baptised on 1 October 1848. The Bakwena watched in dismay. Work in the town stopped, a great meeting was called to discuss what the chief had done, and many people stayed away from the services. Livingstone noted that some of the wives who had been sent away had been among the most regular hearers at the school and the church. The question of polygamy has troubled missions in Africa ever since, and many African church leaders have argued that the missionaries got it wrong: that the demand to put away wives broke families, cast women and children into poverty, and made Christianity seem an enemy of African life. Others have argued that the missionaries were right about the ideal of marriage and wrong about how to reach it. This book cannot settle the question. It can say that Livingstone, who was rarely in doubt, did not seem to see how much he was asking, and that the women who paid the price were not asked at all. The Fall A few months later, early in 1849, it became known that one of Sechele’s former wives was pregnant, and that he was the father. Sechele confessed. Livingstone suspended him from communion. He wrote in sorrow, and the episode seems to have broken something in him. He had put his whole hope for the Bakwena in this one man, and the man had failed. Livingstone never again baptised a convert that we know of. Sechele is, as far as the record shows, the only African he ever baptised. That fact is often repeated, sometimes to make Livingstone look a failure and sometimes to make him look a heroic sower who left the reaping to others. It should be repeated carefully. Livingstone was not the only missionary at work among the Batswana, and the church at Kuruman and elsewhere was growing. He had helpers, Mebalwe and others, who taught and preached. And Sechele did not abandon his faith. He went on reading the Bible, praying and holding worship for his people. In later years he invited other missionaries to the Bakwena, and he preached himself. He remained, in his own way and on his own terms, a Christian until his death in 1892, and Christianity spread among the Bakwena largely through his example and his authority, as he had always said it would. The man Livingstone suspended became, in the long run, the evangelist of his people. Who Is Guiding Whom? The Ethiopian official in Acts was baptised by Philip in a pool by the roadside, and then, the story says, “the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip; and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing” (Acts 8:39, ASV). The missionary disappears from the story. The African goes home with the gospel, and what he does with it there is not recorded, but the Church in Ethiopia remembers him as its first evangelist. Livingstone, too, disappeared from Sechele’s story. Within a few years he had gone north and never came back to live among the Bakwena. What Sechele did with the gospel after that, he did without Livingstone’s guidance. He did it imperfectly, as all of us do. He also did it with a persistence that matched his teacher’s, and he did it in his own language, among his own people, in ways no foreign missionary could have managed. It is worth asking, at the end of this chapter, who was guiding whom. Livingstone taught Sechele to read, and Sechele read Isaiah. But Sechele also taught Livingstone, or tried to: about how a chief’s faith affected a whole people, about the cost of the demands the mission made, about grief for ancestors who had died without the gospel. Livingstone did not always learn. He left Kolobeng convinced that he had failed among the Bakwena and that the way forward lay elsewhere, in the north, among peoples who had never heard a missionary. He may have been right about the north. He was wrong to think he had failed with Sechele.

fields.title: Across the Thirstland
fields.body_html:
“The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.”

— Isaiah 35:1, ASV

The Lake Beyond the Desert

To the north of Kolobeng lay the Kalahari, the great dry country of sand and scrub that the Batswana called the thirstland. For generations, African travellers and hunters had crossed it by routes they knew, and the San and Bakgalagadi peoples lived in it, finding water where Europeans saw none. Beyond it, travellers said, there was a large lake, and beyond the lake rivers and a populous country ruled by Sebetwane, the Makololo chief who had once helped Sechele regain his throne. No European had reached it.

Livingstone wanted to go. Part of his reason was missionary: if there were large populations to the north, the gospel should go to them, and the drought and disappointment at Kolobeng made him feel that his work among the Bakwena had reached a dead end. Part of his reason was curiosity, and part was ambition. He did not separate the three, then or ever.

In June 1849 he set out with two English travellers, William Cotton Oswell and Mungo Murray, wealthy hunters who paid most of the costs of the expedition. Sechele, who wanted to send a message to Sebetwane, provided a guide, a Bakwena man named Ramotobi who knew the route. The party crossed the desert with ox-wagons, digging for water in dry riverbeds and losing oxen to thirst. On 1 August 1849 they reached Lake Ngami.

It was a shallow lake, much smaller than the stories had made it, and the Batawana people who lived beside it had known it all their lives. But to the Royal Geographical Society in London it was a discovery, and the Society awarded Livingstone part of its annual prize for geographical exploration. It was the first public recognition of his travels. It was also the beginning of a change in how the London Missionary Society’s directors, and Livingstone himself, thought about what he was doing.

The Batawana chief would not let him go on to Sebetwane, and Livingstone turned back. But he had seen something on the way that excited him more than the lake. The rivers flowing into Ngami came from the north, and they were full of water even in the dry season. The country to the north, he concluded, was not desert at all. It was well watered and full of people.

A Family on the Road

He went again in 1850, and this time he took his family: Mary, who was pregnant, and their three small children, Robert, Agnes and Thomas. Sechele went with them. Livingstone believed that a missionary should travel as a family, and that a man arriving with his wife and children would be trusted as a man of peace. He also did not want to leave them behind. They reached Lake Ngami again, but the children fell ill with fever, and there was no way north. They turned back to Kolobeng.

In August 1850, soon after their return, Mary gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth. The baby lived about six weeks. Livingstone wrote of her death with simple grief. Mary herself was left partly paralysed on one side of her face by the illness that followed the birth, and she was worn out.

Her mother, Mary Moffat, was appalled to learn that her son-in-law intended to take her daughter north again, pregnant once more, in 1851. She wrote him a letter of fierce protest, rebuking him for his recklessness with his wife and children. It was a brave letter from a mother-in-law to a son-in-law, and nothing in it was unfair. Livingstone went anyway.

Without Water

The 1851 journey, again with Oswell, took the family on a new route across the north of the Kalahari, guided by a San man called Shobo. Shobo lost the way. For four days the party had no water, and the children, Livingstone wrote, were in danger of dying of thirst before their parents’ eyes. The water in the wagons ran down to almost nothing, and Livingstone feared the worst. He recorded what he felt with unusual openness. It would almost have been a relief, he wrote, to have been blamed as the cause of the catastrophe, but their mother spoke not a word of reproach, though her tearful eyes showed the agony within.

On the fifth day some of the men found water and brought it back. The children lived.

That passage about Mary is the most honest thing Livingstone wrote about his marriage in any of his books. He knew that he was to blame. He knew that his wife knew it. He was grateful that she did not say so. He did not, then or later, change course. A modern reader who is moved by her silence will also want to ask whether her silence was strength or exhaustion, and what it cost her to keep it.

Sebetwane

In June 1851 they reached the Chobe River and the country of the Makololo, and Sebetwane came to meet them. He was the most remarkable African ruler Livingstone had met. As a young man, decades earlier, he had led a band of Sotho-speaking people out of the wars that convulsed the interior of southern Africa in the 1820s, fought his way across the Kalahari, and conquered the peoples of the upper Zambezi, building a kingdom of many peoples in the river valleys. He was a warrior and a conqueror, and he was also, by Livingstone’s account, generous, frank and wise, with a great curiosity about the wider world. He welcomed the missionary with delight. Livingstone wrote that he was the finest African chief he had ever met.

He was also ill. An old wound had left him with weak lungs, and soon after Livingstone’s arrival he fell sick with an inflammation of the chest. Livingstone, as a doctor, was afraid to treat him, knowing that if he died under a foreign doctor’s care the doctor would be blamed. He visited him and spoke to him of Christ. On 7 July 1851, two weeks after their meeting, Sebetwane died. Livingstone wrote of him with real sorrow. He had hoped that Sebetwane would open his kingdom to the gospel, and he wondered, in his journal, where the chief’s soul had gone, and grieved that he had been able to say so little to him.

Sebetwane’s son Sekeletu, a young man of about eighteen, succeeded him. He too welcomed Livingstone.

The Zambezi

At the beginning of August, Livingstone and Oswell rode north-east from the Chobe and came, on 4 August 1851, to a great river at Sesheke. It was the upper Zambezi, and no European had known that it flowed so far into the centre of the continent. Livingstone stood on its bank and began to dream. If this river ran to the sea, as he believed it did, then it might be a highway into the heart of Africa, along which missionaries and traders could travel.

He saw something else there that changed his life. Among the Makololo were traders from the west coast, known as Mambari, who were buying captives from Sekeletu’s people in exchange for guns and cloth, to sell to the Portuguese. The Makololo had begun to sell people from the subject peoples they ruled. It was the first time Livingstone had seen the slave trade with his own eyes, and he resolved that the way to end it was to give the people something else to sell. If honest traders could reach the Makololo with the goods they wanted, paying for ivory and other produce, the market for human beings would collapse. He needed a route to the coast.

This was the origin of the conviction he would hold for the rest of his life: that Christianity and legitimate commerce, together, could heal Africa of the slave trade. It was a sincere idea, born of what he had seen. It would also prove to be one of the most dangerous ideas of the century, when other people took it up for other ends.

The Decision

He could not take his family into the swamps and fevers of the Zambezi valley. He could not leave them at Kolobeng, where the drought continued and the Boers to the east were growing hostile. And he would not give up the north. On the way back south, in September 1851, Mary gave birth to another son, William Oswell, named after their companion, on the banks of the Zouga River.

Livingstone made his decision. He would send Mary and the four children to Britain, where they would be safe and the children could be educated, and he would go north alone to look for a route from the Makololo country to the sea. He told the directors of the Society what he intended, and made it plain that he would find a path between the interior and the coast whatever it cost. The cost would be paid, in large part, by his wife and children.

In April 1852, at Cape Town, he put them on a ship for England. He would not see them again for four and a half years.

Blossoming Deserts

Isaiah’s vision of the desert rejoicing and blossoming is a promise about the return of God’s people from exile, along a highway through the wilderness: “And a highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The way of holiness” (Isaiah 35:8, ASV). Livingstone loved this kind of passage. He saw himself as a road-maker for God, opening a highway into Africa along which the gospel could travel, and he believed that the dry places would blossom when it came.

But the prophet’s highway is God’s, not man’s. It is built for “the redeemed,” who return to Zion “with singing.” Livingstone was building something else as well, a road for traders and, though he did not intend it, for empires. And on the way to building it, he left his family by the side of the road. The desert had not yet blossomed for Mary Livingstone. It had nearly killed her children.

fields.title: Kolobeng Plundered
fields.body_html:
“God is our refuge and strength, A very present help in trouble.”

— Psalm 46:1, ASV

The Boers

To the east of Kolobeng lay the country that would become the Transvaal. In the late 1830s and 1840s, thousands of Afrikaner farmers, the Boers, had left the British-ruled Cape Colony and moved north across the Vaal River, setting up republics of their own. They took land from the African peoples who lived there, and they required labour from them. Missionaries and some British officials accused them of taking African children as so-called apprentices, who were in practice little different from slaves. The Boers, for their part, distrusted the missionaries, and especially those of the London Missionary Society, whom they regarded as meddlers who armed Africans against them.

Livingstone detested the Boers, and said so loudly. He was right about the injustice they inflicted, though his language about them was often as sweeping as theirs about Africans. He was also not entirely innocent of their accusation. The Bakwena under Sechele had acquired guns through traders, and Livingstone had helped, believing that a people who could defend themselves would not be enslaved. He had repaired guns for Sechele and kept ammunition at Kolobeng. In 1852 the British government signed the Sand River Convention with the Boers, recognising their independence north of the Vaal and agreeing that neither side would sell arms to the Africans in the region. The Bakwena were left to face the Boers alone.

Dimawe

In late August 1852, while Livingstone was still on his way north from the Cape, delayed at Kuruman by repairs to his wagon, a Boer commando attacked the Bakwena. The pretext was that Sechele had sheltered Mosielele, the Bakgatla chief of Mabotsa, who was wanted by the Boers. Sechele had refused to hand him over, saying, according to a well-known account, that whoever wanted Mosielele could come and take him out of his stomach. The commando attacked Sechele’s people at their stronghold on the hill of Dimawe. The battle lasted several days. Livingstone reported that some sixty Bakwena were killed and that more than two hundred women and children were carried off. The Bakwena, who were well armed, killed a considerable number of the attackers, and they later counted the battle as a victory, because they had not been destroyed. But their town was burned.

The commando also went to Kolobeng. Livingstone’s house was broken into and plundered. His books were torn up and their pages scattered, his medicine bottles smashed, and his furniture, clothing and stores carried off. The Boers said they found a workshop for repairing guns, which confirmed, to them, everything they suspected about him. Livingstone, when he heard the news on his way north at Kuruman, was furious. He wrote angry letters to the Cape newspapers and to the Society. He set out his losses carefully, as a Scottish workman would.

But the house mattered less than what happened to the people. Sechele had lost his town, his cattle, many of his men, and many of his people’s women and children. In 1853 he set out to go to England and appeal to Queen Victoria in person for protection. He got as far as Cape Town, where he made sworn statements about the attack, before his money ran out. The Society would not pay his passage. The colonial authorities were bound by their new treaty with the Boers, and offered no more than polite protests. Sechele went home, rebuilt his town in a new place, and over the following years made his peace with the Boers and became one of the most powerful chiefs in the region. He did not get his help from London. He got it from his own skill and the resilience of his people.

A Very Present Help

The psalm at the head of this chapter was written, it seems, in a time of war, when the city of God was threatened by enemies and the earth itself seemed to shake. “God is our refuge and strength, A very present help in trouble. Therefore will we not fear, though the earth do change, And though the mountains be shaken into the heart of the seas” (Psalm 46:1-2, ASV). The psalm does not promise that the city will not be attacked. It promises that God is present in the attack.

Livingstone was not at Kolobeng when it was plundered. Sechele and his people were at Dimawe. It was their trouble more than his, and the psalm belongs to them first. For Livingstone, the destruction of his station had a different meaning. It cut his last tie with the south. He had no home to go back to, no station, no family in Africa. The road ahead was all that remained, and he took it.

Mary in Britain

Meanwhile Mary and the four children had arrived in Britain in the summer of 1852 with almost no money and nowhere to live. She had grown up in Africa and had few friends in Britain. They went first to Livingstone’s parents in Hamilton, but the arrangement did not work. Mary and her husband’s family did not get on, and there were quarrels whose rights and wrongs are still disputed. Mary moved out.

For the next four years she wandered from one set of lodgings to another, in Hackney, in Manchester, in Kendal, in Epsom, living on a small allowance from the Missionary Society. A Quaker family in Kendal took her in for a time. She was often ill, often lonely, and often without enough money. She wrote to the Society for help and sometimes received it. Her letters to her husband took many months to reach him, when they reached him at all, and his to her were few, because he was in the interior with no way of sending them.

Some of her friends and relatives believed, then and later, that Mary began to drink heavily in these years, and modern biographers have taken the evidence seriously. It cannot now be proved one way or the other, and it should not be stated as a certainty. What is clear is that she was profoundly unhappy, that her health and spirits suffered, and that she felt herself abandoned. There are hints in later letters that her faith itself was shaken. She had married a missionary, expecting to share his work. She found herself a single mother in a strange country, dependent on charity, while her husband became famous for journeys that she had been sent away from.

It is important to say this clearly, because the Victorian biographies did not. Blaikie, writing with the family’s help, passed over these years quickly. The children, too, paid a price. Robert, the eldest, grew up angry and unsettled, and the rest grew up without a father. Paul wrote that a man who does not provide for his own household “hath denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8, ASV). Livingstone did not intend to neglect his family. He sent them to safety. But he left them without the means to live in safety, and without himself, and he did it for a journey that he could have postponed. A Christian biography cannot call that courage without also calling it a failure.

Linyanti

Livingstone went north from Kuruman late in 1852, and after a slow and difficult journey he reached the Makololo town of Linyanti, on the Chobe River, in May 1853. Sekeletu received him warmly. The young chief gave him hospitality, men, oxen and gifts, and over the following months the two men became friends of a sort.

Livingstone wanted to find a healthy site for a mission among the Makololo, somewhere high and free of the fever that killed Europeans in the river valleys. He travelled up the Zambezi into the Barotse valley looking for one, and found none. Everywhere was low, wet and malarial. He himself suffered repeated attacks of fever. Many of the Makololo, too, suffered from it, because they had come from the dry south. The idea of a mission among them, which he had promised the Society, began to look impossible.

He preached regularly to the Makololo, and they listened politely, but there was no response like Sechele’s. Sekeletu was frank about why. Livingstone recorded that the young chief did not wish to learn to read the Bible, because he was afraid that it might change his heart and make him content with only one wife, like Sechele. The story of the Bakwena had travelled north. The price of baptism was known, and Sekeletu was not willing to pay it.

No Value on Anything

In these years Livingstone wrote in his journal one of the resolutions for which he is best remembered. Blaikie printed it, and it has been quoted ever since, with small variations. He resolved to place no value on anything he had or might possess except in relation to the kingdom of Christ. He went on to say that anything that would advance that kingdom should be given away or kept, only as giving or keeping it would best promote the glory of God, to whom he owed all his hopes in time and eternity.

It is a noble resolution, and he lived much of it. He spent little on himself, gave away his possessions freely, and cared nothing for comfort. The question this chapter raises is whether his wife and children counted, in his mind, among the things he possessed, to be given away for the kingdom. He would have been horrified at the suggestion. But it is hard to read his letters from these years without feeling that, in practice, they did. He had laid them on the altar along with his books and his furniture. Jesus said that whoever left house, or wife, or children “for the kingdom of God’s sake” would receive many times more (Luke 18:29-30, ASV). He did not say that the wife and children would be asked whether they agreed.

Livingstone was now alone, at the edge of the known world, with a chief who had given him men and a problem he could not solve. If there was no healthy place for a mission in the Makololo country, then perhaps the answer was a road: a route to the coast along which missionaries and traders could come and go, staying only in the healthy season. He decided to find one. In November 1853 he set out for the Atlantic.

In the late 1830s and 1840s, thousands of Afrikaner farmers, the Boers, had left the British-ruled Cape Colony and moved north across the Vaal River, setting up republics of their own. They took land from the African peoples who lived there, and they required labour from them. Missionaries and some British officials accused them of taking African children as so-called apprentices, who were in practice little different from slaves. The Boers, for their part, distrusted the missionaries, and especially those of the London Missionary Society, whom they regarded as meddlers who armed Africans against them. Livingstone detested the Boers, and said so loudly. He was right about the injustice they inflicted, though his language about them was often as sweeping as theirs about Africans. He was also not entirely innocent of their accusation. The Bakwena under Sechele had acquired guns through traders, and Livingstone had helped, believing that a people who could defend themselves would not be enslaved. He had repaired guns for Sechele and kept ammunition at Kolobeng. In 1852 the British government signed the Sand River Convention with the Boers, recognising their independence north of the Vaal and agreeing that neither side would sell arms to the Africans in the region. The Bakwena were left to face the Boers alone. Dimawe In late August 1852, while Livingstone was still on his way north from the Cape, delayed at Kuruman by repairs to his wagon, a Boer commando attacked the Bakwena. The pretext was that Sechele had sheltered Mosielele, the Bakgatla chief of Mabotsa, who was wanted by the Boers. Sechele had refused to hand him over, saying, according to a well-known account, that whoever wanted Mosielele could come and take him out of his stomach. The commando attacked Sechele’s people at their stronghold on the hill of Dimawe. The battle lasted several days. Livingstone reported that some sixty Bakwena were killed and that more than two hundred women and children were carried off. The Bakwena, who were well armed, killed a considerable number of the attackers, and they later counted the battle as a victory, because they had not been destroyed. But their town was burned. The commando also went to Kolobeng. Livingstone’s house was broken into and plundered. His books were torn up and their pages scattered, his medicine bottles smashed, and his furniture, clothing and stores carried off. The Boers said they found a workshop for repairing guns, which confirmed, to them, everything they suspected about him. Livingstone, when he heard the news on his way north at Kuruman, was furious. He wrote angry letters to the Cape newspapers and to the Society. He set out his losses carefully, as a Scottish workman would. But the house mattered less than what happened to the people. Sechele had lost his town, his cattle, many of his men, and many of his people’s women and children. In 1853 he set out to go to England and appeal to Queen Victoria in person for protection. He got as far as Cape Town, where he made sworn statements about the attack, before his money ran out. The Society would not pay his passage. The colonial authorities were bound by their new treaty with the Boers, and offered no more than polite protests. Sechele went home, rebuilt his town in a new place, and over the following years made his peace with the Boers and became one of the most powerful chiefs in the region. He did not get his help from London. He got it from his own skill and the resilience of his people. A Very Present Help The psalm at the head of this chapter was written, it seems, in a time of war, when the city of God was threatened by enemies and the earth itself seemed to shake. “God is our refuge and strength, A very present help in trouble. Therefore will we not fear, though the earth do change, And though the mountains be shaken into the heart of the seas” (Psalm 46:1-2, ASV). The psalm does not promise that the city will not be attacked. It promises that God is present in the attack. Livingstone was not at Kolobeng when it was plundered. Sechele and his people were at Dimawe. It was their trouble more than his, and the psalm belongs to them first. For Livingstone, the destruction of his station had a different meaning. It cut his last tie with the south. He had no home to go back to, no station, no family in Africa. The road ahead was all that remained, and he took it. Mary in Britain Meanwhile Mary and the four children had arrived in Britain in the summer of 1852 with almost no money and nowhere to live. She had grown up in Africa and had few friends in Britain. They went first to Livingstone’s parents in Hamilton, but the arrangement did not work. Mary and her husband’s family did not get on, and there were quarrels whose rights and wrongs are still disputed. Mary moved out. For the next four years she wandered from one set of lodgings to another, in Hackney, in Manchester, in Kendal, in Epsom, living on a small allowance from the Missionary Society. A Quaker family in Kendal took her in for a time. She was often ill, often lonely, and often without enough money. She wrote to the Society for help and sometimes received it. Her letters to her husband took many months to reach him, when they reached him at all, and his to her were few, because he was in the interior with no way of sending them. Some of her friends and relatives believed, then and later, that Mary began to drink heavily in these years, and modern biographers have taken the evidence seriously. It cannot now be proved one way or the other, and it should not be stated as a certainty. What is clear is that she was profoundly unhappy, that her health and spirits suffered, and that she felt herself abandoned. There are hints in later letters that her faith itself was shaken. She had married a missionary, expecting to share his work. She found herself a single mother in a strange country, dependent on charity, while her husband became famous for journeys that she had been sent away from. It is important to say this clearly, because the Victorian biographies did not. Blaikie, writing with the family’s help, passed over these years quickly. The children, too, paid a price. Robert, the eldest, grew up angry and unsettled, and the rest grew up without a father. Paul wrote that a man who does not provide for his own household “hath denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8, ASV). Livingstone did not intend to neglect his family. He sent them to safety. But he left them without the means to live in safety, and without himself, and he did it for a journey that he could have postponed. A Christian biography cannot call that courage without also calling it a failure. Linyanti Livingstone went north from Kuruman late in 1852, and after a slow and difficult journey he reached the Makololo town of Linyanti, on the Chobe River, in May 1853. Sekeletu received him warmly. The young chief gave him hospitality, men, oxen and gifts, and over the following months the two men became friends of a sort. Livingstone wanted to find a healthy site for a mission among the Makololo, somewhere high and free of the fever that killed Europeans in the river valleys. He travelled up the Zambezi into the Barotse valley looking for one, and found none. Everywhere was low, wet and malarial. He himself suffered repeated attacks of fever. Many of the Makololo, too, suffered from it, because they had come from the dry south. The idea of a mission among them, which he had promised the Society, began to look impossible. He preached regularly to the Makololo, and they listened politely, but there was no response like Sechele’s. Sekeletu was frank about why. Livingstone recorded that the young chief did not wish to learn to read the Bible, because he was afraid that it might change his heart and make him content with only one wife, like Sechele. The story of the Bakwena had travelled north. The price of baptism was known, and Sekeletu was not willing to pay it. No Value on Anything In these years Livingstone wrote in his journal one of the resolutions for which he is best remembered. Blaikie printed it, and it has been quoted ever since, with small variations. He resolved to place no value on anything he had or might possess except in relation to the kingdom of Christ. He went on to say that anything that would advance that kingdom should be given away or kept, only as giving or keeping it would best promote the glory of God, to whom he owed all his hopes in time and eternity. It is a noble resolution, and he lived much of it. He spent little on himself, gave away his possessions freely, and cared nothing for comfort. The question this chapter raises is whether his wife and children counted, in his mind, among the things he possessed, to be given away for the kingdom. He would have been horrified at the suggestion. But it is hard to read his letters from these years without feeling that, in practice, they did. He had laid them on the altar along with his books and his furniture. Jesus said that whoever left house, or wife, or children “for the kingdom of God’s sake” would receive many times more (Luke 18:29-30, ASV). He did not say that the wife and children would be asked whether they agreed. Livingstone was now alone, at the edge of the known world, with a chief who had given him men and a problem he could not solve. If there was no healthy place for a mission in the Makololo country, then perhaps the answer was a road: a route to the coast along which missionaries and traders could come and go, staying only in the healthy season. He decided to find one. In November 1853 he set out for the Atlantic.

fields.title: Twenty-Seven Men
fields.body_html:
“In whose eyes a reprobate is despised, But who honoreth them that fear Jehovah; He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.”

— Psalm 15:4, ASV

The Company

On 11 November 1853, Livingstone left Linyanti for the west coast with twenty-seven men. They were not his servants. They were Sekeletu’s men, chosen by the chief from among the many peoples of his kingdom, and they went because their chief had sent them and because they hoped to open a trade route to the sea for him. Some were Makololo, but most were from the subject peoples of the upper Zambezi. Their leader was a man named Pitsane, and Livingstone came to rely on him heavily. The journey that followed is often described as Livingstone’s journey. It was theirs as much as his. Without them he would not have gone a hundred miles.

The equipment was very small. Livingstone took a few spare clothes, some tea, coffee and sugar, a small tent, a gun and some ammunition, a supply of beads to pay for food and passage, a sextant, a chronometer watch, a thermometer and compasses, a Bible, a nautical almanac and a book of mathematical tables for his calculations, and a magic lantern, a projector with painted glass slides of Bible scenes, which he used to show and explain the gospel stories in the villages. He had very little to trade and almost nothing to give. He was depending, as he would on all his great journeys, on the goodwill of the people through whose land he passed.

Up the River

They went north by canoe up the Zambezi, through the Barotse valley, and then struck north-west overland into the country of the Lunda peoples, towards the watershed where the rivers begin to flow west to the Atlantic. The rains had begun. The country was flooded, the paths were deep in water, and the party was soaked day and night. Livingstone had attack after attack of fever. He grew so weak that he could hardly sit on his riding ox.

The Lunda chiefs received them in various ways. The most memorable was a young woman chief named Manenko, a niece of the great chief Shinte, who insisted on escorting the party to her uncle’s town herself, overruled Livingstone’s own plans, and marched at the head of the column through pouring rain at a pace the men could hardly match, unbothered by the cold they complained of. Livingstone was both exasperated and impressed, and his account of her is one of the liveliest passages in his book. She was not a figure in his story. He was, for those few days, a figure in hers.

Shinte himself received them with great ceremony and real kindness. At his town Livingstone showed his lantern pictures. When the slide of Abraham about to sacrifice Isaac was shown, he recorded, the women watching thought the knife was about to come out of the picture at them, and fled. He laughed at the story, and so did they afterwards. It is worth noticing which Bible story he chose to show first: a father, called by God, about to give up his son.

The Chiboque

Further west, the country changed. Here the people had been in contact with the slave traders of the coast for generations, and they had learned to demand payment from every traveller who passed. The Chiboque, a people near the Kasai River, surrounded Livingstone’s party and demanded a man, an ox, a gun or a tusk as the price of passage, saying that the party had insulted them. They did not want beads. Livingstone understood that a man meant one of his companions, to be sold as a slave.

He sat on his camp stool with his gun across his knees, facing the Chiboque headman, while his men drew close around him and the Chiboque warriors pressed in with spears and guns. He refused to give up a man. He offered a shirt, then beads, then other things. The tension rose, and for a time it seemed that there would be bloodshed. In the end he gave an ox, and they let him go. He was proud afterwards that no blood had been shed. His men had been ready to fight, and he had held them back.

On another occasion, his own men nearly mutinied. Tired, hungry and frightened, some of them refused to go on and became insolent. Livingstone, by his own account, rushed out of his tent with a pistol and threatened to shoot the ringleader. The mutiny collapsed. He believed that discipline had to be kept or the whole party would be lost, and he was probably right. It is also a reminder that he was a leader who could frighten as well as inspire.

The Edge of the World

At the Kwango River, the eastern border of Portuguese influence, a hostile chief demanded more tribute than they could pay. A Portuguese militia sergeant named Cypriano di Abreu, the son of a Portuguese father and an African mother, came to their help, took them across the river, and fed them generously at his home. Livingstone was moved by his kindness. From there the way to the coast lay through territory controlled by the Portuguese, with forts and traders, and on 31 May 1854 the party walked into Luanda, the capital of the Portuguese colony of Angola. Livingstone was so ill that he could barely stand.

The men from the Zambezi had never seen the sea. Livingstone recorded what they said when they first looked at it, and it is one of the most quoted passages in his book. They had marched along with their father, they said, believing what the old people had always told them, that the world had no end; but all at once the world had said to them that it was finished, and there was no more of it. They called Livingstone father, and they had followed him to the end of the world.

Mr Gabriel

At Luanda there was one Englishman, Edmund Gabriel, the British commissioner for the suppression of the slave trade. Gabriel took Livingstone into his house, put him to bed, and nursed him through months of fever and dysentery. Livingstone wrote of the pleasure of lying in a real English bed after six months of sleeping on the ground. When he recovered, he took his men to see the city, the ships in the harbour and the churches. The officers of a British naval squadron showed them over a warship. To earn money, the men found work unloading coal from ships in the port, and they bought cloth and beads to take home.

Luanda itself was a reminder of why Livingstone had come. For more than two centuries it had been one of the greatest slave ports in the world. Hundreds of thousands of people from the interior of Angola and beyond had been marched to its harbour and shipped across the Atlantic, most of them to Brazil. Brazil had stopped importing enslaved Africans only in 1850, under heavy British pressure, and the British squadron whose officers entertained Livingstone was there to stop the trade from reviving. Inland, slavery and forced labour continued, and the traders whose demands had troubled the party at the Kasai were part of the same system. Livingstone looked at the cathedral and the fine houses of the old city and knew what had paid for them.

The naval officers offered Livingstone a passage home to England. His family was there, and he had not seen them for more than two years. He was ill and exhausted, and he had done what he had set out to do: he had reached the coast. He could have sailed, and sent the men home by another route with the help of the Portuguese. No one would have blamed him.

He refused. He had promised Sekeletu that he would bring the men back, and he would not break his word. They did not know the way home, and the country they had come through was dangerous, full of slave traders who would have been glad to seize a party of unprotected men. Livingstone believed that if he left them, they would never see the Zambezi again.

It was a costly decision, and it may well have saved their lives. It also, as it turned out, saved his own. The ship on which he would have sailed, HMS Forerunner, sank off Madeira on her voyage home. Livingstone had sent his journal, maps and letters on her. They went to the bottom, and he had to write them all again.

He That Sweareth to His Own Hurt

Psalm 15 asks who may dwell on God’s holy hill, and answers with a portrait of an honest man: one who walks uprightly, speaks truth in his heart, does not slander his neighbour, and “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.” That is, he keeps his promises even when keeping them costs him.

Livingstone kept his promise to the twenty-seven men. It cost him another two years in Africa, months of fever and danger, and the pain of continued separation from his family. He did it because he had given his word to a chief and to the men themselves, and because the old Highland precept of his family, “Be honest,” meant more to him than his own comfort. It is one of the finest things he ever did, and it is worth setting beside the harder judgements this book has to make. The man who could leave his wife to wander through English lodging-houses would not leave twenty-seven African men on a strange coast.

There is something uncomfortable in that comparison, and it should not be smoothed away. But neither should the decision at Luanda be belittled. It was the act of a man who saw his African companions as people to whom he owed a debt of honour, at a time when many Europeans would have seen them as hired hands to be paid off and left. The men knew it. On the long road home they would show him the same loyalty.

On 20 September 1854, Livingstone and the twenty-seven left Luanda and turned back east, into the interior.

fields.title: The Word of a Gentleman
fields.body_html:
“And Jesus came to them and spake unto them, saying, All authority hath been given unto me in heaven and on earth. Go ye therefore, and make disciples of all the nations … and lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.”

— Matthew 28:18-20, ASV

The Long Way Back

The journey back from Luanda took a year. Livingstone was ill for much of it, with fever and a bout of rheumatic fever that left him unable to travel for weeks. He went slowly, rewriting the journal that had gone down with the Forerunner and taking observations to correct his maps. The men carried the goods they had earned at Luanda, and the gifts that the Portuguese and British had sent for Sekeletu, including a colonel’s uniform and a horse. In September 1855 the party walked back into Linyanti.

The men were heroes. They had been to the sea and come back, and for days they told the people of Linyanti what they had seen: the ocean, the ships, the city with its stone houses, the warship with its guns. Livingstone recorded that they boasted that they had gone to the end of the world and had turned back only when there was no more land. Sekeletu was delighted with his gifts and with the reports. The faithfulness of the twenty-seven had made Livingstone a trusted man among the Makololo.

But Livingstone had concluded that the western route would not do. It was too long, too difficult, too unhealthy, and it passed through country where the slave trade was entrenched. He would try the other way, eastward down the Zambezi to the Indian Ocean. If the river was navigable, it might be the highway he was looking for.

Mosi-oa-Tunya

In early November 1855 he set out again, with a much larger party provided by Sekeletu, more than a hundred men this time, and with a guide and interpreter named Sekwebu, a man who had lived in the country to the east and knew its languages. Sekeletu himself came with them for the first part of the way.

For years Livingstone had heard of a great waterfall on the Zambezi, below the Makololo country, which the people called Mosi-oa-Tunya, “the smoke that thunders,” because of the columns of spray that rose from it and could be seen for miles. In the middle of November 1855, Sekeletu’s men took him by canoe down the river to an island on the very lip of the falls, and he lay down and looked over the edge into the chasm where the whole width of the Zambezi plunges into a narrow gorge.

He described it in Missionary Travels with a rare lyricism. No one could imagine the beauty of the view from anything seen in England, he wrote, and it had never been seen before by European eyes, but scenes so lovely, he thought, must have been gazed on by angels in their flight. He named the falls after Queen Victoria, the only English name, he said, that he gave to anything in the country. He planted peach and apricot stones on the island, and he cut his initials and the date on a tree there, which he said was the only time he had indulged in that kind of vanity.

The renaming of the falls is often taken as a symbol of his whole life, and rightly. The falls had a name already. The people who lived near them had known them for centuries, had worshipped at them, and had brought him there. Livingstone saw, and was moved, and gave them the name of a distant queen, as though they had not been seen until he saw them. He meant it as an honour to the falls, not an insult to the people. But it was the beginning of a habit of mind, his and his country’s, in which what Africans knew did not count until a European had recorded it. Zambia, since independence, has used the old name alongside the new, and the national park around the falls is called Mosi-oa-Tunya.

The Healthy Highlands

Below the falls, the party left the river and crossed the high plateau to the north of the Zambezi, the country of the Batoka people. It was cooler and drier than the river valleys, and Livingstone thought that it was healthy, free from the fever that killed Europeans lower down. Here, he believed, was the place for missions and for European settlement: a high, fertile, well-watered country, with a large population, reached by a great river from the sea. The vision that would drive him for the next eight years was born on this plateau.

The party descended again to the Zambezi and followed it east, through country that grew more hostile as they approached the territory of the Portuguese and their slave-trading allies. Some of the chiefs along the river had been raided by slavers, and they suspected that any large armed party was another raid.

14 January 1856

On 14 January 1856 the party reached the point where the Luangwa River joins the Zambezi, near the ruins of the old Portuguese settlement of Zumbo. The people of the chief on the other side had gathered in large numbers, armed, and Livingstone’s men believed that they would be attacked when they tried to cross. That night he wrote in his journal one of the most famous passages he ever wrote. Blaikie printed it from the manuscript.

He confessed to great turmoil of spirit at the prospect that all his plans for the welfare of that great region and its people might be brought to nothing the next day by the men across the river, whom he described with the contemptuous word his age used for peoples it thought uncivilised. Then he went on. In doing so he missed a long section of the Zambezi above Tete, where the river runs through a narrow gorge called Kebrabasa. He had been told that there were rapids there, but he did not see them. He assumed that they could be passed by a steamer at high water. He would discover, two years later, how wrong he was.

He left most of the Makololo men at Tete, more than a hundred of them, with land to cultivate and the promise of the Portuguese commandant to look after them. A British warship took him from Quelimane to Mauritius. Sekwebu, the guide and interpreter who had brought the party safely down the Zambezi, went with him, meaning to go on to England. He had never been to sea. On the voyage, and at Mauritius, the strangeness of everything overwhelmed him. Livingstone wrote that Sekwebu became insane, and in a fit of terror jumped overboard and was drowned. His body was never found.

Livingstone grieved for him. He had depended on Sekwebu as he had on Pitsane and the others, and he had brought him out of his world into one that destroyed him. fields.title: “I Never Made a Sacrifice”
fields.body_html:
“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed to us-ward.”

— Romans 8:18, ASV

Home

Livingstone landed in England in December 1856 and was reunited with Mary after four and a half years. She had written a poem of welcome for him, which survives, full of love and of the pain of waiting. The children hardly knew him. Robert was ten, Agnes nine, Thomas seven, and William Oswell, whom he had last seen as a baby, was five. His father had died that February, and when Livingstone went to Hamilton to see his mother and sisters, it was to a house in mourning.

He was famous at once. Reports of his crossing of Africa had been reaching Britain for two years, and the public had followed them with excitement. Within days of his arrival he was received at a special meeting of the Royal Geographical Society, which had already awarded him its gold medal, and at a meeting of the London Missionary Society. Over the following months he was given an honorary degree by Oxford and honours by other universities, the freedom of several cities, and an audience with Queen Victoria. He was invited to speak everywhere, and crowds came to see him. He disliked the attention and was a poor speaker, reading his addresses awkwardly in his strong Scottish accent. It made no difference. People wanted to see the man who had walked across Africa.

Missionary Travels

The publisher John Murray persuaded him to write a book, and he spent most of 1857 writing it, in rented rooms in London, with Mary and the children around him. Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa appeared in November 1857. It was a long, dense book, full of natural history and geography as well as adventure, and it sold some seventy thousand copies, an extraordinary number for the time. For the first time in his life, Livingstone had money. He used much of it to provide for his family and to pay for his next journey.

The book made his reputation, and it also made his message. Its pages argued that the interior of Africa was not a desert but a rich, populous, well-watered country, healthy on its high plateaus, full of people who wanted to trade and were willing to hear the gospel. The great obstacle, he argued, was the slave trade, which set people against each other and made all travel dangerous. The answer was to open the country to legitimate commerce by way of the great rivers, especially the Zambezi, so that Africans could sell cotton, ivory and other produce instead of people. Missionaries would follow the traders, and Christianity and civilisation would spread together.

Leaving the Society

Not everyone was delighted. The directors of the London Missionary Society had watched his travels with growing unease. They were a missionary society, supported by the gifts of churchgoers for the preaching of the gospel, and their missionary had spent years exploring rather than preaching. In a letter that reached Livingstone on his way home, the Society’s secretary had written that the directors were restricted in their power to support plans only remotely connected with the spreading of the gospel. Livingstone was deeply offended. He believed that everything he had done was connected with the spread of the gospel, because it was opening a way for it.

The Society was willing, in fact, to support a mission to the Makololo, which he had promised, and it went ahead with one. But Livingstone was ready to move on. The government, impressed by his journeys and attracted by the idea of opening the Zambezi to British trade, offered him an appointment as consul at Quelimane, with responsibility for the east coast and the independent districts of the interior, and the leadership of an official expedition up the Zambezi. He accepted, and in 1857 he resigned from the London Missionary Society.

He insisted that he had not stopped being a missionary. He wrote to friends that he was serving Christ as much in exploring as in preaching, and that a man could be a missionary in many ways. There was truth in that. There was also a change of direction that he did not fully admit, even to himself. From now on he would be paid by the British government, accountable to the Foreign Office, and committed to an expedition whose goals were commercial and scientific as well as Christian. He would never again work for a missionary society.

The Senate House

On 4 December 1857, Livingstone spoke in the Senate House at Cambridge, to a packed audience of students and dons. It was the most important speech of his life, and it was printed soon afterwards. He spoke about Africa, its people, its resources, and its need, and about the slave trade. Then he turned to the subject of sacrifice.

“For my own part,” he said, “I have never ceased to rejoice that God has appointed me to such an office. People talk of the sacrifice I have made in spending so much of my life in Africa. Can that be called a sacrifice which is simply paid back as a small part of a great debt owing to our God, which we can never repay?” He went on: “It is emphatically no sacrifice. Say rather it is a privilege. Anxiety, sickness, suffering, or danger, now and then, with a foregoing of the common conveniences and charities of this life, may make us pause, and cause the spirit to waver, and the soul to sink; but let this only be for a moment. All these are nothing when compared with the glory which shall hereafter be revealed in, and for, us. I never made a sacrifice.”

And he ended with an appeal. He asked his hearers to turn their attention to Africa. He expected, he said, to be cut off in that country within a few years, and he begged them not to let it be shut again now that it was open. “I go back to Africa to try to make an open path for commerce and Christianity,” he said, and he asked them to carry on the work he had begun, and left it with them.

A Privilege

The Cambridge speech had an immediate effect. Students and graduates of Cambridge and Oxford, with support from Durham and Dublin, founded the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa, which would send its first party to the Zambezi in 1861. It was the most direct fruit of Livingstone’s appeal, and in time it became one of the great Anglican missions of East and Central Africa, with a long history of African clergy and churches. Its beginnings, as a later chapter will show, were tragic.

The words about sacrifice have been quoted in thousands of sermons. They deserve to be, because they express something true about the Christian life. Paul wrote, in the verse at the head of this chapter, that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come, and Livingstone was echoing him almost word for word. To serve Christ at a cost is not a loss, when it is set against what Christ has given and what he will give. The missionary who thinks of himself as a martyr has misunderstood the gospel. Livingstone had not.

And yet the words need to be heard alongside the story of the previous four years. Livingstone had not made a sacrifice, he said. Mary had. Her years in English lodgings, alone with four children, were a sacrifice, and she had not chosen them. The children’s years without a father were a sacrifice. Sekwebu, drowned off Mauritius, had made one. The speech was true of Livingstone’s own heart, and it was spoken with real humility. It was not the whole truth about the cost of his calling, because much of that cost had been paid by others.

Commerce and Christianity

The last sentences of the speech have been quoted almost as often as the passage on sacrifice, and they have been criticised more. “I go back to Africa to try to make an open path for commerce and Christianity.” In later years Livingstone’s phrase was turned into a slogan, “Christianity, commerce and civilisation,” and used by many who had no interest in Christianity at all to justify the European takeover of Africa. Traders, settlers and governments followed the paths he opened, and they did not always come in the spirit he hoped.

It is fair to ask what Livingstone himself meant. He did not mean conquest. He believed that Africans should own their own land and govern themselves, and he was a fierce critic of the Boers and later of the Portuguese for taking African land and labour. What he wanted was trade: British merchants buying cotton and ivory from African producers, paying fair prices, and so giving African communities an alternative to selling people. He believed that this would make the slave trade unprofitable and would bring Africans into contact with Christian civilisation, which he assumed would be good for them.

There was real compassion in this, and real naivety. Livingstone believed that British commerce was, at heart, a Christian thing, honest and beneficial, and he underestimated how easily trade becomes exploitation when one side has guns and ships and the other does not. He also assumed, as most Victorians did, that what he called civilisation, meaning British customs and institutions, was the natural companion of the gospel. The history of the next century would show how dangerous that assumption was. Jesus warned, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24, ASV). Livingstone did not think he was serving mammon. He thought he was harnessing it. It is not a thing that can easily be done.

In March 1858 he sailed from Liverpool for the Zambezi, at the head of a government expedition, with a paddle steamer in pieces in the hold and Mary and their youngest son beside him. He was forty-five, the most famous missionary in the world, and no longer a missionary of any society. He was going back, as he had promised, to make an open path.
