The history of the next century would show how dangerous that assumption was. Jesus warned, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24, ASV). Livingstone did not think he was serving mammon. He thought he was harnessing it. It is not a thing that can easily be done. In March 1858 he sailed from Liverpool for the Zambezi, at the head of a government expedition, with a paddle steamer in pieces in the hold and Mary and their youngest son beside him. fields.title: Kebrabasa
fields.body_html:
“A man’s heart deviseth his way; But Jehovah directeth his steps.”

— Proverbs 16:9, ASV

The Expedition

The Zambezi Expedition sailed from Liverpool on 10 March 1858 in the steamer Pearl. In its hold, in three sections, was a small paddle steamer for use on the river, named Ma-Robert, after the name by which Mary Livingstone was known among the Batswana, “mother of Robert.” The expedition had a government grant, a set of official instructions, and a staff of six Europeans besides Livingstone himself: his brother Charles, who had come back from America to serve as general assistant; John Kirk, a young Edinburgh doctor and botanist; Richard Thornton, a geologist of twenty; Thomas Baines, an artist and storekeeper who had experience of southern Africa; Norman Bedingfeld, a naval officer, to command the vessels; and George Rae, a ship’s engineer from Blantyre.

Its aims, set out in the Foreign Office instructions, were to explore the Zambezi and its resources, to open it to British trade, to encourage the people to grow cotton and other crops for export, and to discourage the slave trade. Livingstone also intended to take the Makololo men home from Tete, as he had promised, and to prepare the way for missions on the healthy highlands he had seen.

Mary and their youngest son, Oswell, sailed with them. But on the voyage it became clear that she was pregnant again, and at Cape Town it was decided that she could not go on to the fever-ridden Zambezi delta. She went north to her parents at Kuruman, and there, on 16 November 1858, she gave birth to a daughter, Anna Mary. Livingstone would not see the child until she was five. The other children were in Britain. Mary, once more, was separated from them and from him.

A Leaking Launch

The expedition went wrong almost from the start. The Ma-Robert had been built cheaply, of a new kind of steel plate, and it was badly designed for the river. It burned enormous quantities of wood, so that the crew spent much of each day cutting fuel, and it was so underpowered that canoes paddled past it. Its plates soon began to corrode and leak. The crew nicknamed it the Asthmatic. Livingstone blamed the builder, and with reason.

He also quarrelled almost at once with Bedingfeld, the naval officer, over who commanded the vessels. Bedingfeld resigned and went home within a few months. Livingstone had never commanded Europeans before, apart from his short partnership with Rogers Edwards, and he did not do it well. He gave few clear instructions, expected his men to work as hard as he did without being told, and took any disagreement as disloyalty. He relied heavily on his brother Charles, who was unpopular with the others and whose reports of their failings Livingstone tended to believe.

The delta of the Zambezi was a maze of channels, and it took weeks to find a navigable one. Everyone suffered from malaria. Livingstone had worked out a treatment for fever, a combination of quinine with purgatives, which he called his rousers, and it saved many lives, including his own. It was one of his real contributions to tropical medicine. But it could not keep a party of Europeans healthy in the delta in the rainy season.

The Makololo at Tete

In September 1858 the expedition reached Tete, and Livingstone met the Makololo men he had left there two and a half years before. They were overjoyed to see him. Some of them had died while he was away, and some had settled, married and made new lives at Tete. The rest wanted to go home, and he renewed his promise to take them. It was a promise he kept, in 1860, though by then many more had chosen to stay. The Makololo at Tete were the one part of the expedition’s first year that went as he had hoped.

Kebrabasa

Above Tete lay the gorge of Kebrabasa, the stretch of the Zambezi he had bypassed on his way down in 1856. He had assumed that the rapids there could be passed by a steamer. In November 1858 he went to see them, first in the Ma-Robert, which could not get far, and then on foot, scrambling over the hot black rocks of the gorge with Kirk and a few of the Makololo.

What they found was a narrow channel through which the whole river forced its way between cliffs, in a series of rapids and falls, the worst of them a cataract called Morumbwa. No steamer could pass it. Kirk saw this at once. Livingstone would not accept it. He wrote to the government that a more powerful steamer, at the height of the flood, might pass the rapids, and he asked for a new vessel. Kirk, in his private journal, began to record doubts about his leader’s judgement that would grow sharper as the years went on.

It was the moment when the great plan collapsed. Livingstone had told the British public and government that the Zambezi was a highway into the interior, leading to healthy highlands where missionaries and traders could settle. The highway was blocked, a few hundred miles from the sea, by an obstacle he had not seen because he had walked round it. His whole reputation, and the government’s money, rested on a mistake.

The Heart Deviseth

The proverb at the head of this chapter is one of the wisest in the Bible about planning. “A man’s heart deviseth his way; But Jehovah directeth his steps.” It does not say that planning is wrong. It says that our plans are not the last word. God directs the steps, and sometimes he directs them where we did not intend to go.

Livingstone was a great deviser of ways. His plan for the Zambezi was bold, generous and, in its way, visionary. It was also built on a hasty assumption, and when the assumption proved false he could not let it go. That is the shadow side of the perseverance that this book has praised. The same stubbornness that carried him across Africa made it almost impossible for him to admit that he had been wrong. He did not abandon his plan; he looked for a way round it. Sometimes that is faith. Sometimes it is only pride.

And yet the proverb also suggests something more hopeful. Livingstone’s steps were directed, in the end, somewhere he had not planned to go. Unable to go up the Zambezi, he turned north, up its tributary the Shire River. What he found there would shape the history of a whole country.

The Shire

In January 1859 the expedition steamed up the Shire, a river no European had explored, into a valley of rich farmland and large villages. The Mang’anja people who lived there were at first suspicious, gathering on the banks with bows and poisoned arrows, but they were won over by patient explanation that the strangers came in peace and were not slave traders. Some way upstream, the river was blocked by a series of cataracts, which Livingstone named the Murchison Cataracts after his friend Sir Roderick Murchison of the Royal Geographical Society.

Above the cataracts was high country. In April 1859, Livingstone and Kirk walked up into the highlands and reached Lake Shirwa, a large lake that had not been recorded by Europeans. They saw a cool, fertile plateau with many people, the place, Livingstone thought, for the healthy missionary settlement he had imagined on the Batoka plateau. And they heard of a much larger lake farther north.

In September 1859 they reached it. Lake Nyasa, now Lake Malawi, is one of the great lakes of Africa, some three hundred and sixty miles long. Livingstone and his party were the first Europeans to report it to the world, though Portuguese and Arab-Swahili traders knew of it, and a Portuguese traveller may have reached it earlier. It was a real discovery in the sense that mattered to the British public, and Livingstone presented it as a triumph. It was the most important achievement of the expedition.

It came with a terrible discovery. Along the shores of the lake and in the highlands around it ran one of the main routes of the East African slave trade. Caravans from the lake carried captives east to the coast, to be shipped to Zanzibar and the markets of Arabia and the Persian Gulf. The people of the Shire Highlands lived in fear of raiders, both slave traders from the coast and Yao groups who were themselves moving into the region. Livingstone had found the healthy highlands. He had also found the open sore.

Dismissals

Within the expedition, relations went from bad to worse. In 1859 Livingstone dismissed Richard Thornton, the young geologist, for what he considered idleness. He also dismissed Thomas Baines, the artist, after Charles accused him of stealing expedition stores and giving them away. Baines denied it to the end of his life, and later historians have generally believed him and blamed Charles. Livingstone gave him no real hearing. He sent Baines home in disgrace and refused to retract the charge.

Thornton later rejoined the expedition on his own account and died of fever in Africa in 1863. Baines went on to a long career as an artist and explorer in southern Africa, and his paintings of the Zambezi and the Victoria Falls are among the finest records of the region. Neither man ever received an apology.

It is painful to set these episodes beside the Livingstone of Luanda, who would not abandon twenty-seven African men. The same man who kept his word to Africans at great cost to himself could be unjust and unforgiving to the Europeans who served under him. Part of the reason may be that he expected nothing of Africans that he did not expect of himself, while he expected of his European colleagues everything that he expected of himself, and was angry when they fell short. Part of it was simply that he was not a good leader of men who were not willing to follow him without question. He knew how to persevere. He did not know how to share command.

fields.title: Graves at Linyanti
fields.body_html:
“whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. What is your life? For ye are a vapor that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.”

— James 4:14, ASV

A Promise Kept

In May 1860, Livingstone set out from Tete to take the Makololo home. He had promised Sekeletu, when he set out for the east in 1855, that he would bring them back, and he had promised the men themselves. It was a journey of some six hundred miles upriver, on foot, and it delayed the expedition’s other work by most of a year. Kirk and Charles went with him. Many of the men no longer wanted to go. They had lived at Tete for four years. Some had married local women and had children, some had found work, and some had simply come to prefer the life there. Livingstone did not force them. The party that set out was smaller than the one that had come down, and more men slipped away on the road.

It was characteristic of him that he went at all. The expedition’s instructions did not require it, and the Foreign Office would hardly have noticed if he had sent the men home under an escort. But he had given his word, and he would not delegate it. On the way he passed the Victoria Falls again, and this time he and Charles measured them, dropping a weighted line into the chasm and making careful notes.

The men who stayed behind made their own choices, and some of them made a mark on history that Livingstone could not have foreseen. A group of the Makololo who had served the expedition later settled in the lower Shire valley, in what is now southern Malawi. Armed with the guns the expedition left them and respected for their connection with the Europeans, they gathered followers among the local people and the refugees from the slave raids, and two of them, Ramakukane and Kasisi, became chiefs whose descendants ruled there for generations. They were not Livingstone’s converts or his servants. They were men from the upper Zambezi who saw an opportunity in a disordered land and took it, sometimes protecting the people around them and sometimes ruling them harshly. They belong in this story as reminders that the Africans who travelled with Livingstone were not extras in his drama. They had their own lives, and they lived them.

What He Found

When they reached Sesheke, on the upper Zambezi, in August 1860, Livingstone found the Makololo kingdom in decline. Sekeletu was ill with a disfiguring skin disease, which his people believed had been caused by witchcraft, and he had shut himself away from his subjects. He was suspicious and harsh, and many of his people were afraid of him. The young chief who had befriended Livingstone in 1853 had become, in a few years, a sick and bitter man. Livingstone treated him, with some success, but he could see that the Makololo state, which Sebetwane had built by conquest, was beginning to fall apart. Within a short time of Sekeletu’s death a few years later, the subject peoples rose against the Makololo and destroyed their rule.

He also found out what had happened to the missionaries.

The Makololo Mission

In 1857, after Livingstone’s return to Britain, the London Missionary Society had decided to send missions to two of the peoples he had described: the Matabele in the south, and the Makololo on the Zambezi. Livingstone had urged both. For the Makololo mission the Society chose Holloway Helmore, an experienced missionary who had served for many years among the Batswana, and Roger Price, a young man newly arrived from Britain. They travelled north across the Kalahari with their wives and children, by ox-wagon, a journey of many months, and arrived at Linyanti in February 1860.

Linyanti was low, marshy and full of fever, and they arrived in the rainy season. Within weeks the party was dying. On 7 March, Helmore’s three-year-old son Henry died. Price’s baby daughter died soon after, and so did another of the Helmore children. On 12 March, Anne Helmore died. Holloway Helmore himself died on 21 April. Several of the African wagon drivers and servants who had come with them also died. Price, ill himself, with his wife and the two surviving Helmore children, was allowed by the Makololo to leave, but stripped of many of his goods. On the journey south, Isabella Price died too. Price and the two children were eventually found and brought to safety by another missionary, John Mackenzie.

Of the nine Europeans who had set out for Linyanti, six were dead: Holloway and Anne Helmore, two of their four children, and Roger Price’s wife and baby daughter. The mission was over. It had lasted a few months.

Who Was to Blame?

The disaster caused bitter recriminations, and some of them fell on Livingstone. Roger Price believed that the Makololo had poisoned the party, and some of the Batswana long held the same belief. Livingstone was sure that they had died of malaria, and modern opinion largely agrees with him. But others asked why the missionaries had gone to Linyanti at all, and why they had gone in the wet season, and why Livingstone, who had urged the mission and knew the country, had not been there to meet them, as many believed he had promised.

Livingstone denied that he had made any firm promise to meet them, and pointed out that the expedition had delayed him. He blamed the missionaries for going to the low country rather than looking for the higher ground he had recommended, and for not treating the fever in the way he had found effective. Some of what he said was fair. He had told the Society that the Makololo wanted to move to a healthier place, and that the mission should go with them. He had not told the missionaries to wait at Linyanti in the rainy season.

But it was also true that his own books had painted the country in brighter colours than it deserved, that his own enthusiasm had driven the mission, and that his promise to come to the Makololo, whatever its exact terms, had been part of the reason the Society chose that field. He did not, in his letters, show much sense of his own share in the tragedy. He defended himself, as he usually did, by explaining why others had been wrong. It is a pattern this book has seen before and will see again. Livingstone could bear almost any suffering of his own. He found it very hard to bear the thought that he had caused suffering to others.

A Vapour

The verse at the head of this chapter is from James’s warning to merchants who plan their year: today or tomorrow we will go into such a city, and spend a year there, and trade, and make a profit. “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. What is your life? For ye are a vapor that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.” James goes on: “For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall both live, and do this or that” (James 4:15, ASV).

The Helmores and the Prices went to Linyanti because they believed God had called them there. They planned carefully and travelled far. They did not know what would happen on the morrow. Their lives were indeed a vapour, and it vanished in a few weeks. Christians have always found such deaths hard to understand, and it is right that they should. There is no tidy explanation, and James does not offer one. He offers only humility: the reminder that our plans, however good, are held in God’s hand and not our own.

It is also worth remembering the dead whose names were not recorded. The African wagon drivers and servants who came north with the Helmores and the Prices, men from the mission stations of the south, died at Linyanti too, and the histories of the mission rarely name them. They had their own families and their own reasons for making the journey, and they paid the same price. The church has sometimes kept a list of its missionary martyrs that included only the Europeans. God keeps a fuller one.

That humility was what Livingstone most lacked in these years. He planned for continents. He spoke of the Zambezi, the Shire Highlands and the healthy plateaus as though he could see what would happen on them for a generation to come. He was right about some of it, and the missions that eventually took root in the Shire Highlands bore out part of his vision. But the graves at Linyanti were a warning that Africa did not bend to anyone’s plans, and that the cost of being wrong was paid in the lives of others. Livingstone does not seem to have heard the warning. The worst cost of his plans was still to come.

The Way Back

He left Sekeletu’s country in September 1860 and went back down the Zambezi to Tete. In the Kebrabasa gorge, where he insisted on taking canoes through the rapids, Kirk’s canoe overturned and Kirk lost his notes and much of his equipment, narrowly escaping with his life. Livingstone was not discouraged. At the end of 1860, at the mouth of the river, the Ma-Robert, which had been leaking for two years, finally sank in a sandbank. A new steamer, the Pioneer, sent out by the government at Livingstone’s request, arrived early in 1861. With it came the first party of the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa, led by its new bishop, Charles Frederick Mackenzie.

The young men of Cambridge and Oxford had answered Livingstone’s appeal. They had come to do the work he had begun.

It had lasted a few months. Who Was to Blame? The disaster caused bitter recriminations, and some of them fell on Livingstone. Roger Price believed that the Makololo had poisoned the party, and some of the Batswana long held the same belief. Livingstone was sure that they had died of malaria, and modern opinion largely agrees with him. But others asked why the missionaries had gone to Linyanti at all, and why they had gone in the wet season, and why Livingstone, who had urged the mission and knew the country, had not been there to meet them, as many believed he had promised. Livingstone denied that he had made any firm promise to meet them, and pointed out that the expedition had delayed him. He blamed the missionaries for going to the low country rather than looking for the higher ground he had recommended, and for not treating the fever in the way he had found effective. Some of what he said was fair. He had told the Society that the Makololo wanted to move to a healthier place, and that the mission should go with them. He had not told the missionaries to wait at Linyanti in the rainy season. But it was also true that his own books had painted the country in brighter colours than it deserved, that his own enthusiasm had driven the mission, and that his promise to come to the Makololo, whatever its exact terms, had been part of the reason the Society chose that field. He did not, in his letters, show much sense of his own share in the tragedy. He defended himself, as he usually did, by explaining why others had been wrong. It is a pattern this book has seen before and will see again. Livingstone could bear almost any suffering of his own. He found it very hard to bear the thought that he had caused suffering to others. A Vapour The verse at the head of this chapter is from James’s warning to merchants who plan their year: today or tomorrow we will go into such a city, and spend a year there, and trade, and make a profit. “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. What is your life? For ye are a vapor that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.” James goes on: “For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall both live, and do this or that” (James 4:15, ASV). The Helmores and the Prices went to Linyanti because they believed God had called them there. They planned carefully and travelled far. They did not know what would happen on the morrow. Their lives were indeed a vapour, and it vanished in a few weeks. Christians have always found such deaths hard to understand, and it is right that they should. There is no tidy explanation, and James does not offer one. He offers only humility: the reminder that our plans, however good, are held in God’s hand and not our own. It is also worth remembering the dead whose names were not recorded. The African wagon drivers and servants who came north with the Helmores and the Prices, men from the mission stations of the south, died at Linyanti too, and the histories of the mission rarely name them. They had their own families and their own reasons for making the journey, and they paid the same price. The church has sometimes kept a list of its missionary martyrs that included only the Europeans. God keeps a fuller one. That humility was what Livingstone most lacked in these years. He planned for continents. He spoke of the Zambezi, the Shire Highlands and the healthy plateaus as though he could see what would happen on them for a generation to come. He was right about some of it, and the missions that eventually took root in the Shire Highlands bore out part of his vision. But the graves at Linyanti were a warning that Africa did not bend to anyone’s plans, and that the cost of being wrong was paid in the lives of others. Livingstone does not seem to have heard the warning. The worst cost of his plans was still to come. The Way Back He left Sekeletu’s country in September 1860 and went back down the Zambezi to Tete. In the Kebrabasa gorge, where he insisted on taking canoes through the rapids, Kirk’s canoe overturned and Kirk lost his notes and much of his equipment, narrowly escaping with his life. Livingstone was not discouraged. At the end of 1860, at the mouth of the river, the Ma-Robert, which had been leaking for two years, finally sank in a sandbank. A new steamer, the Pioneer, sent out by the government at Livingstone’s request, arrived early in 1861. With it came the first party of the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa, led by its new bishop, Charles Frederick Mackenzie. The young men of Cambridge and Oxford had answered Livingstone’s appeal. They had come to do the work he had begun.

fields.title: Magomero
fields.body_html:
“The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah is upon me; because Jehovah hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound.”

— Isaiah 61:1, ASV

The Bishop

Charles Frederick Mackenzie was thirty-five, a Cambridge mathematician who had served as a clergyman in Natal and had been consecrated in Cape Town as the first bishop of the Universities’ Mission. He was cheerful, brave, humble and devout, and he admired Livingstone enormously. With him came a small party of clergy and laymen, among them Henry Burrup, Lovell Procter, Henry Rowley, Henry Scudamore, a doctor named John Dickinson, and a lay superintendent named Horace Waller, who would become one of Livingstone’s closest friends. They arrived at the mouth of the Zambezi early in 1861, expecting to be led to the healthy highlands Livingstone had described.

Livingstone did not take them there at once. He had become anxious to find a route into the interior that did not pass through Portuguese territory, where officials were involved in the slave trade and suspicious of British intentions. He insisted on first trying the Rovuma River, far to the north. The Pioneer went a short way up it and found it too shallow. Months were lost. Only in the middle of 1861 did the mission party reach the Shire Highlands, by the familiar route up the Shire.

The Slave Party at Mbame’s

In the middle of July 1861, as the expedition and the missionaries were walking up into the highlands, they arrived at the village of a chief named Mbame. As they rested there, a long line of captives came into the village: men, women and children, the men fastened by the neck in heavy forked sticks, the women and children tied together with ropes, driven by armed men who were blowing horns as if in triumph. When the drivers saw the Englishmen, they fled. Livingstone recognised one of them as a man who had belonged to a former Portuguese commandant of Tete.

The captives were released. The Englishmen cut the ropes and sawed through the slave-sticks, and the people, who had been expecting to be sold, were told that they were free. The Narrative describes how the captives knelt and clapped their hands in thanks. They told what had happened on the march. A woman, they said, had been killed because she could not carry both her load and her baby, and the baby had been killed with her. A man who had collapsed from exhaustion had been killed with an axe and left by the path. There were eighty-four of them, most of them women and children.

Among the children freed in these weeks, by the usual account, was a Yao boy of about ten or eleven named Chuma, who had been taken from his home and family by raiders. He was put into the care of the mission. Thirteen years later, he would help carry Livingstone’s body to the sea.

Liberty to the Captives

Jesus began his ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth by reading from the scroll of Isaiah the passage at the head of this chapter, and saying, “To-day hath this scripture been fulfilled in your ears” (Luke 4:21, ASV). In Luke’s version, the words are “to proclaim release to the captives … to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luke 4:18, ASV). Christians have argued for centuries about how literally to take them. Is Jesus speaking of freedom from sin, or freedom from chains?

At Mbame’s village, for once, the answer was both, and there was no need to choose. Eighty-four people who had been bound were set free, and the men who freed them did it in the name of Christ. It is one of the clearest moments in Livingstone’s life, and one of the few in which his campaign against the slave trade bore immediate, visible fruit. It was also, as the following weeks showed, the beginning of a terrible entanglement.

Fighting

The freed captives became the nucleus of the mission’s first settlement, at a place called Magomero, where a Mang’anja chief named Chigunda welcomed the missionaries. But the Shire Highlands were in turmoil. Groups of Yao people, themselves displaced by wars and famine to the east, were moving into the highlands, raiding Mang’anja villages and selling captives to the coastal traders. The Mang’anja were defenceless against them.

A few days after the release at Mbame’s, Livingstone, Mackenzie and their party came upon a Yao raiding band that had just burned a village. Livingstone tried to talk to them. The Yao, according to his account, opened fire, and the expedition fired back. Several of the raiders were killed. It was the first time that Livingstone had led men into a fight in which people were killed, and he was deeply troubled by it. He had always said that a missionary should never use force. Now he had.

He advised Mackenzie not to become involved in the fighting between the Yao and the Mang’anja. Then he went back to the river, to continue exploring Lake Nyasa. Mackenzie, left among people who begged him to protect them and who were being killed and enslaved before his eyes, decided that he could not stand by. He accompanied Mang’anja forces on several armed expeditions against Yao raiders, and freed more captives. A bishop of the Church of England had gone to war.

When the news reached Britain, there was outrage. Some blamed Mackenzie for betraying his calling. Some blamed Livingstone, who had led the first fight and then left the bishop to face its consequences. Livingstone, characteristically, defended his own conduct and was cautious in defending Mackenzie’s. It is hard, at this distance, to judge either man. They were trying to protect people from being enslaved, in a country without law, with no help from any government. Most Christians would not want to say that they should have done nothing. Most would also want to say that the consequences of using force were unpredictable and grave, and that the mission paid for them.

The Island at the Ruo

At the end of 1861, Livingstone arranged with Mackenzie to meet him in January at the point where the Ruo River joins the Shire, on a certain date. Mackenzie was expecting his sister and the wife of Henry Burrup to arrive from Britain, and Livingstone was going down to the coast to bring them up, together with Mary Livingstone and the sections of a new steamer, the Lady Nyassa, which Livingstone had paid for himself.

Livingstone did not keep the appointment. The Pioneer was delayed, and then went aground on sandbanks in the lower Shire. Mackenzie and Burrup, meanwhile, set out down the river by canoe to meet him. Their canoe overturned, and they lost their medicines. They waited on an island near the mouth of the Ruo, in the rainy season, without quinine. Both fell ill with fever. Mackenzie died on 31 January 1862. Burrup, who struggled back to Magomero, died soon after.

Livingstone heard the news when the Pioneer finally reached the Ruo. Mary was with him, and so were Miss Mackenzie and Mrs Burrup, who had come all the way from England to join their brother and husband and now learned that they were dead. Livingstone wrote in his journal that the death of Mackenzie would hurt the mission terribly, and that he feared it would hurt his own cause too. Some of the missionaries never forgave him for not keeping the appointment. He said that he could not help it. Both things were true.

Waller

The mission did not die at once, but it never recovered. More of its members died in the following year, including Scudamore and Dickinson. In 1863 a new bishop, William Tozer, arrived, decided that the Shire Highlands were impossible, and withdrew the mission first to a mountain station and then, in 1864, to Zanzibar. Livingstone was bitter about the retreat, and said so. In Zanzibar, the Universities’ Mission began again, among freed slaves and on the mainland opposite, and from there, over the next century, it built churches across what are now Tanzania, Malawi and Mozambique, with African priests and bishops. It returned to Lake Nyasa in the 1880s. The tragedy at Magomero was not the end of the story.

Horace Waller stayed until the end. When the mission withdrew, he refused to abandon the freed captives who had been in its care, and he took a number of them south to the Cape, where he found homes and work for them. He was a big, warm, practical man, and he and Livingstone formed a friendship that lasted the rest of Livingstone’s life. It was Waller who would edit Livingstone’s last journals, and who would sit with Chuma and Susi in England, writing down their account of his death.

Two of the freed boys stayed with Livingstone himself. Chuma and another boy, Wikatani, travelled with the expedition for the rest of its time on the Zambezi and the Shire, and became part of his household. Livingstone was fond of them both, and they of him. Their story, and Chuma’s especially, runs through the rest of this book. It is worth noticing that the most lasting fruit of the Magomero mission was not a church building or a station, but a handful of freed children who grew up into men and women of their own.

Isaiah’s great passage about liberty to the captives goes on to promise that those who were freed will “build the old wastes” and “raise up the former desolations” (Isaiah 61:4, ASV). The people freed at Mbame’s did not build the Shire Highlands. Many of them died, in the famine and fighting of the following years. But one of them, the boy Chuma, would live to carry the man who freed him a thousand miles through Africa. The prophet’s promise was kept, in a way the prophet’s readers would not have predicted.

fields.title: Shupanga
fields.body_html:
“Jehovah is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, And saveth such as are of a contrite spirit.”

— Psalm 34:18, ASV

Ma-Robert

This book has said a good deal about what Mary Livingstone suffered. It should also say who she was, because the story of her marriage has usually been told from her husband’s side, and she has too often appeared in it only as the woman who waited.

She was the daughter of missionaries and had grown up among the Batswana. She spoke Setswana from childhood, as her husband never quite did. At Mabotsa, Chonuane and Kolobeng she ran the infant school, taught sewing, made soap and candles and clothes, kept a household going in a country where every necessity had to be made by hand or carried hundreds of miles, and nursed the sick. She bore five children in less than six years, in mud-walled houses and ox-wagons, one of them on the bank of a river in the bush, and a sixth some years later. She went with her husband across the thirstland in 1850 and again in 1851, pregnant both times. The Batswana called her Ma-Robert, mother of Robert, in the respectful way of the country, and the people of Kolobeng remembered her with affection. She was not a frail Victorian lady dragged unwillingly into Africa. She was an African missionary’s daughter, tough and capable, who knew exactly what the life involved.

What broke her was not Africa. It was separation: the years in Britain without her husband, and then, after 1858, the years at Kuruman and in Scotland, away from him again, with her children divided between continents. In the letters of these years there are signs of depression, of anger, and of a faith that had grown dark. Those who saw her in Scotland in 1860 and 1861 found her unhappy and restless. She was determined to rejoin her husband. She left her children with relatives and friends in Scotland, among them her baby Anna Mary, and sailed for the Zambezi.

The Arrival

She arrived at the mouth of the Zambezi at the end of January 1862, on the brig Hetty Ellen, together with the sections of the Lady Nyassa, the steamer Livingstone had paid for out of the profits of his book to carry on Lake Nyasa, and with Miss Mackenzie and Mrs Burrup, who were coming to join the bishop and his colleague. With them, too, was a young Scottish minister, James Stewart, who had come to see whether the Free Church of Scotland should start a mission in the region.

It was the worst possible time. The rainy season had begun. The Pioneer, laden with the women, their baggage and part of the steamer, struggled for weeks up the Zambezi and the Shire against the shallows. When at last they reached the Ruo, they learned that Mackenzie and Burrup were dead. The two women went back down to the coast and home. Mary stayed.

The Lady Nyassa had to be assembled before it could be used, and Livingstone decided to put it together at Shupanga, on the south bank of the lower Zambezi, where there was an old Portuguese house and a good landing place. For three months the expedition worked there, in the heat and the rain, bolting together the iron hull. Mary lived in the house at Shupanga with her husband. For a few weeks, after so many years, they were together.

27 April 1862

Around the middle of April, Mary fell ill with fever. At first it seemed like the many fevers she had survived before. Then it grew worse. She became delirious, and the treatments that usually worked, Livingstone’s own quinine and purgatives, had no effect. Kirk, who was with them, did what he could. On 27 April 1862, in the evening, she died, with her husband beside her. She was forty-one.

She was buried the next day under a great baobab tree near the house at Shupanga, after a short service. A stone was later put up to mark the place.

The First Heavy Stroke

Livingstone was devastated. He had seen death all his life, as a doctor and a traveller, and he had lost his baby daughter Elizabeth at Kolobeng. But nothing had prepared him for this. His journal, as Blaikie printed it, records his grief with a simplicity that is more moving than any eloquence. What follows gives its substance closely, though not word for word.

He wrote that this was the first heavy blow he had suffered, and that it took away all his strength. He had wept over her, he wrote, and she deserved many tears. He had loved her when he married her, and the longer he lived with her the more he loved her. He thought of the children, who had all been tenderly attached to her, and asked God to pity them. He himself, he wrote, was left alone in the world by one whom he had felt to be a part of himself.

A few days later he wrote again, addressing her as though she could hear him. He remembered how often they had longed for a quiet home, since they had been cast adrift at Kolobeng. And he wrote a sentence that tells us more about him than any account of his journeys: for the first time in his life, he said, he felt willing to die.

The verse at the head of this chapter promises that God is near to the broken-hearted. Livingstone’s heart was broken at Shupanga, perhaps more completely than at any other time in his life. He did not lose his faith. His journal entries are full of prayer, of hope for heaven, of trust that Mary had gone a little before him. But they are also full of a grief that does not hurry to be comforted, and they show a man who had suddenly, too late, seen what his marriage had cost.

Regret

He wrote to Mary’s mother, and to his children, and to friends. In some of these letters he defended himself, saying that Mary had insisted on coming, as she had, and that he could not have prevented it. In others the defence slips, and something else comes through: the knowledge that she had come because he had left her alone so long that she could not bear it, and that she had died in the country he had brought her to, in the service of plans that had already gone wrong.

It would be cruel to blame him for her death. Malaria killed thousands of Europeans and countless Africans in the Zambezi valley, and there was no reliable protection against it. Mary chose to come, against advice, because she wanted to be with her husband. But it would be dishonest not to say that the shape of her whole married life, its separations and wanderings and loneliness, was given to it by his choices, and that those choices were made with too little thought for her. Livingstone knew that, at Shupanga. Whether he ever said it plainly, even to God, we cannot know. Grief and guilt are often too tangled for anyone to separate.

The psalm promises more than God’s nearness to the broken-hearted. It says that he “saveth such as are of a contrite spirit.” Contrition is grief that sees its own share in the wound. There are hints of contrition in Livingstone’s journal after Mary’s death. There is not much of it in the rest of his life. He went back to work, as he always did, and work was both his comfort and his escape.

The Grave Under the Baobab

Mary Livingstone was not the only person to die at Shupanga. The Zambezi valley in those years was full of graves, of missionaries and sailors and expedition members, and of the African people of the river, who died of fever, famine and the slave raids in far greater numbers. Mary’s grave was marked, and visited, and remembered. Most of the others were not.

But her grave deserves its marker. She was a missionary in her own right, born to the work and faithful in it for most of her life. She endured more than most of the heroes of the missionary movement, and she has been remembered less. Victorian accounts made her a footnote to her husband. Some later accounts made her a victim, or a problem. She was a woman who loved a difficult man and the Africa in which she had been born, who suffered greatly, whose faith wavered and, as far as we can tell, held, and who died where she had wanted to be, beside him.

Paul writes of believers “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Corinthians 6:10, ASV). It is a fair epitaph for Mary Moffat Livingstone. She had very little in this world. She gave a great deal. The church has been slow to say so.

Back to Work

Within days of the funeral, Livingstone was at work again on the Lady Nyassa. The steamer was launched in June 1862. But the river had fallen, and it could not be taken up the Shire until the rains returned at the end of the year. Livingstone went off to try the Rovuma again, hoping still for a route to Lake Nyasa outside Portuguese control. The expedition, which had lost its purpose at Kebrabasa, was now losing its members and its credit with the government at home. It had perhaps a year left to run, and the worst of that year would fall not on its members but on the people of the Shire valley.

At Mabotsa, Chonuane and Kolobeng she ran the infant school, taught sewing, made soap and candles and clothes, kept a household going in a country where every necessity had to be made by hand or carried hundreds of miles, and nursed the sick. She bore five children in less than six years, in mud-walled houses and ox-wagons, one of them on the bank of a river in the bush, and a sixth some years later. She went with her husband across the thirstland in 1850 and again in 1851, pregnant both times. The Batswana called her Ma-Robert, mother of Robert, in the respectful way of the country, and the people of Kolobeng remembered her with affection. She was not a frail Victorian lady dragged unwillingly into Africa. She was an African missionary’s daughter, tough and capable, who knew exactly what the life involved. What broke her was not Africa. It was separation: the years in Britain without her husband, and then, after 1858, the years at Kuruman and in Scotland, away from him again, with her children divided between continents. In the letters of these years there are signs of depression, of anger, and of a faith that had grown dark. Those who saw her in Scotland in 1860 and 1861 found her unhappy and restless. She was determined to rejoin her husband. She left her children with relatives and friends in Scotland, among them her baby Anna Mary, and sailed for the Zambezi. The Arrival She arrived at the mouth of the Zambezi at the end of January 1862, on the brig Hetty Ellen, together with the sections of the Lady Nyassa, the steamer Livingstone had paid for out of the profits of his book to carry on Lake Nyasa, and with Miss Mackenzie and Mrs Burrup, who were coming to join the bishop and his colleague. With them, too, was a young Scottish minister, James Stewart, who had come to see whether the Free Church of Scotland should start a mission in the region. It was the worst possible time. The rainy season had begun. The Pioneer, laden with the women, their baggage and part of the steamer, struggled for weeks up the Zambezi and the Shire against the shallows. When at last they reached the Ruo, they learned that Mackenzie and Burrup were dead. The two women went back down to the coast and home. Mary stayed. The Lady Nyassa had to be assembled before it could be used, and Livingstone decided to put it together at Shupanga, on the south bank of the lower Zambezi, where there was an old Portuguese house and a good landing place. For three months the expedition worked there, in the heat and the rain, bolting together the iron hull. Mary lived in the house at Shupanga with her husband. For a few weeks, after so many years, they were together. 27 April 1862 Around the middle of April, Mary fell ill with fever. At first it seemed like the many fevers she had survived before. Then it grew worse. She became delirious, and the treatments that usually worked, Livingstone’s own quinine and purgatives, had no effect. Kirk, who was with them, did what he could. On 27 April 1862, in the evening, she died, with her husband beside her. She was forty-one. She was buried the next day under a great baobab tree near the house at Shupanga, after a short service. A stone was later put up to mark the place. The First Heavy Stroke Livingstone was devastated. He had seen death all his life, as a doctor and a traveller, and he had lost his baby daughter Elizabeth at Kolobeng. But nothing had prepared him for this. His journal, as Blaikie printed it, records his grief with a simplicity that is more moving than any eloquence. What follows gives its substance closely, though not word for word. He wrote that this was the first heavy blow he had suffered, and that it took away all his strength. He had wept over her, he wrote, and she deserved many tears. He had loved her when he married her, and the longer he lived with her the more he loved her. He thought of the children, who had all been tenderly attached to her, and asked God to pity them. He himself, he wrote, was left alone in the world by one whom he had felt to be a part of himself. A few days later he wrote again, addressing her as though she could hear him. He remembered how often they had longed for a quiet home, since they had been cast adrift at Kolobeng. And he wrote a sentence that tells us more about him than any account of his journeys: for the first time in his life, he said, he felt willing to die. The verse at the head of this chapter promises that God is near to the broken-hearted. Livingstone’s heart was broken at Shupanga, perhaps more completely than at any other time in his life. He did not lose his faith. His journal entries are full of prayer, of hope for heaven, of trust that Mary had gone a little before him. But they are also full of a grief that does not hurry to be comforted, and they show a man who had suddenly, too late, seen what his marriage had cost. Regret He wrote to Mary’s mother, and to his children, and to friends. In some of these letters he defended himself, saying that Mary had insisted on coming, as she had, and that he could not have prevented it. In others the defence slips, and something else comes through: the knowledge that she had come because he had left her alone so long that she could not bear it, and that she had died in the country he had brought her to, in the service of plans that had already gone wrong. It would be cruel to blame him for her death. Malaria killed thousands of Europeans and countless Africans in the Zambezi valley, and there was no reliable protection against it. Mary chose to come, against advice, because she wanted to be with her husband. But it would be dishonest not to say that the shape of her whole married life, its separations and wanderings and loneliness, was given to it by his choices, and that those choices were made with too little thought for her. Livingstone knew that, at Shupanga. Whether he ever said it plainly, even to God, we cannot know. Grief and guilt are often too tangled for anyone to separate. The psalm promises more than God’s nearness to the broken-hearted. It says that he “saveth such as are of a contrite spirit.” Contrition is grief that sees its own share in the wound. There are hints of contrition in Livingstone’s journal after Mary’s death. There is not much of it in the rest of his life. He went back to work, as he always did, and work was both his comfort and his escape. The Grave Under the Baobab Mary Livingstone was not the only person to die at Shupanga. The Zambezi valley in those years was full of graves, of missionaries and sailors and expedition members, and of the African people of the river, who died of fever, famine and the slave raids in far greater numbers. Mary’s grave was marked, and visited, and remembered. Most of the others were not. But her grave deserves its marker. She was a missionary in her own right, born to the work and faithful in it for most of her life. She endured more than most of the heroes of the missionary movement, and she has been remembered less. Victorian accounts made her a footnote to her husband. Some later accounts made her a victim, or a problem. She was a woman who loved a difficult man and the Africa in which she had been born, who suffered greatly, whose faith wavered and, as far as we can tell, held, and who died where she had wanted to be, beside him. Paul writes of believers “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Corinthians 6:10, ASV). It is a fair epitaph for Mary Moffat Livingstone. She had very little in this world. She gave a great deal. The church has been slow to say so. Back to Work Within days of the funeral, Livingstone was at work again on the Lady Nyassa. The steamer was launched in June 1862. But the river had fallen, and it could not be taken up the Shire until the rains returned at the end of the year. Livingstone went off to try the Rovuma again, hoping still for a route to Lake Nyasa outside Portuguese control. The expedition, which had lost its purpose at Kebrabasa, was now losing its members and its credit with the government at home. It had perhaps a year left to run, and the worst of that year would fall not on its members but on the people of the Shire valley.

fields.title: Recalled
fields.body_html:
“we are pressed on every side, yet not straitened; perplexed, yet not unto despair; pursued, yet not forsaken; smitten down, yet not destroyed.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:8-9, ASV

The Valley of Death

When the rains came at the end of 1862, Livingstone took the Pioneer back up the Shire, towing the Lady Nyassa, which he intended to carry in pieces past the Murchison Cataracts and reassemble on Lake Nyasa. He found the valley transformed.

Three years earlier, the Shire valley had been one of the most fertile and populous places he had seen, with large villages and fields of cotton and grain. Now it was a wilderness. A severe drought had destroyed the harvests. At the same time, slave-raiding bands working for a Portuguese-African trader named Mariano, together with Yao raiders from the east, had swept through the region, burning villages and carrying off thousands of people. Those who escaped had fled into the hills or the marshes, where many starved. The Narrative records that the bodies of the dead floated down the river past the steamer every day, and that in the mornings the paddle wheels had to be cleared of corpses. The expedition members walked through deserted villages full of skeletons.

Livingstone was shattered by what he saw. The country he had opened, and had described to the world as the most promising field for missions and trade in Central Africa, had become a graveyard. He blamed the Portuguese, whose officials, he believed, protected and profited from the slave traders, and he wrote about them in the Narrative with an anger that caused a diplomatic incident. Some historians have since asked whether the expedition itself contributed to the disaster, by opening the Shire to outsiders, arming the Makololo who stayed behind, and drawing attention to the region. The drought and the raids had causes of their own that had nothing to do with Livingstone. But it is a painful fact that the valley he had hoped to save was devastated within a few years of his arrival.

Pressed on Every Side

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s description of his own ministry, written to a church that doubted him: pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not in despair; persecuted, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed. Paul does not pretend that he is not pressed or perplexed. He insists only that the pressure has not destroyed him, because the power at work in him is God’s, not his own.

The years 1862 to 1864 were the worst of Livingstone’s life up to that point. His wife was dead. His bishop was dead. His expedition was failing, his colleagues were leaving, and the country he loved was being destroyed before his eyes. He was perplexed, and he was struck down. He was not, by any account, destroyed. He kept a journal through it all, and it records grief and anger and much self-justification, but it also records prayer, and a stubborn refusal to believe that God had abandoned Africa or him. It was in these years that he began to say, more clearly than before, that his great work was not to found missions or open trade routes but to expose the slave trade to the world, so that the world would act to stop it.

The Recall

The expedition’s members were leaving one by one. Kirk and Charles Livingstone, both seriously ill, went home in May 1863. Kirk had served loyally for five years, and Livingstone parted from him on good terms, but Kirk’s private journals from the expedition record sharp criticisms of his leader’s judgement, his temper, and his treatment of the others. They were not written for publication, and they were not unfair.

In July 1863 a letter arrived from the Foreign Secretary, Lord Russell, recalling the expedition. The government had spent a great deal of money on it, and it had produced, as far as the government could see, a blocked river, a dead bishop, a failed mission, angry Portuguese allies and a series of resignations. The expedition was to end by the close of the year. Livingstone accepted the decision without protest, though he was bitterly hurt.

Before he left, he made one more journey on foot, in the second half of 1863, walking west and north from the Shire towards the slave routes west of Lake Nyasa. He wanted to see where the captives came from and where they went. He saw enough. When he came back, he took the two steamers down the Shire on the floods of early 1864 and handed the Pioneer over to the navy.

Across the Indian Ocean

That left the Lady Nyassa, his own ship, bought with the profits of Missionary Travels. He could have sold it to the Portuguese, but he would not, because he feared it would be used in the slave trade. He decided to sell it in India instead. In April 1864 he sailed it out of Zanzibar for Bombay, two and a half thousand miles across the Indian Ocean, in a small river steamer never meant for the open sea. His crew was a handful of Europeans and a group of young African men from the Zambezi, among them Chuma and Wikatani, the two boys freed in the Shire Highlands. Livingstone had never captained a ship. He navigated by his own observations, and the monsoon was about to break. The voyage took about six weeks. They arrived safely in June 1864, to the astonishment of everyone who saw the little ship come into Bombay harbour.

It was a reckless thing to do, and it was also one of the most remarkable feats of seamanship of the time. It is a fair picture of Livingstone at his best and worst: brave, resourceful, unwilling to let a principle go, and so careless of risk that he took a dozen other lives into his hands on a gamble. The African crew members, who had never been to sea before, showed as much courage as he did. Chuma and Wikatani were left in Bombay to be educated at a mission school, and Livingstone went on to England.

Robert

He reached London in July 1864. Waiting for him was the news of his eldest son.

Robert Livingstone was eighteen. He had been the most troubled of the children, angry, unsettled and resentful of his father’s absence. In 1863 he had been sent to Natal, in South Africa, with the intention that he would go on to join his father on the Zambezi. He did not go on. Instead he took ship for America and, in Boston, enlisted in the Union army in the American Civil War under a false name, Rupert Vincent. He wrote to his father that he had taken another name so as not to bring further dishonour on his family. He was wounded, captured, and taken to the Confederate prison at Salisbury, North Carolina, where he died in December 1864. His father did not learn the details of his death until later.

It is a heartbreaking story, and it belongs in a book about Livingstone, because Robert’s life was shaped by his father’s calling as surely as Mary’s was. Livingstone loved his children and wrote them many affectionate and earnest letters, full of advice and of prayers for their souls. But he was rarely present, and when he was, he was a stern and demanding father, as his own father had been. Paul wrote, “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but nurture them in the chastening and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4, ASV). Robert was provoked, and the nurture came mostly by letter. Livingstone grieved for him, and he seems to have blamed Robert more than himself. That, too, was characteristic.

Newstead

He spent most of the following year in Britain. For several months he lived at Newstead Abbey, the old home of Lord Byron in Nottinghamshire, as the guest of William Frederick Webb, a friend from his hunting days at Kolobeng. There, with his brother Charles, he wrote the Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi, published in 1865. It defended the expedition, attacked the Portuguese, and passed lightly over its quarrels and failures. It did not sell nearly as well as Missionary Travels.

He spent time with his children, who were growing up without him. In June 1865 his mother died in Hamilton, and he went north to bury her. He spoke at the British Association, attacking the Portuguese slave trade. And he began to plan his next journey.

The idea came from Sir Roderick Murchison and the Royal Geographical Society. The great unsolved question of African geography was the source of the Nile. Several explorers had claimed to find it, at Lake Victoria or Lake Albert, and the claims were disputed. Murchison suggested that Livingstone should go to the region between Lake Nyasa and Lake Tanganyika, find the watershed, and settle the question. Livingstone agreed, on one condition: that he should go as a missionary, not only as a geographer. He wrote that he would not go simply as a geographer, but as a missionary, and do geography by the way. He also intended to see the slave routes for himself, and to expose them.

The government gave him a small grant and the title of consul, without a salary, to the rulers of the interior. His friend James Young gave him a thousand pounds. In August 1865 he left Britain for the last time. He was fifty-two. He went by way of Paris, where he left his daughter Agnes at school, and Bombay, where he sold the Lady Nyassa at a loss and recruited men. In January 1866 he arrived at Zanzibar.

fields.title: The Sentence of Death
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”

— Hebrews 11:8, ASV

The Last Party

Livingstone left Zanzibar in March 1866 and landed near the mouth of the Rovuma River, on the mainland coast of what is now southern Tanzania. His party was an odd one. There were thirteen sepoys, Indian soldiers from the Bombay Marine Battalion, lent by the government of Bombay. There were ten men from the island of Anjouan in the Comoros, known as the Johanna men, under a headman named Musa, who had served on the Zambezi. There were nine African youths from a mission school at Nasik, in western India, run by the Church Missionary Society for children freed from slave ships. There were two men from Shupanga on the Zambezi, one of whom was Susi, who had worked for the expedition as a woodcutter and had sailed with Livingstone to Bombay. And there were the two Yao boys freed in the Shire Highlands, Chuma and Wikatani, now young men, who had come back from their school in Bombay to join him. With them came camels, buffaloes, mules and donkeys, which Livingstone wanted to test against the tsetse fly.

The animals died within months, of tsetse and of neglect. The sepoys, who had no wish to be in Africa and found the work hard, quarrelled with the others, mistreated the animals, lagged behind, and were eventually sent back to the coast. Livingstone was not a good manager of a mixed and unwilling party, and he admitted as much in his journal.

The Road of the Slaves

The route inland from the Rovuma to Lake Nyasa was one of the main slave roads of East Africa. Livingstone had come to see it, and he saw it. His journal records, day after day, the evidence along the path: a woman tied by the neck to a tree and left dead; others shot or stabbed and lying in the path; people who had collapsed under their loads and been killed, or simply abandoned to starve. He was told that the traders killed those who could not keep up, in anger at losing the money they had paid for them, and to frighten the others into marching faster. The country was depopulated. Villages had been burned, fields abandoned, and those who remained lived in fear.

He wrote it all down, without rhetoric, as evidence. He meant his journal to be read, and he meant it to make Britain act. In the years that followed, these plain entries did more for the campaign against the East African slave trade than any speech he made.

Wikatani and Musa

In August 1866, near the southern end of Lake Nyasa, Wikatani found his own people. He had been taken from this region as a child, and now he met relatives he had thought were lost to him. He asked to stay with them, and Livingstone let him go, with some sadness and with gifts. It was the kind of ending Livingstone had hoped the gospel might bring to freed captives: a return home, with something learned and nothing lost. We do not know what became of Wikatani afterwards.

A month later, Musa and the Johanna men deserted. They had heard rumours that the country ahead was being raided by the Ngoni, a militarised people who had moved north from southern Africa a generation before, and they were afraid. When Livingstone insisted on going on, they turned back. To excuse their desertion, they told the authorities at Zanzibar that Livingstone had been killed by the Ngoni, and they gave a detailed description of his death. The story was believed. Obituaries were published in Britain. The Royal Geographical Society sent out a small expedition under E. D. Young, a naval officer who had served on the Zambezi, which went up the Shire to Lake Nyasa in 1867 and found evidence that Livingstone had passed safely and that Musa had lied. By then Livingstone was hundreds of miles away.

The Medicine Chest

The party, now small, pressed north-west into the high country between Lake Nyasa and Lake Tanganyika. It was the rainy season. Food was scarce, because the slave raids had destroyed the harvests, and they were often hungry. Christmas 1866 was spent with almost nothing to eat. Livingstone grew thin and weak.

Then, on 20 January 1867, two porters who had joined the party on the way ran off in the night. They took with them, among other things, the box that held all of Livingstone’s medicines, including the quinine on which his life depended. He wrote in his journal that he felt as though he had now received the sentence of death, as poor Bishop Mackenzie had.

It was very nearly true. From that day, Livingstone had no defence against malaria, and it attacked him again and again. In the following months he suffered severe fevers, and on one occasion he lost consciousness and fell, waking to find that he could not remember what had happened. He was fifty-three, worn by twenty-five years of African travel, and he had just lost the means of keeping himself alive.

He did not turn back. He went on, with Susi, Chuma, the Nasik youths and whatever porters he could find, towards the great lakes of the interior. The verse at the head of this chapter describes Abraham, who went out “not knowing whither he went.” Livingstone knew, in one sense, exactly where he was going: north, to the watershed, to find the source of the Nile. In another sense he had no idea. He did not know if he would live. He did not know whether anyone at home knew that he was alive. He went on, he believed, because God had called him, and because the slave trade had to be seen and written down.

With the Traders

Here the story takes a turn that the Victorian biographies passed over quickly, and that modern historians have rightly emphasised. Without medicines, without money, without enough men or goods to pay his way, Livingstone could not travel alone in the interior. The only people who could protect and feed him were the very people he had come to expose: the Arab-Swahili traders from Zanzibar who dealt in ivory and slaves.

From 1867 onwards, he travelled for long periods with their caravans, ate their food, accepted their help and their hospitality, and depended on their goodwill. One of them was a powerful young trader named Hamed bin Muhammed, later famous under the name Tippu Tip, who would become the most powerful man in the eastern Congo. Livingstone found many of the traders courteous and generous to him personally, and he wrote of their kindness. He also watched what they did to the people of the country, and recorded it.

It was a terrible position for a man whose life’s cause was the destruction of the slave trade. He could not stop what he saw. He could only write it down, and accept the protection of those who did it. He was not complicit in their trade. But he was dependent on it, and he knew it. The man who had set captives free at Mbame’s village now ate at the table of the slavers, because otherwise he would die.

Lakes

In April 1867 he reached the southern end of Lake Tanganyika. In November he reached Lake Mweru, to the west, and visited the capital of the Lunda king Kazembe, a powerful ruler whose court had been visited by Portuguese travellers decades before. In July 1868 he reached Lake Bangweulu, a vast shallow lake surrounded by swamps, the farthest south of the great lakes of the region. He was the first European to describe it. He did not know that he would die near its shores five years later.

He was now convinced that the rivers flowing out of this region, through Lake Bangweulu and Lake Mweru and northward as the great river called the Lualaba, were the true sources of the Nile. His party was an odd one. There were thirteen sepoys, Indian soldiers from the Bombay Marine Battalion, lent by the government of Bombay. There were ten men from the island of Anjouan in the Comoros, known as the Johanna men, under a headman named Musa, who had served on the Zambezi. fields.title: Nyangwe
fields.body_html:
“O Jehovah, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save.”

— Habakkuk 1:2, ASV

Manyema

The country west of Lake Tanganyika, which the traders called Manyema, was in 1869 the new frontier of the ivory and slave trade. The Arab-Swahili traders from Zanzibar had only recently pushed into it, and they were taking ivory by trade where they could and by force where they could not. The people of Manyema, who had no guns, were raided, robbed and enslaved. Livingstone went into this country in the second half of 1869, with a handful of followers, in the company of traders, looking for the Lualaba.

He liked many of the people he met there, and his journal records their gardens, their markets, their crafts and their courtesy, as well as the fear in which they lived. The traders told lurid stories about the Manyema to justify how they treated them, and Livingstone sometimes repeated those stories and sometimes doubted them. What he did not doubt was that the people had done nothing to deserve what was being done to them.

It was the most miserable period of his life. He was ill again and again. In 1870, at a place called Bambarre, his feet broke out in ulcers that ate into the flesh, so that he could not walk, and he was laid up for months in a hut. Most of the porters who had come with him had deserted. For a time only three of his followers stayed with him: Susi, Chuma, and a young man from the Nasik school called Gardner. They nursed him, foraged for food, and kept him alive.

In those months of illness, with nothing else to read, he read the Bible through four times. His journal records the readings, and the thoughts they prompted. It was the longest sustained reading of Scripture in his life, and it was done in a hut in Manyema, by a lame and lonely man who had no idea whether anyone outside Africa knew he was alive.

Men From Zanzibar

Early in 1871 a party of men arrived from Zanzibar to join him. They had been hired by an Indian merchant on behalf of the British consulate, where Livingstone’s old colleague John Kirk was now the consul. They were slaves of Indian merchants, hired out by their owners, and they had no wish to go into the interior with a sick old man. They were insubordinate from the start, refused to go where he wanted, and stirred up trouble with the people of the country. Livingstone came to believe that Kirk had sent him bad men deliberately, or at least carelessly, and his letters from this time are full of bitter accusations against his former friend. They were unfair. Kirk had done what he could from Zanzibar. But Livingstone was ill, isolated and suspicious, and the old pattern of blaming others was stronger than ever.

With these men, in March 1871, he reached Nyangwe, a large market town on the bank of the Lualaba. The river was wide and flowed north. Livingstone was sure that it was the Nile. He needed canoes to follow it, and he spent months trying to buy them, without success. The traders did not want him to go further, and the people of the town, who were afraid of everyone from the east, would not sell to him.

15 July 1871

Nyangwe held a great market every few days, to which hundreds of people, most of them women, came from the surrounding country to buy and sell food, pottery, cloth and other goods. On 15 July 1871 Livingstone went to the market as usual. By his published account, a quarrel broke out over a fowl. Then the men of a trader named Dugumbe, who had recently arrived at Nyangwe with a large armed following, opened fire on the crowd.

The massacre that followed was the most terrible thing Livingstone ever saw. The gunmen fired into the market and along the river bank. People fled to the river and tried to escape in canoes, which overturned in the crush, and many who could not swim were drowned. The gunmen went on firing at those in the water. Then Dugumbe’s men crossed the river and burned the villages on the other side. Livingstone estimated that between three and four hundred people were killed, most of them women. Others have given different numbers. Whatever the count, it was a slaughter of unarmed people on a market day.

His published journal records his horror and his grief, his conviction that he had witnessed something from hell, and his prayer. As he wrote, he could hear the wailing for the dead from across the river. He wrote a short prayer that God’s kingdom would come. It is the petition of the Lord’s Prayer, but it comes here as a cry, almost a protest: a man who had spent his life asking God to bring his kingdom to Africa, watching the opposite of the kingdom come in front of him, and crying out for God to act.

How Long?

The prophet Habakkuk began his book with the same cry. “O Jehovah, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save.” Habakkuk had seen injustice in his own people, and then he was told that God was sending the Babylonians, a people more violent still. He did not understand. He stood on his watchtower and waited for an answer, and the answer he was given was not an explanation, but a promise: “the righteous shall live by his faith,” and “the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah, as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:4, 14, ASV).

Livingstone was given no explanation for Nyangwe either. He could do nothing for the dead. He could not stop Dugumbe. He could only write what he had seen, and send it to the world, and pray. He did all three. His account of the massacre reached Britain in 1872 and was printed widely. It shocked the public and strengthened the campaign that was already gathering in Parliament against the East African slave trade, and it contributed to the pressure that led, in 1873, to the closing of the great slave market at Zanzibar. It was, in the end, perhaps the most effective thing he ever wrote.

What the Field Diary Showed

For more than a century, Livingstone’s account of Nyangwe was known only from the Last Journals, edited by Waller from the large journal that Livingstone wrote up from his pocket notebooks. In the early twenty-first century, scholars working on the Livingstone Online project used spectral imaging to read his original field diary for 1871, written in improvised ink on scraps of newspaper and faded almost to nothing. What they found complicated the story.

The field diary, written day by day, shows that the situation at Nyangwe before the massacre was more tangled than the published version suggests. Livingstone had been travelling and living under the protection of traders, including men associated with Dugumbe. The men from Zanzibar who were supposed to be his own followers had been involved in violence against local people in the weeks before. He seems to have feared, in the days after the massacre, that he himself would be associated with what had happened, and that the people of the country would see him as one of the traders. The later journal, written up with more care, gives a clearer and more morally straightforward account, in which Livingstone is purely a horrified observer.

The historians who studied the diary did not conclude that Livingstone had lied about the massacre, which certainly happened as a massacre, or that he bore responsibility for it. They did conclude that the published account was shaped, by Livingstone and then by Waller, to present him as more separate from the traders than he really was. It is a sobering finding. It is also, in a way, a very human one. A man who has seen something terrible, and has been closer to it than he wishes, will often tell the story in a way that puts more distance between himself and the evil. That is not the same as lying. But it is not the whole truth either, and a biography that wants the whole truth has to say so.

The Way Back

After the massacre Livingstone could not stay at Nyangwe. He would not travel with Dugumbe’s men, and without them he could not go north. He turned back towards Ujiji, sick and broken in spirit. On the way, in August 1871, his party was ambushed in the forest by people who took them for slave traders, and he narrowly escaped death three times in a single day: a spear thrown at him missed him by inches, another passed close behind him, and a great tree, set on fire and cut nearly through, crashed down a yard from where he walked. He recorded each escape in his journal, and thanked God.

He reached Ujiji in late October 1871, according to his own reckoning, which by then had gone astray by several weeks. He was a skeleton. He found that the goods that had been sent there for him had been sold off by the man left in charge of them, who had assumed that he was dead. He had almost nothing left. He sat down in his house at Ujiji, among the few faithful men who had brought him back, and wondered how he would live.

He did not know that a young American journalist, with a large, well-supplied caravan, was marching towards Ujiji at that moment, looking for him.

fields.title: “I Presume”
fields.body_html:
“As cold waters to a thirsty soul, So is good news from a far country.”

— Proverbs 25:25, ASV

The Journalist

Henry Morton Stanley was not, as he liked to suggest, an American. He had been born John Rowlands in north Wales in 1841, the illegitimate son of a young mother who did not keep him. He grew up partly in a workhouse, went to sea as a teenager, landed in New Orleans, took the name of a merchant who befriended him, fought on both sides of the American Civil War, and became a newspaper correspondent. In 1869, according to his own account, James Gordon Bennett, the owner of the New York Herald, summoned him and told him to go and find Livingstone, whatever it cost. Bennett wanted a story. Livingstone had not been heard from for years, and many believed he was dead.

Stanley took his time. He covered other assignments first, and reached Zanzibar only in January 1871. There, with Bennett’s money, he assembled a large and well-equipped caravan, with nearly two hundred porters and soldiers, and set out for the interior in March. It was a hard march. Stanley drove his men brutally, with the whip, and several died on the way. He was ill himself, and fought his way through a war between Arab-Swahili traders and the forces of a chief named Mirambo. Late in 1871 he approached Ujiji.

An Englishman

Livingstone’s journal records how the news reached him. Susi came running as fast as he could, gasped out that he had seen an Englishman, and ran off again to meet the stranger. Stanley’s caravan was marching into Ujiji with the American flag at its head and the porters firing their guns in salute. The whole town came out to see.

Stanley’s account of the meeting is one of the most famous passages in the literature of travel. He describes walking through the crowd towards a pale, grey-bearded old man in a faded blue cap and a red-sleeved waistcoat, standing in front of his house with a few of his men. He wanted to run to him, he says, and to embrace him, but he did not know how an Englishman would receive such a thing. So, in Stanley’s own account, he walked up deliberately, took off his hat, and said, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?”

Livingstone said yes, by Stanley’s account, with a kind smile, lifting his cap slightly. They shook hands, and Stanley thanked God that he had been permitted to see him. Livingstone replied that he was thankful to be there to welcome him.

The four famous words have been quoted, parodied and repeated for a century and a half. It is worth knowing how fragile our evidence for them is. They come from Stanley alone. The pages of his diary for the days around the meeting are missing, and his first newspaper report and his book do not give exactly the same wording. Even the date is uncertain.
