Stanley had brought food, medicine, cloth, letters and news. Livingstone had been near starvation, and within days, with good food and company, he began to recover. The two men spent about four months together. He described Livingstone’s gentleness, his humour, his patience, his love of a joke, his kindness to his men and theirs to him, and his refusal to complain. And he described his faith. Livingstone’s religion, Stanley wrote, was not of the theoretical kind, but a constant, earnest, sincere practice, neither demonstrative nor loud, but quiet and practical and always at work. Every Sunday Livingstone held a short service for his men. He read the Bible daily. He did not preach at Stanley, but Stanley was moved by what he saw.

On 14 March 1872, Stanley left Unyanyembe for the coast. fields.title: Chitambo’s Village
fields.body_html:
“Precious in the sight of Jehovah Is the death of his saints.”

— Psalm 116:15, ASV

The Company

On 25 August 1872, Livingstone left Unyanyembe for the last time. His plan was to go south along the eastern side of Lake Tanganyika, then round the southern end of Lake Bangweulu, and then north-west to the Lualaba, to trace the fountains that he still believed fed the Nile. He reckoned that it would take a few months.

His company numbered something over sixty people. At its heart were the men who had been with him for years: Susi, who had joined him on the Zambezi; Chuma, freed as a boy in the Shire Highlands; and a few others who had come back with him from Manyema. With them were the young men from Nasik, among them Jacob Wainwright, Carus Farrar and Matthew Wellington. There was a boy named Majwara, who served Livingstone personally and slept at the door of his hut. There were women too, the wives of some of the men, among them Halima, the wife of one of the Shupanga men, who cooked for Livingstone and whom he valued highly, and a young woman called Ntaoeka. And there were the porters hired at the coast. These people are named here because, in the next nine months, they would decide what happened to David Livingstone, living and dead.

The Swamps

The journey went badly from the start. Livingstone’s geography was confused; his calculations of position had gone wrong, and he thought Lake Bangweulu lay farther east than it did. The party went too far east and found itself, when the rains came at the end of 1872, approaching the lake from the wrong side, in a vast country of swamps and flooded grassland.

From January to April 1873 they waded. For days on end the path lay through water, sometimes knee-deep, sometimes waist-deep, sometimes up to the chest, with the rain falling on them and leeches in the water. They crossed rivers by canoe when they could find canoes, and by wading when they could not. The local people were often unwilling to help, and sometimes hostile, because they had suffered from slave raiders. Food was scarce. The porters grew sullen and some deserted. And Livingstone was dying.

He had suffered for years from dysentery, and now he began to bleed heavily from the bowels. He grew weaker and weaker from loss of blood. He could no longer walk far. By April he could not walk at all, and the men carried him in a litter, a kitanda, made of a framework of poles with grass and a blanket, slung between two men. Even that jolting was agony. His journal entries, which had always been full and careful, grow shorter and shorter, and the handwriting falters.

On 19 March 1873 he turned sixty, in the swamps. He wrote a few lines of thanks to God for sparing him so far on the journey of life, wondered whether he could still hope for success when so many obstacles had arisen, and prayed that Satan would not prevail over him. Even now, his mind was on finishing the work.

The Last Entries

On 21 April he tried to ride a donkey, but was forced to lie down, and was carried back to the village exhausted. On 27 April he wrote his last entry. It begins, “Knocked up quite, and remain—recover—sent to buy milch-goats,” and notes that they were on the banks of the Molilamo. After that, nothing. The notebook, in Waller’s phrase, dropped from his hand.

On 29 April the men carried him across the Molilamo River and to the village of a chief named Chitambo, in a district called Ilala, south of Lake Bangweulu in what is now Zambia. They built him a hut, and laid him in it on a bed of sticks and grass. Chitambo came to visit him on 30 April, but Livingstone was too ill to talk, and asked him to come back the next day.

The Last Night

What we know of that night comes from the men who were there, as they later told it to Horace Waller in England, and as he printed it in the Last Journals. Their account is the source of everything that follows. It was given by men who loved Livingstone and who had every reason to remember him well, and it was shaped by Waller, who loved him too. It is not a record taken at the time. It is testimony, and it should be read as testimony: precious, and not beyond question.

About eleven o’clock at night, Susi said, Livingstone called him, and asked him about the noise he could hear in the village, which was the people shouting to scare buffaloes away from their crops. A little later he asked whether this was the Luapula River, and Susi told him that they were in Chitambo’s village, near the Molilamo. He asked how many days it was to the Luapula, and Susi said he thought three days. Livingstone sighed and seemed to fall asleep. Around midnight he called Susi again, asked for hot water and for his medicine chest, and with great difficulty chose a dose of calomel. Then, in Susi’s memory, he told Susi that all was well and that he could go out now. Those were the last words anyone heard him say.

4 a.m.

The boy Majwara was sleeping at the door of the hut, as he always did. Some time before dawn he woke and saw his master kneeling by the bed. He thought Livingstone was praying, and did not disturb him. Later he looked again, and saw that he had not moved. Frightened, he went and woke Susi, Chuma and some of the others. He told them, in the words Waller recorded, that when he had lain down Livingstone had been just as he was now, and that it was because he did not move that he feared he was dead.

The men came to the hut and looked in. Livingstone was kneeling by the side of the bed, his body stretched forward, his head buried in his hands upon the pillow. For a minute they watched him, and saw no sign of breathing. Then Matthew Wellington went softly forward and laid his hands on Livingstone’s cheeks. The face was cold. He had been dead for some time.

The Date

The date of his death is not certain. Waller, working from the men’s account and the last journal entries, gave it as 1 May 1873, and that is the date on his grave in Westminster Abbey and in most books. But the men themselves, when they carved an inscription on a tree at Chitambo’s village a few days later, gave the date as 4 May, and some of the early reports from the coast gave that date too. Livingstone’s own dating had been unreliable for years, and the men were keeping their own count. Most historians accept 1 May, but the disagreement cannot now be settled, and it is a small sign of how much of this last scene rests on the memories of people who had other things on their minds than calendars.

On His Knees

The picture of Livingstone dying on his knees in prayer became the most famous image of his life. It was painted, engraved, preached on and printed in countless books. It made him, for the Victorian public, the perfect missionary saint: a man who had given everything, and who died in the act of prayer, alone in the heart of Africa.

It is right to hold the picture carefully. It comes from the testimony of Majwara, Susi, Chuma and Matthew, filtered through Waller. Some modern writers have suggested that a man bleeding to death from dysentery might have knelt by the bed for other reasons, or simply collapsed. We cannot know. What we can say is that the men who found him believed that he had died praying, and that this belief fits everything they knew of him. He had prayed every day of his life. He had knelt by his bed every night that he could. If he knelt there that night, in his last weakness, it would have been in character. If he died there, it was in a posture he had taken ten thousand times before.

The psalm at the head of this chapter says that the death of God’s saints is precious in his sight. The psalmist was not saying that their deaths are beautiful, or that they come without pain. He was saying that God notices, and cares, and counts them costly. Livingstone died in a grass hut, in a swamp, far from his family, of a slow and painful disease, with his work unfinished and his great geographical theory wrong. By the measure of the world, it was a miserable end. By the measure of the psalm, it was precious. God was not absent from Chitambo’s village. He was present in the faith of a dying man, whatever his posture, and in the love of the people who sat with him.

The Watchers

That is the last thing to notice about this night. Livingstone did not die alone. The legend of the lonely hero in the heart of Africa forgets that there were sixty people around him, and that a handful of them had stayed with him for years, through famine and fever and the swamps, when they could easily have gone home. A boy slept at his door. A man answered his call at midnight and helped him find his medicine. A young man from Nasik laid his hands gently on his face. They were his family at the end, in a way his own children could not be.

In the morning, the men gathered outside the hut and talked about what to do. They were hundreds of miles from the coast, in hostile country, with a dead white man who was famous, as they knew, in a world they had only glimpsed. Some of the Nasik men could read and write; most of the others could not. No one would have blamed them if they had buried him there and gone home. What they decided to do instead is one of the great stories of loyalty in the history of Africa, and it is theirs, not his.

Some modern writers have suggested that a man bleeding to death from dysentery might have knelt by the bed for other reasons, or simply collapsed. We cannot know. What we can say is that the men who found him believed that he had died praying, and that this belief fits everything they knew of him. He had prayed every day of his life. He had knelt by his bed every night that he could. If he knelt there that night, in his last weakness, it would have been in character. If he died there, it was in a posture he had taken ten thousand times before. The psalm at the head of this chapter says that the death of God’s saints is precious in his sight. Livingstone died in a grass hut, in a swamp, far from his family, of a slow and painful disease, with his work unfinished and his great geographical theory wrong. By the measure of the world, it was a miserable end. By the measure of the psalm, it was precious. God was not absent from Chitambo’s village. He was present in the faith of a dying man, whatever his posture, and in the love of the people who sat with him. The Watchers That is the last thing to notice about this night. Livingstone did not die alone. A boy slept at his door. A man answered his call at midnight and helped him find his medicine. A young man from Nasik laid his hands gently on his face. They were his family at the end, in a way his own children could not be. In the morning, the men gathered outside the hut and talked about what to do. They were hundreds of miles from the coast, in hostile country, with a dead white man who was famous, as they knew, in a world they had only glimpsed. Some of the Nasik men could read and write; most of the others could not. No one would have blamed them if they had buried him there and gone home. What they decided to do instead is one of the great stories of loyalty in the history of Africa, and it is theirs, not his.

fields.title: Faithful Hands
fields.body_html:
“And devout men buried Stephen, and made great lamentation over him.”

— Acts 8:2, ASV

The Council

The men who gathered outside the hut at Chitambo’s village on the morning of Livingstone’s death had several choices. They could bury him where he lay, as Africans and Europeans alike were usually buried in the interior, and go home. They could leave his body and his papers with the chief and walk away. Or they could try to take him to the coast, more than a thousand miles away, through country that was often hostile, where the carrying of a corpse would arouse fear and suspicion in every village they passed.

They decided to take him home. According to the account they later gave Waller, they met together and agreed to put themselves under the leadership of Susi and Chuma, the two men who had been with Livingstone longest, and to obey them as they had obeyed him. They agreed that the body would be preserved and carried to Zanzibar, together with his papers, instruments and belongings, so that his people could bury him in his own country and his work would not be lost. Nobody ordered them to do it. There was no one to order them. They chose it.

It is impossible to know all their reasons. They loved him; that much is clear from everything they said and did. Some of them also understood that he was an important man in the British world, and that it would go hard with them if they returned to Zanzibar without his body and his papers, and were suspected of having harmed him. Both motives may have been at work. Neither diminishes what they did.

The Heart in Africa

At first they kept the death secret from the people of the village, fearing that the chief would impose heavy fines or that the villagers would be alarmed by a death among strangers. When Chitambo learned of it, however, he behaved with great courtesy. He came with his people to mourn, with drums and the firing of guns, in the manner of the country, and he allowed the men to build a separate enclosure outside the village where the body could be prepared.

The men had no embalmer. One of them, Farijala, had worked for a doctor in Zanzibar and had watched him at work. With the help of Carus Farrar, he opened the body and removed the heart and other internal organs. These were placed in a tin box and buried in the earth beneath a large mpundu tree near the hut. A short service was read over them; Jacob Wainwright, who could read English, is said to have read the burial service from the Book of Common Prayer. Then Jacob carved an inscription in the bark of the tree, giving Livingstone’s name and the date of his death, as the men reckoned it, 4 May 1873, together with some words of their own.

The body was filled with salt and laid out to dry in the sun for about two weeks. Then it was wrapped in calico, enclosed in a cylinder of bark, sewn up in sailcloth, tarred against the weather, and lashed to a pole so that two men could carry it. His papers, journals, maps, instruments and the rest of his belongings were packed into loads.

The burial of his heart in Africa has become one of the best-loved details of his story, and it is often said that his African friends buried it there because his heart belonged to Africa. The Royal Geographical Society, which still holds the section of the tree with Jacob’s inscription, records that this is what his companions said. It may also have been a practical necessity of preserving the body. Both things can be true. It is fitting, whatever the reason, that the heart of the man who loved Africa, and whose love was often clumsy and costly, should lie in African earth, buried by African hands.

A Thousand Miles

The journey to the coast took about five months. The company went north-east, back past Lake Bangweulu, across the high country towards Lake Tanganyika, and then east towards Unyanyembe. They suffered illness, hunger and hostility. Several of them died on the way. In some places the people would not let them pass with a corpse, and the men resorted to a stratagem: they made up a bundle that looked like a body, sent it back along the path as if returning it for burial, and disguised the real body as an ordinary bale of goods. At least once they had to fight their way through a village.

In October 1873, near Unyanyembe, they met an English expedition under a naval officer named Verney Lovett Cameron, which the Royal Geographical Society had sent out to relieve Livingstone. Cameron and his companions learned from Susi and Chuma that the man they had come to help was dead. Cameron advised them to bury the body there, saying that it would be safer and simpler. The men refused. They had carried him this far, and they would carry him to the sea. Cameron took some of Livingstone’s instruments, and the men went on.

They reached the coast at Bagamoyo, opposite Zanzibar, in February 1874, nine months after his death. They handed the body and the papers over to the acting British consul. A British warship took the body across to Zanzibar.

Devout Men

The verse at the head of this chapter records the burial of Stephen, the first Christian martyr, stoned to death in Jerusalem. It is a single sentence in the book of Acts, and it is one of the tenderest in the New Testament. “And devout men buried Stephen, and made great lamentation over him.” Luke does not name them. We do not know who they were, whether apostles or ordinary believers, or how they recovered the body. We know only that they loved him and grieved for him and buried him with honour, at some risk to themselves.

The men and women who carried Livingstone to the coast were not all Christians, though several of them were or would become so. They were, in the sense that matters here, devout: devoted to the man they had followed and to the duty they had taken on. Unlike the men who buried Stephen, many of them can be named, and they should be. Susi and Chuma led them. Jacob Wainwright, Carus Farrar and Matthew Wellington were among the young men from Nasik. Majwara was the boy at the door. Halima cooked for the company, as she had for Livingstone. Farijala prepared the body. There were dozens of others whose names are in the lists that Waller compiled and that later scholars have gathered, and some whose names are lost.

The inscription on Livingstone’s grave in Westminster Abbey begins, “Brought by faithful hands over land and sea.” The hands over land were theirs.

England

When the body reached Zanzibar, the British authorities paid off most of the men and sent them home. They were given their wages and a few gifts. Very few of them were taken to England for the funeral. Only Jacob Wainwright went with the body, on the ship that carried it to Southampton. Many people have since thought it a shameful thing that the men who had carried Livingstone a thousand miles were left at Zanzibar while British dignitaries carried him the last few hundred yards. It was.

The body reached Southampton in April 1874 and was taken by special train to London, where it lay at the rooms of the Royal Geographical Society. There it was examined by the surgeon Sir William Fergusson and others, in the presence of friends who had known Livingstone, among them his father-in-law, Robert Moffat. They found in the upper left arm the false joint left by the lion at Mabotsa thirty years before, and were satisfied that the body was his. The men who had carried it had never doubted it.

The funeral took place on 18 April 1874. Jacob Wainwright walked among the eight pallbearers, the only African among them, beside Stanley and old friends and companions of Livingstone’s travels. The Abbey records that he threw a palm branch into the grave. A choirboy who was present is said to have remembered, years later, seeing Stanley restrain him at the graveside, overcome with grief.

Susi and Chuma came to Britain some weeks later, after the funeral, through the efforts of Livingstone’s friends. They visited his family, met many of those who had known him, and spent time with Horace Waller at Newstead Abbey, helping him to sort Livingstone’s papers and telling him, day after day, the story of the last months and the long journey. Waller wrote it down, and it became the closing chapters of the Last Journals. Almost everything we know of Livingstone’s death and of the journey to the coast comes from their memories.

What Became of Them

Chuma went back to Zanzibar and worked for the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa, the mission whose first bishop had died at the Ruo in 1862, and later led caravans for other expeditions into the interior. He died of tuberculosis in Zanzibar in 1882, still a young man. Susi also returned to Zanzibar and worked for the same mission, as a trusted helper of its bishops on their journeys. In 1886, after years of instruction, he was baptised, and he took the name David, after his old master. He died in 1891. Jacob Wainwright returned to East Africa and worked with the Church Missionary Society; he died in 1892.

Their later lives were not famous. They were faithful. In that, they were more like the real Livingstone than the legend ever was.

fields.title: A Grain of Wheat
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.”

— John 12:24, ASV

The Market Closed

On 5 June 1873, about a month after Livingstone’s death at Chitambo’s village, and long before anyone outside the interior knew of it, the Sultan of Zanzibar, Barghash bin Said, signed a treaty with Britain. It made the export of slaves by sea from his mainland territories illegal, and it closed the great public slave market of Zanzibar, through which tens of thousands of people from the interior had passed every year. The treaty was the work of many hands: a British government mission led by Sir Bartle Frere, the persistent pressure of the consul at Zanzibar, John Kirk, Livingstone’s old colleague, and years of campaigning in Britain. The campaign had been fed, more than by anything else, by Livingstone’s letters and journals, and especially by his account of the massacre at Nyangwe. He did not live to know of it.

The treaty did not end the slave trade in East Africa. The overland trade went on for years, and slavery itself continued on the island and the coast until the end of the century and beyond. But it was the beginning of the end, and it came because people in Britain had been made to see what Livingstone had seen. All he could add in his solitude, he had written, was a prayer for blessing on anyone who would help heal the open sore. The prayer was being answered while he was dying.

In September 1873 the Universities’ Mission to Central Africa bought the site of the old market, and on Christmas Day that year the foundation stone of a church was laid there. Christ Church Cathedral, Zanzibar, stands on the place where people were bought and sold. Tradition says that its altar stands where the whipping post once stood. Whether or not that is exact, the building is a sermon in stone, and it was built by the mission that Livingstone’s Cambridge lecture had called into being.

The Missions

His death did what his life had not. The news of how he had died, and of how his men had carried him home, moved British Christians as nothing else could have done. Within a few years, missions were founded in the regions he had explored. In 1875 the Free Church of Scotland established a mission on Lake Nyasa, named Livingstonia, which under the leadership of Robert Laws became a great centre of education, training African teachers, ministers, doctors and craftsmen for half a century. In 1876 the Church of Scotland founded a mission in the Shire Highlands and called it Blantyre, after his birthplace; the town that grew up around it is now one of the principal cities of Malawi. The Universities’ Mission returned to Lake Nyasa in the 1880s. The London Missionary Society sent missionaries to Lake Tanganyika. Others followed.

These missions had their own failures, and their own entanglement with what came after. But out of them grew churches that are now among the largest and most vigorous in Africa, led by African ministers and bishops, worshipping in African languages, and sending out their own missionaries. It is worth saying again what this book has said several times: those churches were built mostly by African evangelists, teachers and catechists, men and women whose names are not in the history books, carrying the gospel to their own people in ways that no foreign missionary could. Livingstone had argued, in his first years at Kuruman, that this was how Africa would be evangelised. He was right. He did not live to see it, and it did not happen through him. It happened through the kind of people who carried him to the coast.

The Shadow of Empire

His death also did something he would not have wanted. In the 1880s the European powers divided Africa among themselves, in what came to be called the Scramble for Africa. Livingstone’s name was used, over and over again, to justify British claims. In the Shire Highlands, the Scottish missionaries and their supporters lobbied the British government to take the region under its protection, to keep it from the Portuguese and to stop the slave raids. In 1891 Britain declared a protectorate over the region, later called Nyasaland. The country north of the Zambezi, where Livingstone had walked and died, was taken over by Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company and became Northern Rhodesia. The phrase “Christianity, commerce and civilisation” became a slogan of empire.

Colonial rule brought some of the things Livingstone had hoped for: the end of the slave trade, roads, schools, hospitals. It also brought much that he had opposed all his life: the taking of African land by European settlers and companies, forced labour, heavy taxes, racial discrimination, and the denial of self-government. In 1915, in Nyasaland, a Baptist minister named John Chilembwe, who had grown up in the world the missions made and had been taught by missionaries, led an armed rising against the injustices of colonial rule and was killed. In the Congo basin, which Livingstone had thought was the Nile, Stanley’s work for King Leopold opened the way for one of the worst atrocities of the colonial era.

It would be unjust to blame Livingstone for all of this. He did not want Africa conquered, and his ideal of African communities trading freely with Britain while governing themselves was different from what happened. But it would be dishonest to pretend that his vision had nothing to do with it. He called for Britain to come to Africa. He believed that British influence was a Christian influence. He did not see how easily that belief could be used by people who cared nothing for Christ. Christians who admire him should learn from that blindness. The gospel can be carried on the back of power, but power does not stay its servant for long.

When Zambia and Malawi became independent in 1964, they did something that surprised many observers. They kept his name. The town of Livingstone, near the Victoria Falls, kept it, and his statue still stands there. Blantyre kept its name. Many African Christians, then and now, have honoured him as a man who hated the slave trade, treated Africans as equals, and died among them. Others have seen him as a forerunner of colonial rule and asked why his memory should be kept. Both views have their reasons, and Africans have every right to make up their own minds about him. It is not for a British biographer, or for any outsider, to tell them which to hold.

The One Convert

And what of his missionary work, judged by the standard he would have used? He baptised one convert whom we know of, and suspended him from communion within months. By any ordinary measure, his career as a missionary was a failure, and he knew it. In his own lifetime he was criticised for abandoning the missionary calling for exploration, and the criticism had force.

But Sechele did not fall away. He went on reading his Bible, holding worship, and teaching his people, and the Bakwena became a Christian people in large part because of him. That was Livingstone’s doing as well as Sechele’s. And the missions founded after Livingstone’s death in the lands he had explored brought the gospel to millions. Was that his work? Not directly. He did not found them, staff them or lead them. But they would not have existed without him. He was, in his own words at Cambridge, a man who began a work and left it for others to carry out.

The verse at the head of this chapter is Jesus’s saying about the grain of wheat: unless it falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Jesus spoke it of his own death, and he went on to apply it to all who follow him: “He that loveth his life loseth it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal” (John 12:25, ASV). Livingstone’s life did not bear much visible fruit while he lived. It bore fruit after he died, in the missions, in the closing of the slave market, in the churches of Malawi and Zambia and Tanzania, and in the lives of people like Chuma and Susi, who learned the faith in his company and kept it. His heart, literally, was buried in African earth. It is not too much to say that it bore fruit there.

The Man Himself

This book has tried to tell the truth about him, and the truth is mixed. He was brave, persevering, honest about money, generous to the poor, and devoted to the cause of African freedom. He kept his word to the men who carried him across Africa. He respected Africans more than most Europeans of his day, and he gave his life to a continent he loved. He prayed every day, read his Bible through again and again, and dedicated himself to Christ at sixty as he had at twenty.

He was also proud, stubborn and often unjust. He could not work with equals, and he blamed others for his own mistakes. He neglected his wife and children for his work, and they paid a terrible price. He told his own story in ways that flattered him, and he was sometimes careless with the truth about his failures. He believed too easily that his own plans and God’s were the same. And he set going a vision of Africa’s future that others turned to purposes he would have hated.

The Victorian legend made him a saint. Some modern accounts have made him a villain, or a fool. He was neither. He was a sinner who had been forgiven and who knew it, a servant of Christ who often mistook his own will for his Master’s, and a man who went on, through failure after failure, because he believed that he had been sent. “We are unprofitable servants,” Jesus taught his disciples to say; “we have done that which it was our duty to do” (Luke 17:10, ASV). Livingstone would not have quarrelled with that verdict. In the best known of his last prayers, he asked only to be accepted, and to finish his task. God accepts the unprofitable. The task was finished by others, as it always is.

In the 1880s the European powers divided Africa among themselves, in what came to be called the Scramble for Africa. Livingstone’s name was used, over and over again, to justify British claims. In the Shire Highlands, the Scottish missionaries and their supporters lobbied the British government to take the region under its protection, to keep it from the Portuguese and to stop the slave raids. In 1891 Britain declared a protectorate over the region, later called Nyasaland. The country north of the Zambezi, where Livingstone had walked and died, was taken over by Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company and became Northern Rhodesia. The phrase “Christianity, commerce and civilisation” became a slogan of empire. Colonial rule brought some of the things Livingstone had hoped for: the end of the slave trade, roads, schools, hospitals. It also brought much that he had opposed all his life: the taking of African land by European settlers and companies, forced labour, heavy taxes, racial discrimination, and the denial of self-government. In 1915, in Nyasaland, a Baptist minister named John Chilembwe, who had grown up in the world the missions made and had been taught by missionaries, led an armed rising against the injustices of colonial rule and was killed. In the Congo basin, which Livingstone had thought was the Nile, Stanley’s work for King Leopold opened the way for one of the worst atrocities of the colonial era. It would be unjust to blame Livingstone for all of this. He did not want Africa conquered, and his ideal of African communities trading freely with Britain while governing themselves was different from what happened. But it would be dishonest to pretend that his vision had nothing to do with it. He called for Britain to come to Africa. He believed that British influence was a Christian influence. He did not see how easily that belief could be used by people who cared nothing for Christ. Christians who admire him should learn from that blindness. The gospel can be carried on the back of power, but power does not stay its servant for long. When Zambia and Malawi became independent in 1964, they did something that surprised many observers. They kept his name. The town of Livingstone, near the Victoria Falls, kept it, and his statue still stands there. Blantyre kept its name. Many African Christians, then and now, have honoured him as a man who hated the slave trade, treated Africans as equals, and died among them. Others have seen him as a forerunner of colonial rule and asked why his memory should be kept. Both views have their reasons, and Africans have every right to make up their own minds about him. It is not for a British biographer, or for any outsider, to tell them which to hold. The One Convert And what of his missionary work, judged by the standard he would have used? He baptised one convert whom we know of, and suspended him from communion within months. By any ordinary measure, his career as a missionary was a failure, and he knew it. In his own lifetime he was criticised for abandoning the missionary calling for exploration, and the criticism had force. But Sechele did not fall away. He went on reading his Bible, holding worship, and teaching his people, and the Bakwena became a Christian people in large part because of him. That was Livingstone’s doing as well as Sechele’s. And the missions founded after Livingstone’s death in the lands he had explored brought the gospel to millions. Was that his work? Not directly. He did not found them, staff them or lead them. But they would not have existed without him. He was, in his own words at Cambridge, a man who began a work and left it for others to carry out. The verse at the head of this chapter is Jesus’s saying about the grain of wheat: unless it falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Jesus spoke it of his own death, and he went on to apply it to all who follow him: “He that loveth his life loseth it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal” (John 12:25, ASV). Livingstone’s life did not bear much visible fruit while he lived. It bore fruit after he died, in the missions, in the closing of the slave market, in the churches of Malawi and Zambia and Tanzania, and in the lives of people like Chuma and Susi, who learned the faith in his company and kept it. His heart, literally, was buried in African earth. It is not too much to say that it bore fruit there. The Man Himself This book has tried to tell the truth about him, and the truth is mixed. He was brave, persevering, honest about money, generous to the poor, and devoted to the cause of African freedom. He kept his word to the men who carried him across Africa. He respected Africans more than most Europeans of his day, and he gave his life to a continent he loved. He prayed every day, read his Bible through again and again, and dedicated himself to Christ at sixty as he had at twenty. He was also proud, stubborn and often unjust. He could not work with equals, and he blamed others for his own mistakes. He neglected his wife and children for his work, and they paid a terrible price. He told his own story in ways that flattered him, and he was sometimes careless with the truth about his failures. He believed too easily that his own plans and God’s were the same. And he set going a vision of Africa’s future that others turned to purposes he would have hated. The Victorian legend made him a saint. Some modern accounts have made him a villain, or a fool. He was neither. He was a sinner who had been forgiven and who knew it, a servant of Christ who often mistook his own will for his Master’s, and a man who went on, through failure after failure, because he believed that he had been sent. “We are unprofitable servants,” Jesus taught his disciples to say; “we have done that which it was our duty to do” (Luke 17:10, ASV). Livingstone would not have quarrelled with that verdict. In the best known of his last prayers, he asked only to be accepted, and to finish his task. God accepts the unprofitable. The task was finished by others, as it always is.

fields.title: Appendix a: Lessons from the Life of David Livingstone
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. Livingstone is a harder subject for this kind of list than most of the people in this series, because some of his lessons are warnings. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider the outcome of the lives of those who went before us and to imitate their faith, not every choice they made. Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on his example alone.

1. God Uses Working People

A boy who went into a cotton mill at ten, and studied Latin at night with the books snatched from his hands at midnight, became a doctor, a minister and one of the best-known Christians of his century. “God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27, ASV).

2. Hard Work Is a Form of Service

Livingstone believed that the mill had trained him for Africa. Work done with all our strength can be offered to God, even work we did not choose. “Whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, ASV).

3. Faith and the Study of Creation Belong Together

He came to faith when he saw that the God of the Bible and the God of the rocks and stars were the same. He worshipped as he measured. “The heavens declare the glory of God; And the firmament showeth his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1, ASV).

4. Weakness Does Not Disqualify

He forgot his sermon at Ongar and was nearly rejected by his Society. God did not make him eloquent; he gave him other gifts. “Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak” (Exodus 4:12, ASV).

5. Learn the People’s Language and Ways

He lived for six months among the Bakwena without hearing English, so as to learn Setswana and the life of the people. “I am become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, ASV).

6. Honour Those Who Save Your Life

Mebalwe ran at the lion with a gun that would not fire. Livingstone’s life, again and again, was saved by Africans whom his books barely named. “Salute Prisca and Aquila my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus, who for my life laid down their own necks” (Romans 16:3-4, ASV).

7. Hear the Hard Questions

Sechele asked why the gospel had come so late to his ancestors. Livingstone had no easy answer, and he wrote the question down. “Being ready always to give answer to every man that asketh you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, yet with meekness and fear” (1 Peter 3:15, ASV).

8. Faith Cannot Be Forced

He refused Sechele’s offer to beat the Bakwena into belief, and he was right. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith Jehovah of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6, ASV).

9. Count the Cost Others Will Pay

His family paid for his journeys with poverty, loneliness and separation. A calling that destroys those closest to us needs to be examined, not only admired. “But if any provideth not for his own, and specially his own household, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8, ASV).

10. Keep Your Word

He would not leave twenty-seven men on the coast at Luanda, though a ship was waiting to take him home. “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psalm 15:4, ASV).

11. Rest on the Promise of Christ

On the night of 14 January 1856 he found peace not in a change of circumstances but in a word, which he called the word of a gentleman of the strictest honour. “And lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world” (Matthew 28:20, ASV).

12. Service Is a Privilege

“I never made a sacrifice,” he told Cambridge. Those words are true of what Christ gives, though we must remember those who paid the price for us. “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed to us-ward” (Romans 8:18, ASV).

13. Beware of Borrowed Power

His call for “commerce and Christianity” was taken up by those who wanted Africa for themselves. The gospel must not be confused with the interests of any nation. “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24, ASV).

14. Hold Your Plans Loosely

He built a vision on a river he had not seen, and Kebrabasa blocked it. Plans are good; certainty about them is dangerous. “A man’s heart deviseth his way; But Jehovah directeth his steps” (Proverbs 16:9, ASV).

15. Learn to Share Command

He could lead Africans across a continent and could not lead six Europeans up a river. Humility in leadership is not weakness. “In lowliness of mind each counting other better than himself” (Philippians 2:3, ASV).

16. Admit When You Are Wrong

Livingstone found it very hard to say that he had been mistaken about Kebrabasa, about Baines, about the Helmores, about Kirk. Confession is a door to freedom. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9, ASV).

17. Speak for the Captive

He wrote down what he saw on the slave roads, plainly and without exaggeration, and his writing helped close the Zanzibar market. “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV).

18. Grief Is Not Unbelief

At Shupanga he wept for Mary and felt, for the first time, willing to die. God is near in such grief. “Jehovah is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart” (Psalm 34:18, ASV).

19. Be Present to Your Children

Robert died in a prison camp in America under a false name, having hardly known his father. Children need more than letters. “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but nurture them in the chastening and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4, ASV).

20. Lament Is a Form of Prayer

At Nyangwe he could only cry out for God’s kingdom to come. The Bible gives us words for such moments. “O Jehovah, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear?” (Habakkuk 1:2, ASV).

21. Tell the Whole Truth

His field diary shows that he told the story of Nyangwe in a way that put more distance between himself and the traders than there had been. Christians, of all people, can afford to tell the whole truth. “Putting away falsehood, speak ye truth each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25, ASV).

22. God Remembers the Unnamed

Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright, Majwara, Halima and the others carried him a thousand miles, and most of them were sent home before the funeral. “For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and the love which ye showed toward his name” (Hebrews 6:10, ASV).

23. Fruit May Come After We Are Gone

One known convert in his lifetime; churches of millions after his death. “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit” (John 12:24, ASV).

24. We Are Unprofitable Servants

At sixty, in the swamps, he gave himself to Christ again and asked only to finish his task. The task was finished by others. “We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which it was our duty to do” (Luke 17:10, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make David Livingstone an object of admiration, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Many chapters raise hard questions about family, leadership, power and mission. They are meant to be discussed honestly, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Saint, the Explorer, and the Record

Central idea

The real Livingstone, as his own writings and the record show him, is more complicated and more instructive than the Victorian legend.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:7; John 8:32.

Reflection

1. Why do Christians need their heroes to be flawless? 2. What do we lose when we polish a life?

Chapter 1 - Shuttle Row

Central idea

A one-room home in a mill village gave him a Highland pride in honesty, a father’s stern faith and a mother’s cheerful thrift.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 16:5-6; Proverbs 22:6.

Reflection

1. What did you inherit from your family that helps you serve God? 2. What did you inherit that you have had to unlearn?

Chapter 2 - The Piecer

Central idea

Ten years in the mill formed endurance and a working man’s sympathy, and also a habit of judging others by work done.

Scriptures to revisit

Ecclesiastes 9:10; Colossians 3:23.

Reflection

1. How do you regard work you did not choose? 2. Where might your strengths make you hard on others?

Chapter 3 - Colour Blindness Cured

Central idea

His faith became his own when he saw that the God of Scripture and the God of creation are one.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 19; Romans 1:20.

Reflection

1. Have you ever felt that faith and learning were at war? 2. What would it mean for you to see the world “in colour”?

Chapter 4 - Slow of Speech

Central idea

A poor preacher, nearly rejected by his Society, was sent anyway, and given other gifts.

Scriptures to revisit

Exodus 4:10-13; Psalm 121.

Reflection

1. What weakness do you think disqualifies you? 2. How has God used you in spite of it?

Chapter 5 - Another Man’s Foundation

Central idea

He longed to go where Christ was not named, and saw early that Africa would be evangelised by Africans.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 15:20-24; 2 Timothy 2:2.

Reflection

1. Is pioneering always better than building on others’ work? 2. Whom are you training to carry the gospel further than you can?

Chapter 6 - The Lion at Mabotsa

Central idea

He was saved from the lion by Mebalwe’s courage, and drew from the attack a lesson about God’s mercy.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:17; Psalm 23:4.

Reflection

1. Whose courage has protected you without much credit? 2. What do you make of his idea of a merciful provision?

Chapter 7 - Sechele

Central idea

A chief who read Isaiah asked hard questions, paid a great price for baptism, fell, and became the evangelist of his people.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 8:26-39; 1 Peter 3:15.

Reflection

1. How would you answer Sechele’s question about his ancestors? 2. What did you make of the demand that he send away his wives?

Chapter 8 - Across the Thirstland

Central idea

Lake Ngami and the Zambezi opened a vision of the interior, at a heavy cost to his wife and children.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 35; 1 Timothy 5:8.

Reflection

1. When does a calling justify risk to others? 2. What did you hear in Mary’s silence?

Chapter 9 - Kolobeng Plundered

Central idea

The Boer raid ended his station, while Mary and the children wandered through English lodgings.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 46; Luke 18:29-30.

Reflection

1. Who in your church is carrying a hidden cost for someone else’s ministry? 2. Can a resolution to place no value on anything go wrong?

Chapter 10 - Twenty-Seven Men

Central idea

At Luanda he refused a passage home rather than break his promise to the men who had brought him to the sea.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 15; Matthew 5:37.

Reflection

1. What promise is it costing you to keep? 2. Why do you think he kept faith with these men more easily than with his family?

Chapter 11 - The Word of a Gentleman

Central idea

On the night of 14 January 1856 he found peace in the promise of Christ, not in any change of circumstances.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 28:18-20; Psalm 56:3-4.

Reflection

1. Which promise of Christ do you most need to take as the word of a gentleman? 2. What did you notice about the renaming of Mosi-oa-Tunya?

Chapter 12 - “I Never Made a Sacrifice”

Central idea

Fame, the Cambridge appeal, and the vision of commerce and Christianity together.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 8:18; Matthew 6:24.

Reflection

1. Is it true that serving Christ is never a sacrifice? 2. Where might the gospel in your culture be confused with commerce or national interest?

Chapter 13 - Kebrabasa

Central idea

A plan built on an unseen river collapsed, and he could not admit it, nor lead his colleagues well.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 16:9; Philippians 2:3-4.

Reflection

1. When has perseverance turned into stubbornness in your life? 2. How do you respond when someone under you disagrees?

Chapter 14 - Graves at Linyanti

Central idea

The Helmore and Price families died at Linyanti, and he defended himself rather than grieving his share.

Scriptures to revisit

James 4:13-15; Hebrews 6:10.

Reflection

1. How should Christians speak of missionary deaths? 2. Whose names are missing from the stories your church tells?

Chapter 15 - Magomero

Central idea

Captives were freed at Mbame’s village, and the mission was drawn into fighting and lost its bishop.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 61:1-4; Luke 4:16-21.

Reflection

1. Is it ever right for Christians to use force to free the oppressed? 2. What did the freeing of Chuma mean in the long run?

Chapter 16 - Shupanga

Central idea

Mary died beside him at Shupanga, and he saw, too late, what their marriage had cost her.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 34:18; 2 Corinthians 6:10.

Reflection

1. What does contrition look like after a loss we helped to cause? 2. How would you tell Mary Livingstone’s story?

Chapter 17 - Recalled

Central idea

The Shire valley was devastated, the expedition recalled, and his son Robert lost.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:8-9; Ephesians 6:4.

Reflection

1. How do you keep faith when your work appears to have done harm? 2. What would Robert have needed from his father?

Chapter 18 - The Sentence of Death

Central idea

Without medicines, he went on, and became dependent on the slave traders he had come to expose.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 11:8-10; 2 Corinthians 1:8-9.

Reflection

1. Have you ever had to depend on people whose ways you oppose? 2. What does it mean to go out “not knowing whither”?

Chapter 19 - Nyangwe

Central idea

He witnessed a massacre, wrote it down, prayed, and helped move a nation; his first notes show a more tangled story.

Scriptures to revisit

Habakkuk 1:2-4; 2:4, 14; Ephesians 4:25.

Reflection

1. What is the place of lament in your prayers? 2. Why do we tell stories that put distance between ourselves and evil?

Chapter 20 - “I Presume”

Central idea

Stanley’s arrival brought him new life, and Livingstone refused to go home; he dedicated himself again on his birthday.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 25:25; Romans 12:1.

Reflection

1. Who has brought you “good news from a far country”? 2. What would it mean for you to dedicate your “whole self” again today?

Chapter 21 - Chitambo’s Village

Central idea

He died in a grass hut, probably kneeling, among people who had stayed with him for years.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 116:15; 2 Timothy 4:6-8.

Reflection

1. How do you hold a cherished story that cannot be proved? 2. Who will be with you at the end?

Chapter 22 - Faithful Hands

Central idea

Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright and their companions chose to carry his body a thousand miles to the coast.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 8:2; Ruth 1:16-17.

Reflection

1. What did their choice reveal about them, and about him? 2. How can churches honour the unnamed who carry the work?

Chapter 23 - A Grain of Wheat

Central idea

His life bore fruit after his death, in the closing of the slave market and the churches of Central Africa, and in the shadow of empire.

Scriptures to revisit

John 12:24-26; Luke 17:10.

Reflection

1. What in his life would you imitate, and what would you avoid? 2. What might God do with your life after you are gone?

Chapter 2 - The Piecer Central idea Ten years in the mill formed endurance and a working man’s sympathy, and also a habit of judging others by work done. Scriptures to revisit Ecclesiastes 9:10; Colossians 3:23. Reflection 1. How do you regard work you did not choose? 2. Where might your strengths make you hard on others? Chapter 3 - Colour Blindness Cured Central idea His faith became his own when he saw that the God of Scripture and the God of creation are one. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 19; Romans 1:20. Reflection 1. Have you ever felt that faith and learning were at war? 2. What would it mean for you to see the world “in colour”? Chapter 4 - Slow of Speech Central idea A poor preacher, nearly rejected by his Society, was sent anyway, and given other gifts. Scriptures to revisit Exodus 4:10-13; Psalm 121. Reflection 1. What weakness do you think disqualifies you? 2. How has God used you in spite of it? Chapter 5 - Another Man’s Foundation Central idea He longed to go where Christ was not named, and saw early that Africa would be evangelised by Africans. Scriptures to revisit Romans 15:20-24; 2 Timothy 2:2. Reflection 1. Is pioneering always better than building on others’ work? 2. Whom are you training to carry the gospel further than you can? Chapter 6 - The Lion at Mabotsa Central idea He was saved from the lion by Mebalwe’s courage, and drew from the attack a lesson about God’s mercy. Scriptures to revisit 2 Timothy 4:17; Psalm 23:4. Reflection 1. Whose courage has protected you without much credit? 2. What do you make of his idea of a merciful provision? Chapter 7 - Sechele Central idea A chief who read Isaiah asked hard questions, paid a great price for baptism, fell, and became the evangelist of his people. Scriptures to revisit Acts 8:26-39; 1 Peter 3:15. Reflection 1. How would you answer Sechele’s question about his ancestors? 2. What did you make of the demand that he send away his wives? Chapter 8 - Across the Thirstland Central idea Lake Ngami and the Zambezi opened a vision of the interior, at a heavy cost to his wife and children. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 35; 1 Timothy 5:8. Reflection 1. When does a calling justify risk to others? 2. What did you hear in Mary’s silence? Chapter 9 - Kolobeng Plundered Central idea The Boer raid ended his station, while Mary and the children wandered through English lodgings. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 46; Luke 18:29-30. Reflection 1. Who in your church is carrying a hidden cost for someone else’s ministry? 2. Can a resolution to place no value on anything go wrong? Chapter 10 - Twenty-Seven Men Central idea At Luanda he refused a passage home rather than break his promise to the men who had brought him to the sea. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 15; Matthew 5:37. Reflection 1. What promise is it costing you to keep? 2. Why do you think he kept faith with these men more easily than with his family? Chapter 11 - The Word of a Gentleman Central idea On the night of 14 January 1856 he found peace in the promise of Christ, not in any change of circumstances. Scriptures to revisit Matthew 28:18-20; Psalm 56:3-4. Reflection 1. Which promise of Christ do you most need to take as the word of a gentleman? 2. What did you notice about the renaming of Mosi-oa-Tunya? Chapter 12 - “I Never Made a Sacrifice” Central idea Fame, the Cambridge appeal, and the vision of commerce and Christianity together. Scriptures to revisit Romans 8:18; Matthew 6:24. Reflection 1. Is it true that serving Christ is never a sacrifice? 2. Where might the gospel in your culture be confused with commerce or national interest? Chapter 13 - Kebrabasa Central idea A plan built on an unseen river collapsed, and he could not admit it, nor lead his colleagues well. Scriptures to revisit Proverbs 16:9; Philippians 2:3-4. Reflection 1. When has perseverance turned into stubbornness in your life? 2. How do you respond when someone under you disagrees? Chapter 14 - Graves at Linyanti Central idea The Helmore and Price families died at Linyanti, and he defended himself rather than grieving his share. Scriptures to revisit James 4:13-15; Hebrews 6:10. Reflection 1. How should Christians speak of missionary deaths? 2. Whose names are missing from the stories your church tells? Chapter 15 - Magomero Central idea Captives were freed at Mbame’s village, and the mission was drawn into fighting and lost its bishop. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 61:1-4; Luke 4:16-21. Reflection 1. Is it ever right for Christians to use force to free the oppressed? 2. What did the freeing of Chuma mean in the long run? Chapter 16 - Shupanga Central idea Mary died beside him at Shupanga, and he saw, too late, what their marriage had cost her. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 34:18; 2 Corinthians 6:10. Reflection 1. What does contrition look like after a loss we helped to cause? 2. How would you tell Mary Livingstone’s story? Chapter 17 - Recalled Central idea The Shire valley was devastated, the expedition recalled, and his son Robert lost. Scriptures to revisit 2 Corinthians 4:8-9; Ephesians 6:4. Reflection 1. How do you keep faith when your work appears to have done harm? 2. What would Robert have needed from his father? Chapter 18 - The Sentence of Death Central idea Without medicines, he went on, and became dependent on the slave traders he had come to expose. Scriptures to revisit Hebrews 11:8-10; 2 Corinthians 1:8-9. Reflection 1. Have you ever had to depend on people whose ways you oppose? 2. What does it mean to go out “not knowing whither”? Chapter 19 - Nyangwe Central idea He witnessed a massacre, wrote it down, prayed, and helped move a nation; his first notes show a more tangled story. Scriptures to revisit Habakkuk 1:2-4; 2:4, 14; Ephesians 4:25. Reflection 1. What is the place of lament in your prayers? 2. Why do we tell stories that put distance between ourselves and evil? Chapter 20 - “I Presume” Central idea Stanley’s arrival brought him new life, and Livingstone refused to go home; he dedicated himself again on his birthday. Scriptures to revisit Proverbs 25:25; Romans 12:1. Reflection 1. Who has brought you “good news from a far country”? 2. What would it mean for you to dedicate your “whole self” again today? Chapter 21 - Chitambo’s Village Central idea He died in a grass hut, probably kneeling, among people who had stayed with him for years. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 116:15; 2 Timothy 4:6-8. Reflection 1. How do you hold a cherished story that cannot be proved? 2. Who will be with you at the end? Chapter 22 - Faithful Hands Central idea Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright and their companions chose to carry his body a thousand miles to the coast. Scriptures to revisit Acts 8:2; Ruth 1:16-17. Reflection 1. What did their choice reveal about them, and about him? 2. How can churches honour the unnamed who carry the work? Chapter 23 - A Grain of Wheat Central idea His life bore fruit after his death, in the closing of the slave market and the churches of Central Africa, and in the shadow of empire. Scriptures to revisit John 12:24-26; Luke 17:10. Reflection 1. What in his life would you imitate, and what would you avoid? 2. What might God do with your life after you are gone?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of David Livingstone
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted. Livingstone’s own dating became unreliable in his last years, and several dates from that period are uncertain.

1813 - Birth

David Livingstone is born on 19 March at Blantyre Works, Lanarkshire, the second of seven children of Neil Livingstone, tea dealer, and Agnes Hunter.

1823 - The Mill

At ten he goes to work as a piecer in the Blantyre cotton mill, and attends the evening school.

c. 1832 - Spinner and Convert

Promoted to spinner. About this time he comes to a personal faith, helped by Thomas Dick’s Philosophy of a Future State.

c. 1834 - China

Karl Gützlaff’s appeal for medical missionaries to China moves him to train as a doctor.

1836-1838 - Glasgow

Studies medicine and chemistry at the Andersonian University, Greek at Glasgow University, and theology under Ralph Wardlaw, working in the mill in summer.

1838-1839 - Ongar

Accepted on probation by the London Missionary Society; studies under Richard Cecil at Chipping Ongar; probation extended; accepted in 1839.

1839-1840 - London

The Opium War closes China. Meets Robert Moffat and turns to southern Africa.

1840 - Ordination and Departure

Qualifies as a Licentiate of the Faculty of Physicians and Surgeons of Glasgow in November; ordained on 20 November at Albion Chapel, London; sails on the George on 8 December.

1841 - Kuruman

Lands at Simon’s Bay in March; reaches Kuruman on 31 July. First journey north with Rogers Edwards.

1842-1843 - The North

Travels among the Bakwena and Bamangwato; lives for about six months among the Bakwena to learn Setswana. Meets Sechele. Founds Mabotsa with Edwards in 1843.

1844 - The Lion

Mauled by a lion at Mabotsa in February; saved by the intervention of Mebalwe. Engaged to Mary Moffat.

1845 - Marriage

Marries Mary Moffat at Kuruman on 9 January. Quarrel with Edwards; moves to Chonuane, Sechele’s town.

1846-1851 - Children

Robert born 1846 (Mabotsa), Agnes 1847 (Chonuane), Thomas 1849 (Kolobeng), Elizabeth 1850 (died at about six weeks), William Oswell 1851 (on the Zouga River).

1847 - Kolobeng

The Bakwena move to Kolobeng. Years of drought begin.

1848 - Sechele’s Baptism

Sechele is baptised on 1 October after sending away all but one of his wives. Early in 1849 he is suspended from communion. He is the only African Livingstone is known to have baptised.

1849 - Lake Ngami

With W. C. Oswell and Mungo Murray, guided by Sechele’s man Ramotobi, reaches Lake Ngami on 1 August.

1850-1851 - With the Family

Second journey to Ngami with Mary and the children (1850). In 1851 reaches the Makololo; Sebetwane dies on 7 July; reaches the upper Zambezi at Sesheke on 4 August. Sees the slave trade for the first time.

1852 - Separation and Dimawe

Mary and the children sail for Britain from the Cape in April. In late August a Boer commando attacks the Bakwena at Dimawe, and Livingstone’s house at Kolobeng is plundered.

1853 - Linyanti

Sechele travels to Cape Town to appeal for help. Livingstone reaches Linyanti in May; leaves for the west coast with twenty-seven men on 11 November.

1854 - Luanda

Reaches Luanda on 31 May. Declines a passage home; HMS Forerunner, carrying his papers, sinks off Madeira. Leaves Luanda on 20 September.

1855 - Victoria Falls

Back at Linyanti in September. Leaves for the east in November; sees Mosi-oa-Tunya, which he names the Victoria Falls, in mid-November.

1856 - Across Africa

The night of 14 January at the Luangwa confluence. Father dies in February. Reaches Tete on 2 March and Quelimane on 20 May. Sekwebu drowns at Mauritius. Reaches England on 9 December.

1857 - Fame

Resigns from the London Missionary Society. Missionary Travels published in November. Speaks in the Senate House, Cambridge, on 4 December.

1858 - The Zambezi Expedition

Sails from Liverpool on 10 March as consul and leader of a government expedition. Mary stays at the Cape and Kuruman; Anna Mary is born at Kuruman on 16 November. Kebrabasa rapids found impassable in November.

1859 - Shire and Nyasa

Explores the Shire River; Lake Shirwa (April); Lake Nyasa (September). Thornton and Baines dismissed.

1860 - Linyanti Again

Helmore and Price families stricken at Linyanti (February to April). Livingstone takes the Makololo home, reaching Sesheke in August.

1861 - The Universities’ Mission

Bishop Mackenzie and the mission arrive. The Rovuma is tried and found too shallow. Captives freed at Mbame’s village in July, Chuma among them by the usual account; mission settles at Magomero.

1862 - Shupanga

Mackenzie dies on 31 January. Mary arrives at the end of January and dies at Shupanga on 27 April. The Lady Nyassa is launched.

1862-1863 - Famine and Recall

Drought and slave raids devastate the Shire valley. Kirk and Charles Livingstone go home in May 1863; the recall reaches Livingstone in July.

1864 - Bombay and Home

Sails the Lady Nyassa from Zanzibar to Bombay (April to June). Reaches London in July. His son Robert, serving in the Union army as Rupert Vincent, dies at Salisbury prison, North Carolina, in December.

1865 - Last Departure

Writes the Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi at Newstead Abbey. His mother dies in June. Leaves Britain for the last time in August.

1866 - The Last Journey Begins

Reaches Zanzibar in January; lands near the Rovuma in March. Wikatani stays with his people near Lake Nyasa (August). Musa and the Johanna men desert and report his death.

1867 - Without Medicines

Medicine chest stolen on 20 January. Reaches Lake Tanganyika (April) and Lake Mweru (November). E. D. Young’s search party disproves Musa’s story.

1868 - Bangweulu

Reaches Lake Bangweulu in July.

1869 - Ujiji and Manyema

Reaches Ujiji, gravely ill, on 14 March; finds his stores plundered. Goes west into Manyema.

1870 - Bambarre

Laid up for months with ulcerated feet; reads the Bible through four times while in Manyema.

1871 - Nyangwe and Stanley

Reaches Nyangwe on the Lualaba in March. Witnesses the massacre on 15 July. Returns to Ujiji in late October. Meets H. M. Stanley at Ujiji (10 November by Stanley’s book; 3 November in other Stanley texts; Livingstone’s own dating points to late October).

1872 - Unyanyembe

With Stanley explores the north of Lake Tanganyika (late 1871) and travels to Unyanyembe (February). Stanley leaves on 14 March. Birthday dedication on 19 March. Porters arrive in August, with Jacob Wainwright and others from Nasik. Leaves Unyanyembe on 25 August.

1873 - Death

Wades the Bangweulu swamps (January to April). Last journal entry on 27 April. Dies at Chitambo’s village, Ilala, probably on 1 May (his companions carved 4 May on the tree). His heart is buried under a mpundu tree. The Zanzibar slave market is closed by treaty on 5 June. His companions meet Cameron near Unyanyembe in October.

1874 - Westminster Abbey

The body reaches Bagamoyo in February. Buried in Westminster Abbey on 18 April; Jacob Wainwright among the pallbearers. Susi and Chuma come to England and help Horace Waller. The Last Journals published.

1875-1876 - The Missions

Livingstonia (Free Church of Scotland) founded on Lake Nyasa (1875); Blantyre Mission (Church of Scotland) founded in the Shire Highlands (1876).

1880 - Blaikie

W. G. Blaikie publishes The Personal Life of David Livingstone.

1882-1892 - The Companions

Chuma dies at Zanzibar (1882). Susi is baptised David (1886) and dies (1891). Sechele dies (1892). Jacob Wainwright dies (1892).

1891 - Protectorate

Britain declares a protectorate over the Shire Highlands and Lake Nyasa region, later Nyasaland.

1964 - Independence

Malawi and Zambia become independent. Both keep many of the places named in his memory.
